Introduction to Metaheuristics Methods

2.1 Introduction

This chapter delves into the fundamental concepts of optimization, with a special focus on the methodologies underlying metaheuristic optimization techniques. It offers a comparative analysis between traditional optimization methods and metaheuristic approaches, highlighting their differences and respective advantages. Additionally, the chapter provides an in-depth discussion on the taxonomy of metaheuristic methods, categorizing and defining various strategies under this broad umbrella. An important part of this chapter is the examination of several key mechanisms intrinsic to the methodology of metaheuristic techniques, enhancing the reader’s understanding of how these methods function in practice. As illustrative examples, the chapter specifically analyzes two simple metaheuristic strategies: random search and simulated annealing, demonstrating their application and effectiveness. To aid in comprehension, the chapter is enriched with several MATLAB implementations. These practical code examples not only facilitate a deeper grasp of the discussed concepts but also serve as a valuable resource for readers to apply these techniques in their own optimization problems, bridging the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical application.

Optimization has increasingly become a pivotal aspect of various disciplines, driven by the universal aim to enhance quality while maintaining competitiveness in pricing. This surge in its relevance is anchored in the quest to create superior products or services without escalating costs. Fundamentally, optimization is about identifying the most effective solution from an extensive array of potential options (Baldick 2006). It involves a meticulous process of analyzing, comparing, and selecting the optimum choice that aligns with specific objectives, whether in engineering, business, healthcare, or other fields. This approach not only ensures efficiency and effectiveness but also fosters innovation and progress across sectors.

An optimization problem is typically structured as a process where the primary goal is to determine the optimal value, denoted as x*, which either minimizes or maximizes a given objective function, f(x). This function represents a specific criterion that needs to be optimized, such as cost, efficiency, or performance. The process involves carefully adjusting the variables within the function, in this case x, to find the value x* that leads to the best possible outcome for f(x). This optimal value is contingent upon satisfying a set of constraints or conditions that define the feasible region for the problem. These constraints might include resource limitations, physical laws, or specific requirements that the solution must adhere to. Thus, solving an optimization problem involves not only maximizing or minimizing the objective function but also ensuring that the solution complies with all necessary constraints. This can be formulated as follows:

(2.1)

In the area of optimization, x is commonly used to denote the vector of decision variables, where each element in this vector represents a specific variable that can be adjusted or controlled within the problem. The number of these variables is represented by d, indicating the dimensionality of the problem. The set of all possible combinations of these decision variables is referred to as X, known as the candidate solutions set, search space, or solution space. This space encompasses all the potential solutions that can be considered for finding the optimal result. Often, the range of each decision variable in x is restricted by lower (li) and upper (ui) bounds, which define the feasible region of the solution space. This can be mathematically expressed as X = {x ∈ ℝd|li ≤ xi ≤ ui, i = 1, …, d}, where each xi within the vector x must lie between its respective lower and upper bounds for all d dimensions. These boundaries ensure that the search for the optimal solution is conducted within a realistic and practical framework.

In optimization, the objective function f(x) can either be subjected to minimization or maximization, depending on the specific goals of the problem. Whether the aim is to reduce costs, minimize error, maximize efficiency, or achieve the highest possible performance, the nature of the objective dictates the approach. Interestingly, these two types of optimization problems – minimization and maximization – are interconvertible through a simple mathematical relation. By negating the objective function, a minimization problem can be transformed into a maximization one, and vice versa. This is expressed as: if the goal is to maximize f(x), it is equivalent to minimizing −f(x), and if the task is to minimize f(x), this can be approached as maximizing −f(x). This relationship allows for flexibility in the formulation and solution of optimization problems, enabling problem-solvers to adapt the approach that best suits their computational tools or theoretical preferences. This convertibility is a fundamental aspect of optimization theory, broadening the applicability and versatility of optimization techniques across different scenarios. This concept can be formulated as follows (Pedregal 2004):

(2.2)

To illustrate the above concepts, the following minimization problem is presented as an example:

(2.3)

In the presented formulation, we encounter an optimization problem centered around the minimization of a function that hinges on a single decision variable, denoted as d = 1. This simplifies the scenario to a one-dimensional optimization task. The search space X, in this case, is defined by a specific interval, extending from −4 to 1. This range delineates the boundaries within which the solution must be found. The core objective of the problem is to pinpoint the specific value of x within this interval for which the function f(x) attains its minimum value. This value of x is the crux of the optimization process, and it is referred to as the optimal value, symbolized as x*. To aid in understanding and visualizing this optimization task, a graphical representation of the function f(x) is provided, typically in the form of a curve plotted within the defined interval of [−4, 1]. This visual depiction, often labeled as Figure 2.1 in texts, serves to illustrate how the function behaves across the search space and where its minimum value lies, thereby highlighting the optimal solution x*.

From Figure 2.1, which graphically illustrates the function f(x) in the optimization problem, we can observe two distinct points, labeled as solutions A and B. These points represent two different minima of the function f(x). The presence of multiple prominent minima is a characteristic feature of what are known as multimodal functions. In multimodal functions, there are several points where the function reaches a minimum value, but these minima are of different natures. The minimum at point A is of particular significance as it represents the global optimal solution x* for the problem, meaning it is the lowest point across the entire search space. On the other hand, point B signifies a local minimum. A local minimum, like B, is a point where the function reaches a minimum value in a nearby region but is not the absolute lowest when considering the entire search space. This distinction is crucial in optimization as the ultimate goal is often to find the global minimum (point A), which represents the best overall solution, rather than a local minimum (point B), which is only optimal in a limited context.

2.2 Classic Optimization Methods

Typically, the function f(x) in optimization problems may exhibit a non-linear relationship with the decision variables x, adding a layer of complexity to the problem-solving process. To navigate this intricacy, optimization methodologies often employ iterative processes that meticulously explore the search space to identify efficient solutions. There are two primary families of algorithms used for tackling such complex, non-linear optimization problems: classical techniques and metaheuristic schemes. Classical methods are grounded in mathematical rigor and often utilize the gradient of the function f(x) to generate new candidate solutions. These techniques rely on differential calculus and are adept at navigating smoothly varying landscapes of the objective function. However, their effectiveness can be limited in scenarios where the function is not differentiable or is highly irregular. On the other hand, metaheuristic methods offer a more flexible approach. These methods do not require derivative information of the function for searching the optimal decision vector. Instead, they implement a set of heuristic rules to guide the search process. The beauty of metaheuristics lies in their inspiration from natural or societal phenomena. These algorithms mimic processes observed in nature, like evolution, or behaviors seen in social dynamics, enabling them to efficiently navigate complex, multimodal search spaces. This adaptability makes metaheuristics particularly useful in scenarios where classical methods falter, such as in problems with discontinuous or highly irregular objective functions.

Classical optimization algorithms, known for their specific performance characteristics, necessitate that the objective function f(x) adheres to two fundamental requirements to be applicable. First, the function must be twice differentiable. This means that not only should the first derivative of f(x) exist, but also its second derivative should be computable. The availability of these derivatives is crucial because classical algorithms often rely on gradient (first derivative) and curvature (second derivative) information to guide the search towards the optimal solution. The second requirement is that the function should be unimodal. In a unimodal function, there is only one local minimum or maximum, which is also the global minimum or maximum. This characteristic is important because classical algorithms are designed to converge to a single optimal point; in the presence of multiple local minima or maxima (as in multimodal functions), these algorithms may not reliably find the global optimum. Instead, they might converge to a local optimum that is not the best possible solution over the entire search space. Therefore, for classical optimization algorithms to perform effectively and as intended, both the twice differentiability and unimodality of the objective function f(x) are imperative.

This section offers a foundational overview of gradient-based optimization techniques, a cornerstone of classical optimization methods. While the focus of the book is primarily on the in-depth exploration of metaheuristic methods, the inclusion of classical optimization is intended to provide a basic understanding of these traditional techniques. Gradient-based optimization is pivotal in understanding the broader landscape of optimization methods, as it relies on the use of derivatives to guide the search for optimal solutions. However, given that this book primarily delves into metaheuristics, the coverage of classical optimization is relatively brief and not exhaustive. For readers seeking a more comprehensive and detailed study of gradient-based and other classical optimization techniques, it is recommended to consult additional specialized texts. These texts can offer deeper insights into the mathematical foundations, algorithmic structures, and application contexts of classical optimization methods, thereby complementing the knowledge gained from this book’s focus on metaheuristic approaches.

2.3 Descending Gradient Method

The gradient descent method (Dennis 1978), often referred to simply as the gradient method, stands as one of the earliest techniques employed for minimizing multidimensional objective functions. This method serves as the foundational pillar upon which several other more advanced optimization algorithms are built. The gradient descent method operates on a straightforward principle: it iteratively moves towards the minimum of the function by navigating in the direction of the steepest descent, as indicated by the negative of the function’s gradient. Despite a notable drawback of slow convergence, especially in scenarios involving complex or high-dimensional functions, the gradient descent method remains the most frequently utilized approach for optimizing nonlinear functions. This enduring popularity is largely attributable to its simplicity and the relative ease with which it can be programmed. Its conceptual clarity and straightforward implementation make it an accessible and reliable choice for a wide range of optimization problems, particularly for those new to the field or in situations where more sophisticated methods are not necessary. The gradient descent method’s enduring relevance in optimization underscores its importance in both theoretical and applied aspects of the field.

In the gradient descent method, the process begins with an initial point, denoted as x0, which serves as the starting position in the search for the optimal solution. From this point, the decision vector is iteratively updated through a series of steps, with the aim of progressively moving closer to the optimal solution, symbolized as x*. The number of iterations, referred to as Niter, is a crucial aspect of this process, as it determines how many times the decision vector is adjusted in pursuit of the optimal point. The iterative modification of the decision vector in the gradient descent method is governed by a specific mathematical expression. This expression encapsulates the essence of the method: at each step, the decision vector is updated by moving in the opposite direction of the gradient of the function at the current point. Mathematically, this update rule can be formulated as follows (Hocking 1991):

(2.4)

where k represents the current iteration and represents the step size of the search.

In Eq. 2.4 the term g(f(x)) represents the gradient of the function f(x). The gradient g of a function f(x) at point x expresses the direction in which the function f(x) shows its maximum growth. Thus, in the case of a minimization problem, the direction of descent can be obtained in the opposite direction of g (multiplying by −1). Under this rule, it is guaranteed that f(xk + 1) < f(xk), which implies that the new solution generated is better than the previous one.

In theoretical and didactic settings, the formulation of an optimization problem typically includes a well-defined objective function f(x). This clear definition serves as a crucial component for demonstrating and teaching the principles of optimization. However, in practical applications, the exact formulation of f(x) is often not deterministically known or explicitly defined. Instead, the values of the function are typically known only at specific points that are relevant or required by the optimization algorithm during its execution. This scenario is particularly common in real-world problems where the function might be based on empirical data, simulations, or complex systems where an analytical expression of f(x) is not feasible.

Under these practical circumstances, where the function f(x) and its gradient g are not analytically defined, numerical methods come into play for calculating the gradient. These methods estimate the gradient based on the function values at strategically chosen points. Techniques such as finite difference approximations are commonly used, where small perturbations are applied to the decision variables to estimate the rate of change of the function. This approach allows for the gradient estimation in situations where direct analytical computation is not possible. Although numerical methods for gradient calculation might introduce some approximation errors and require additional function evaluations, they are invaluable tools for tackling a wide range of optimization problems encountered in diverse practical scenarios. The ability to estimate gradients numerically broadens the applicability of optimization algorithms, making them versatile and effective even when dealing with complex, non-deterministic objective functions.

The gradient of a multidimensional function f(x) (x = (x1, …, xd) ∈ ℝd) represents the way in which the function varies with respect to one of its d dimensions. Thus, the gradient expresses the way in which f(x) varies with respect to x1. Such a gradient is properly defined as:

The minimization process of a function f(x1, x2) using the gradient descent method is succinctly encapsulated in pseudocode format, labeled as Algorithm 2.1. This algorithmic representation outlines the step-by-step procedure for applying gradient descent to a function with two decision variables. The procedure initiates by randomly selecting a decision vector xk (where k = 0) within the defined search space. This search space for both variables x1 and x2 is delineated by the interval [−1, 1]. Once the initial decision vector xk is established, the next step involves calculating the gradients and at the current point xk. These gradients represent the direction and rate of the steepest increase of the function at xk for each variable separately. With the gradient information at hand, the algorithm proceeds to generate a new solution. This is achieved by applying the update equation, referred to as Eq. 2.4 in the pseudocode. Since the function f(x1, x2) comprises two decision variables, the solution update process outlined in Eq. 2.4 considers each variable independently. This decoupled approach allows for the adjustment of each variable in the decision vector based on its respective gradient. The update, thus, is executed for each variable x1 and x2 separately, according to the calculated gradients and the specified update rule. This decoupled update mechanism ensures that both variables are optimally adjusted, leading to an effective search for the minimum of the function f(x1, x2) in the multidimensional decision space. Under such conditions, the update rules are defined as follows:

To assist readers in practically implementing Algorithm 2.1, Code 2.1 provides a specific MATLAB script tailored for this purpose. This script is not just a direct translation of the pseudocode into MATLAB syntax; it also includes additional features that enhance understanding and visualization of the algorithm’s operation. The first step in the MATLAB code involves plotting the function f(x1, x2). This visualization is crucial as it allows readers to grasp the characteristics of the function they are attempting to minimize, such as its shape, gradients, and potential minima. Understanding these aspects is vital for comprehending how the gradient descent method navigates the search space. Following the visualization step, the code executes an iterative process. This process involves updating the candidate solutions starting from the initial value x0 and progressively moving towards the optimal value x*. During each iteration, the trajectory of these candidate solutions is calculated and displayed. This dynamic representation shows how the algorithm explores the search space, adjusts its direction based on the gradients, and converges towards the minimum. To provide a concrete example of how the algorithm functions in practice, Figure 2.4, generated by Code 2.1, illustrates this trajectory on a MATLAB contour plot. This graphical representation demonstrates the path taken by the algorithm from its starting point to the point where it finds the optimal value x*. Such a visual aid is immensely helpful for readers, particularly those new to the concept of gradient descent, as it offers a clear, step-by-step illustration of the algorithm in action, showcasing the practical application of the theoretical concepts discussed earlier.

 Code 2.1

% Descending gradient method
% Clear memory
clear all
% The function to be optimized 2.8 is defined as follows
funstr='10-(exp(-1*(x∧2+3*y∧2)))';
f=vectorize(inline(funstr));
range=[-1 1 -1 1];
% Function is plotted to reference
Ndiv=50;
dx=(range(2)-range(1))/Ndiv; dy=(range(4)-range(3))/Ndiv;
[x,y] =meshgrid(range(1):dx:range(2),range(3):dy:range(4));
z=(f(x,y));
figure(1);   surfc(x,y,z);
% The number of iterations is defined
k=0;
niter=200;
% The size of the disturbance for gradients is established.
hstep = 0.001;
% Optimization step is set
alfa=0.05;
% Generation of the starting point
xrange=range(2)-range(1);
yrange=range(4)-range(3);
x1=rand*xrange+range(1);
x2=rand*yrange+range(3);
figure
% The iterative optimization process is established
while (k<niter)
% The function is evaluated
zn=f(x1,x2);
% Gradients gx1 and gx2 are calculated.
vx1=x1+hstep;
vx2=x2+hstep;
gx1=(f(vx1,x2)-zn)/hstep;
gx2=(f(x1,vx2)-zn)/hstep;
% The solution produced is plotted
contour(x,y,z,15); hold on;
plot(x1,x2,'.','markersize',10,'markerfacecolor','g');
drawnow;
hold on;
% The new solution is calculated
x1=x1-alfa*gx1;
x2=x2-alfa*gx2;
k=k+1;
end

2.4 Metaheuristic Methods

Classical gradient-based methods are often considered among the fastest algorithms for nonlinear optimization problems (Reinhardt et al. 2013). A significant advantage of these techniques is their ability to guarantee the attainment of the optimal solution to the optimization problem under certain conditions. This assurance of reaching the optimal solution is a compelling feature, especially in scenarios where precision is paramount (Hussain et al. 2019). However, the applicability of these methods is notably constrained by specific prerequisites: the objective function must be twice differentiable and unimodal. In reality, many optimization problems present objective functions that do not meet one or both of these criteria. It’s not uncommon for real-world objective functions to exhibit multimodal behavior, characterized by the presence of several local minima. In such cases, applying gradient-based methods can be problematic, as these methods might get trapped in one of the local minima, impeding any further exploration of the search space for a potentially better solution. An illustration of a multimodal function can be seen in Figure 2.5a, which exemplifies how multiple minima can exist within a single function. Additionally, there are numerous reasons why an objective function might not be differentiable, which further limits the suitability of gradient-based methods. Even a simple operation like rounding, for instance, can transform a differentiable function into a non-differentiable one. This is depicted in Figure 2.5b, where the rounded version of the function presented in Figure 2.3 is shown. Such transformations highlight the complexities and limitations encountered in real-world optimization scenarios, where objective functions may not always conform to the ideal conditions assumed by classical gradient-based optimization methods.

Metaheuristic methods (Simon 2013), a subset of metaheuristic methods, are distinguished by their non-reliance on the gradient information of the objective function. This characteristic significantly broadens their applicability, especially in complex optimization scenarios. By not being constrained to functions that are differentiable or have a clearly defined gradient, these methods can handle a wide array of objective functions, no matter how intricate or unconventional they may be. The flexibility of metaheuristic methods allows them to accommodate objective functions that are tailored to the specific requirements of the application at hand. This adaptability is particularly advantageous in cases where the objective function encompasses simulations or experimental models, scenarios often encountered in fields like engineering, biology, and economics. These functions might be too complex, noisy, or even discontinuous to fit the criteria necessary for gradient-based methods. In evolutionary computation, solutions evolve over time, following principles inspired by natural evolution, such as selection, mutation, and crossover. This process does not require any gradient information; instead, it evaluates the quality of solutions based on a fitness function, which is analogous to the objective function in optimization. The ability to work directly with the objective function, regardless of its mathematical properties, enables metaheuristic methods to tackle a diverse range of optimization problems, including those with complex, multimodal, and non-differentiable objective functions. This makes them highly versatile and powerful tools in the arsenal of optimization techniques, capable of addressing challenges that are beyond the reach of traditional gradient-based methods.

Metaheuristic methods, a key category of metaheuristic approaches, are uniquely characterized by their independence from derivative information of the objective function during the search for the optimal decision vector x that minimizes (or maximizes) a given objective function. Unlike gradient-based methods, which rely on the derivative information to guide their search, these methods utilize heuristic rules to create patterns for exploring the solution space. These heuristic rules often draw inspiration from simulations of various natural or social processes, such as biological evolution, social behavior patterns, or physical phenomena. The distinct advantage of metaheuristic methods lies in their ability to tackle a wide range of problems, including those where the objective function is complex, non-linear, non-differentiable, or even unknown. However, this advantage comes with a trade-off. Since metaheuristic methods do not leverage the derivative information of the objective function, they generally lack precise, immediate guidance on the direction and magnitude of search steps. This lack of direct, relevant information about the objective function’s landscape means that these methods might require more iterations or evaluations to converge to an optimal or near-optimal solution, leading to slower convergence compared to gradient-based techniques. Despite this slower pace, the strength of metaheuristic methods lies in their robustness and versatility. They are particularly valuable in scenarios where traditional methods fail or are impractical, such as optimization problems with complex, irregular, or dynamic objective functions. By employing heuristic rules and mimicking natural or social processes, metaheuristic methods provide effective, though sometimes slower, strategies for finding solutions in diverse and challenging optimization landscapes.

Metaheuristic methods are inherently stochastic in nature (Bartholomew-Biggs 2008), meaning they employ random processes as a fundamental component in determining the directions and strategies of their search. This stochastic element introduces a level of unpredictability and diversity in the search process (Deb 2001), which is crucial for exploring complex and multimodal solution spaces effectively. However, the random nature of these methods also poses a significant challenge for their analytical study. Due to the inherent randomness, it becomes difficult to apply traditional analytical techniques to rigorously analyze and predict the behavior of such methods (Fletcher and Powell 1963). Consequently, many of the properties and understandings of metaheuristic methods have been gleaned through empirical means – experimentation and observation – rather than purely theoretical analysis (Yang 2010).

While some evolutionary computational algorithms are specifically designed to mimic biological phenomena – genetic algorithms, for example, are inspired by the process of natural selection – they are not confined to these biological paradigms in their operational principles. In their broader conception, these methods are fundamentally optimization techniques. They leverage concepts from biological evolution not as an end in themselves, but as a means to develop robust and versatile strategies for finding optimal or near-optimal solutions in complex optimization problems. This approach allows them to transcend the specifics of biological processes and function effectively as general-purpose optimization tools, adaptable to a wide array of problems across various domains. This versatility and the ability to handle diverse and challenging optimization scenarios underscore the significance of metaheuristic methods in the field of optimization.

The term “population optimization algorithms” is often used by some authors to describe metaheuristic techniques. This nomenclature highlights a key characteristic of many such methods: they typically operate with a population of candidate solutions to tackle the optimization problem. In this context, each candidate solution functions akin to an independent agent, each executing its own search strategy. The underlying concept is that over time, through processes reminiscent of natural selection and genetic variation, this population evolves, progressively improving the solutions until it converges to or nears the optimal solution. However, the term “population optimization algorithms” may not fully encapsulate the breadth of metaheuristic methods. This is because not all metaheuristic techniques rely on a population of solutions. For instance, methods like simulated annealing or certain evolutionary strategies work with a single candidate solution that is iteratively modified. In these methods, the focus is on the evolution of this single solution through successive iterations, rather than the evolution of a population of solutions. This distinction is crucial as it points to the more general nature of metaheuristic methods. While population-based approaches like genetic algorithms are a significant part of this category, the field also encompasses methods that operate on a single solution trajectory. Thus, metaheuristic methods, in their broader sense, extend beyond the concept of population-based optimization, encompassing a wider range of strategies and approaches. This more inclusive perspective acknowledges the diversity and flexibility of metaheuristic methods, recognizing their applicability across a spectrum of optimization scenarios, whether they involve single or multiple candidate solutions.

The term “computational intelligence” is sometimes employed to encompass metaheuristic techniques, distinguishing them from other areas within the broader domain of artificial intelligence, such as expert systems. This distinction is rooted in the differing fundamental approaches of these methodologies. Expert systems, a traditional discipline within artificial intelligence, primarily model deductive reasoning. They are designed to replicate the decision-making process of a human expert, relying on a predefined set of rules and logic to draw conclusions from specific inputs. In contrast, metaheuristic methods are more aligned with inductive reasoning. These methods, inspired by biological evolution, learn and evolve through a process of trial and error, exploration, and adaptation, rather than following rigid, pre-established rules. However, the scope of computational intelligence extends beyond just metaheuristic or metaheuristic methods. It is a broader concept that also includes approaches, such as neural networks and fuzzy systems. Neural networks, for instance, are designed to simulate the way the human brain processes information, and are widely used in areas like pattern recognition, classification, and prediction. Fuzzy systems, on the other hand, deal with reasoning that is approximate rather than precise, mimicking the way humans make decisions in a vague and uncertain environment. This wide spectrum of methodologies under the umbrella of computational intelligence is not limited to optimization problems. These approaches find applications across various domains, including data mining, machine learning, signal processing, and control systems, among others. The term “computational intelligence” thus represents a more comprehensive concept, acknowledging the diverse, adaptive, and often heuristic nature of these methods, and their applicability to a vast array of problems beyond just optimization.

The term “bio-inspired algorithms” is frequently used by researchers to refer to metaheuristic methods, but this characterization can be somewhat misleading. While it’s true that many metaheuristic techniques draw inspiration from biological processes – such as genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization – this is not universally the case. For instance, methods like differential evolution and the imperialistic competitive algorithm do not directly derive their mechanisms from natural phenomena. Differential evolution is based more on mathematical principles of optimization, and the imperialistic competitive algorithm models a socio-political process rather than a biological one. Furthermore, there are approaches within evolutionary computation, such as evolutionary strategies and oppositional learning, that maintain only a tenuous or abstract connection to biological processes. Evolutionary strategies, for example, focus on the optimization of strategy parameters and oppositional learning is based on mathematical concepts that do not necessarily mirror natural processes. Given these variations, it becomes evident that metaheuristic methods encompass a broader and more diverse set of algorithms than what the term “bio-inspired” might imply. While bio-inspired algorithms are a significant and well-recognized subset of evolutionary computation, the field as a whole extends beyond just mimicking biological processes. It includes a range of techniques and strategies, some of which are inspired by nature, others by different scientific or mathematical principles, making metaheuristic a more general and inclusive concept than the narrower category of bio-inspired algorithms. This diversity allows metaheuristic methods to be versatile and adaptable, capable of addressing a wide variety of problems across different disciplines.

The term “heuristic algorithms” is often used interchangeably with “evolutionary computation” by some authors, though the two encompass slightly different concepts. The word “heuristic” originates from the Greek term meaning “to find” or “to discover.” Heuristic algorithms are methods that employ intuitive rules or strategies based on common sense or practical experience to solve problems. The primary goal of these algorithms is not necessarily to find the optimal solution but to discover a sufficiently acceptable or satisfactory solution within a reasonable timeframe and with feasible computational resources. Heuristic algorithms are characterized by their problem-solving approach, which is more about applying practical methods that work well in practice, rather than strictly following theoretical or mathematical guidelines. These methods are particularly useful in scenarios where an exhaustive search for the optimal solution is impractical due to complexity or computational constraints. The term “meta-heuristic” refers to a broader family of heuristic algorithms. Meta-heuristics are high-level frameworks or strategies that guide the search process, often incorporating mechanisms to escape local optima and explore the search space more diversely. These may include both population-based approaches and single-solution methods. Given these definitions, it can be argued that most, if not all, of the algorithms discussed in metaheuristic literature fall under the umbrella of meta-heuristics. This encompasses a wide range of algorithms, each with its unique strategies and mechanisms, but all sharing the common goal of efficiently and effectively finding good-enough solutions to complex problems. Therefore, while “evolutionary computation” and “heuristic algorithms” might sometimes be used synonymously, it’s important to recognize that they represent a spectrum of approaches within the broader field of meta-heuristic methods.

Many researchers draw a distinction between evolutionary computational methods and swarm algorithms, although the two share some similarities. Swarm algorithms are based on the concept of collective intelligence, modeling the behavior of groups of animals or insects, such as ants, birds, or fish. This approach leverages the idea that simple rules followed by individuals can lead to complex, intelligent behavior emerging at the group level. Two notable examples in this category are Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), inspired by the foraging behavior of ants, and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), influenced by the social behavior of bird flocking or fish schooling. Despite their distinct inspiration, the operational mechanisms of swarm algorithms bear a resemblance to those of metaheuristic methods. Both involve a population of individuals (ants in ACO, particles in PSO, or candidate solutions in evolutionary algorithms) exploring the search space, albeit guided by different principles and processes. In swarm algorithms, the movement and decision-making of each individual are influenced by the collective experience of the group, whereas evolutionary methods typically rely more on mechanisms like mutation, crossover, and selection. Given their operational similarities and the shared goal of optimizing complex problems, this book considers swarm algorithms as a part of the broader category of metaheuristic methods. This classification is based on the perspective that the underlying principles of adaptation, learning, and evolution in a population, whether inspired by natural evolution or collective animal behavior, fall under the same overarching theme of evolutionary computation. This inclusive perspective allows for a more comprehensive understanding of these methods and their applications in solving a wide array of optimization problems.

The discussions above illuminate that the terminology used to define metaheuristic methods is notably imprecise and varies depending on the context. This lack of precise definition stems from the diverse origins and inspirations of these methods, as well as their evolving nature. In this book, with the intention of encompassing all perspectives and providing a unifying definition, metaheuristic methods are characterized in a broader sense. They are defined as algorithms that modify one or several candidate solutions over numerous iterations, without relying on the gradient information of the objective function. This approach to metaheuristic acknowledges the intrinsic variety within metaheuristic methods. The key element here is the combination of stochastic processes and deterministic models to guide the modification or search strategy. The stochastic component introduces randomness and diversity, allowing the algorithm to explore the solution space broadly and avoid getting trapped in local optima. On the other hand, deterministic models provide a structured approach to refining solutions and converging towards optimality. This blend of randomness and systematic strategy enables these methods to effectively tackle complex optimization problems that are intractable for traditional gradient-based approaches. By adopting this inclusive and integrative definition, the book aims to capture the essence of metaheuristic methods (Cuevas and Rodríguez 2020) as flexible, adaptive, and robust optimization tools. This perspective not only bridges various subfields within the domain of metaheuristics but also provides a coherent framework for understanding and applying these methods across a wide range of problem-solving scenarios.

A key focus here is to clearly define the nomenclature commonly employed by metaheuristic methods, which is essential for a comprehensive understanding. Metaheuristic algorithms, inspired by natural evolutionary processes (Venkataraman 2009), incorporate a variety of terms and concepts unique to their domain. These include notions, such as “population” (Matyas 1965), referring to a set of candidate solutions; “generation,” indicating the iteration steps in the algorithm; “selection,” describing the process of choosing more promising solutions; “mutation” and “crossover,” mechanisms for introducing variability and new characteristics into the solutions; and “fitness,” a measure of how well a solution satisfies the optimization criteria.

By dissecting these terms and concepts, the section aims to provide a clear and detailed overview of how metaheuristic algorithms function, how they approach the task of optimization, and the rationale behind their strategies. This elucidation not only aids in understanding the operational mechanics of these algorithms but also helps in appreciating their versatility and effectiveness in solving complex optimization problems. The goal is to present these concepts in a manner that is both accessible to newcomers and valuable to those with existing knowledge in the field, ensuring a comprehensive grasp of metaheuristics as a powerful tool in the optimization arsenal.

(2.10)

In optimization problems, x typically represents the vector of decision variables, and d specifies the number of these variables. This vector, x, is a crucial element as it encapsulates all the variables that can be adjusted or controlled in order to optimize a given objective function. The concept of d, the dimensionality of the problem, is equally important as it indicates how many such variables are involved in the problem, thereby defining the complexity and scope of the optimization task.

The set X is another fundamental concept, representing the set of all possible candidate solutions. This set is also referred to as the search space or solution space. It is essentially the domain within which the optimization algorithm operates, encompassing all the potential combinations of the decision variables that can be considered for arriving at the optimal solution.

In many instances, the search space is not unlimited but is instead bounded by lower and upper bounds for each of the decision variables. These bounds are denoted by (the lower bound) and (the upper bound) for each variable xi in the decision vector x. The mathematical representation of this bounded search space can be expressed as X = {x ∈ ℝd|li ≤ xi ≤ ui, i = 1, …, d}. This expression signifies that for every decision variable xi in the vector x, there exists a permissible range defined by its corresponding lower and upper bounds, and . These bounds ensure that the solutions explored by the optimization algorithm are feasible and within the practical constraints of the problem.

To tackle the optimization problem described in Eq. 2.10, a metaheuristic algorithm employs either a single candidate solution xk or a population Pk consisting of N candidate solutions . This population undergoes an evolutionary process, changing and adapting over a predetermined maximum number of iterations, niter, transitioning from an initial state to a final, optimally evolved state.

In the initial state of the algorithm, the set of candidate solutions is randomly initialized within the bounds of the search space X. This initialization is crucial as it sets the starting point for the evolutionary process. At each subsequent generation or iteration (as it is often referred to in the nomenclature of metaheuristic algorithms), a set of evolutionary operators is applied to the current population Pk to create a new generation of candidate solutions Pk + 1.

The effectiveness of each candidate solution (where i ranges from 1 to N) is assessed using the objective function , which quantifies the quality of the solution with respect to the optimization problem. This value is known as the fitness value of in the context of metaheuristic algorithms. During the evolution process, the algorithm typically tracks the best solution, denoted as m, which emerges from the pool of all candidate solutions. This best solution holds a special designation and is continuously updated as the algorithm progresses.

The ultimate goal of this evolutionary process is that, by the final iteration, this position m will represent the optimal solution to the problem. Figure 2.6 in the reference material offers a graphical representation of this optimization process from the perspective of metaheuristic algorithms. This visual aid helps in understanding how the population of candidate solutions evolves and converges towards the best solution over time, providing a clear illustration of the dynamic and iterative nature of metaheuristic methods.

2.5 Exploitation and Exploration

Exploration and exploitation (Hussain et al. 2019) are two fundamental strategies in the realm of optimization, especially within metaheuristic and metaheuristic algorithms. Exploration is characterized by the search for new solutions in the solution space (Xu and Xu 2021). It involves venturing into uncharted or less-explored areas with the aim of discovering potentially better solutions. This approach is inherently risky, as the outcomes of exploring new possibilities are uncertain and can lead to solutions of varying quality, including those that may not improve upon existing ones. However, the potential reward of exploration is significant; it offers the chance to stumble upon the best possible solution, or at least, solutions that are substantially better than those previously known.

Exploitation, on the other hand, is a more conservative strategy (Morales-Castañeda et al. 2020). It focuses on utilizing existing solutions that have already proven to be effective in similar situations. This approach leverages the knowledge gained from past successes to refine and improve upon these solutions. Exploitation is less risky compared to exploration, as it relies on tried-and-tested solutions, making the outcomes more predictable. However, the downside is that the improvements made through exploitation are often incremental, leading to smaller gains in optimization.

For an optimization agent or search strategy, striking a balance between exploration and exploitation is crucial. On one hand, the ability to explore is necessary to discover novel and potentially superior solutions, despite the inherent risks. On the other hand, the ability to exploit is important for capitalizing on known successful solutions, albeit with marginal gains (Črepinšek et al. 2013). The optimal blend of exploration and exploitation depends on the specific characteristics of the problem and the stage of the search process. Initially, a greater emphasis on exploration may be beneficial to gain a broad understanding of the solution space, while later stages might benefit more from exploitation to fine-tune and enhance the already identified promising solutions. This dynamic interplay between exploration and exploitation is a key aspect of effective search strategies in optimization algorithms.

A metaheuristic approach, in its essence, is designed to orchestrate the dual processes of exploration and exploitation within the search space (Yang et al. 2022). In the context of metaheuristic methods, these two processes play distinct yet complementary roles. Exploration is the process of venturing into new areas of the search space to uncover novel solutions. It involves probing areas that are less known or entirely unknown, with the aim of discovering potentially better solutions that have not been considered before. This aspect of the search is crucial for broadening the scope of the solutions and avoiding premature convergence to suboptimal results.

Exploitation, in contrast, focuses on the local refinement of the best solutions already identified in the search process (Lin and Gen 2009). The goal here is to fine-tune these solutions, enhancing their quality and efficiency. This process leverages the information and insights gained from the successful solutions so far, to incrementally improve them. Exploitation is vital for intensifying the search around promising areas, thereby increasing the precision and effectiveness of the solutions.

However, focusing solely on either exploration or exploitation can be detrimental to the optimization process. Pure exploration, while opening up new possibilities, may degrade the accuracy of the solutions, as it tends to overlook the refinement of already good solutions. Conversely, pure exploitation, although effective in improving existing solutions, can severely limit the search strategy. It often leads to a scenario where the algorithm gets trapped in local optima, unable to escape and explore potentially better solutions elsewhere.

Therefore, the key challenge and strength of an evolutionary metaheuristic method lie in its ability to strike a delicate balance between exploration and exploitation (Binkley and Hagiwara 2008). This balance is critical for ensuring that the algorithm is able to thoroughly investigate the search space while also capitalizing on the promising solutions it finds. The exploration–exploitation balancing act has not been conclusively solved in the field, and as such, each metaheuristic method implements its own unique approach to address this challenge. Different algorithms employ various strategies and mechanisms to manage this balance, often tailored to the specific nature of the optimization problems they are designed to solve. This ongoing quest to effectively balance exploration and exploitation continues to be a central theme in the development and refinement of metaheuristic algorithms.

2.6 Acceptance and Probabilistic Selection

Acceptance and probabilistic selection are two fundamental operations commonly employed in virtually all metaheuristic methods, playing a crucial role in guiding the search process toward effective solutions.

The probabilistic acceptance operation is a strategy where the execution of a particular action is contingent upon a certain probability. This approach introduces a stochastic element into the decision-making process, allowing for a degree of randomness that can be vital for exploring the search space more broadly. For instance, in some algorithms, a worse solution might be accepted over a better one with a certain probability. This mechanism can help the algorithm escape from local optima by permitting moves that are not immediately beneficial but may lead to more promising areas of the search space in the long run.

Probabilistic selection, on the other hand, relates to the process of choosing an element from a set of possible solutions, where elements of higher quality have a greater likelihood of being selected compared to those of lower quality. This operation is central to the concept of “survival of the fittest” in evolutionary methods. It ensures that solutions which are closer to the optimal (or have better fitness) are more likely to be retained and propagated through generations. By preferentially selecting higher-quality solutions, the algorithm incrementally improves the overall quality of the population.

Both these operations – probabilistic acceptance and probabilistic selection – are instrumental in achieving a balance between exploration and exploitation. While probabilistic acceptance facilitates exploration by introducing randomness and flexibility, probabilistic selection steers the algorithm towards exploitation, concentrating the search around the most promising solutions found so far. The interplay of these operations allows metaheuristic methods to navigate complex search spaces effectively, adapting and evolving their strategies to find optimal or near-optimal solutions.

Probabilistic acceptance is a pivotal operation commonly employed in metaheuristic methods to guide the application of various operators in the solution search process. This operation hinges on the principle of executing a particular action, let’s call it Action A, based on a predetermined probability, denoted as PA.

The essence of probabilistic acceptance lies in the fact that PA determines the frequency with which Action A is applied within the algorithm. To ensure this operation aligns with the principles of probability, PA must fall within the range of valid probability values, which is the interval [0, 1]. In other words, PA can take any value from 0 (indicating that Action A will never be executed) to 1 (implying that Action A will always be executed).

The process of deciding whether to accept or reject Action A under these conditions unfolds in the following manner: Firstly, a random number rA is generated. This number is drawn from a uniform distribution spanning the interval [0, 1], denoted as U[0, 1]. The value of rA is then compared to the probability PA. If rA is less than or equal to PA, then Action A is executed. If, however, rA is greater than PA, Action A is not executed and therefore has no effect on the solution search process at that instance.

This probabilistic mechanism introduces an element of randomness and variability into the algorithm, which can be crucial for navigating complex solution spaces. It allows the algorithm to occasionally explore less optimal paths or accept less promising solutions, providing the flexibility needed to escape local optima and potentially discover more globally optimal solutions. This makes probabilistic acceptance an integral part of the dynamic and adaptive nature of metaheuristic algorithms.

Since metaheuristic algorithms operate iteratively, the probability PA plays a pivotal role in dictating the frequency at which a certain action, referred to as Action A, is executed throughout the course of these iterations. This probability essentially determines how often the algorithm will opt to perform Action A.

When the value of PA is set close to zero, it implies that Action A is designated to be a rare occurrence within the algorithm’s execution. In this scenario, the algorithm will seldom resort to applying Action A, making it an infrequent aspect of the search process. Conversely, if PA is set close to one, the situation is quite different. Here, Action A becomes a common event, being executed almost every time the opportunity arises. Such a high probability ensures that Action A is a regular and influential part of the algorithm’s behavior.

From an implementation standpoint, the process of determining whether to execute Action A at each iteration is typically handled through the generation of a uniformly distributed random number (generated by the function rand). This is achieved using a function like rand which generates a random number in the range of [0, 1] (denoted as U[0, 1]). The generated random number is then compared to PA. If the random number is less than or equal to PA, Action A is executed in that iteration; otherwise, it is skipped. This use of a random number from a uniform distribution ensures that the decision to execute Action A maintains the stochastic nature inherent to metaheuristic algorithms, allowing these methods to balance exploration and exploitation effectively in their search for optimal solutions.

To demonstrate the concept of probabilistic acceptance in practice, a program, as illustrated in Code 2.2, was developed. This program is designed to run for a total of 10,000 iterations, with a set probability PA = 0.7 dictating the execution frequency of a specific action, ActionA. According to this setup, ActionA is expected to be executed approximately 70% of the time throughout these iterations, while in the remaining 30% of the iterations, ActionA will not be executed.

In practical terms, when the program is run, a uniformly distributed random number between 0 and 1 is generated in each iteration. If this random number is less than or equal to 0.7 (reflecting the value of PA), then ActionA is executed; if it is greater than 0.7, Action A is not executed. As a result, over the span of 10,000 iterations, one would expect the variable ActionA (which counts the number of times ActionA is executed) to reach a value close to 7000, given the 70% probability of execution. Correspondingly, the variable NoActionA (which counts the number of times ActionA is not executed) would approximate 3000, aligning with the 30% probability of non-execution.

This program exemplifies how probabilistic acceptance works in an iterative process. It highlights the impact of the chosen probability value on the frequency of an action’s execution and provides a clear, quantifiable insight into how often an action occurs under specified probabilistic conditions. The outcome, with ActionA around 7000 and NoActionA around 3000, serves as a practical illustration of the probabilistic decision-making inherent in metaheuristic algorithms.

 Code 2.2

% Probabilistic acceptance
% Clear memory
clear all
% Variables are initialized
ActionA=0;
NoActionA =0;
% Starts the iterative decision process
for i=1:10000
    % A random number is generated U[0, 1]
    rA=rand;
    % Probabilistic acceptance
    if (rA<=0.7)
        ActionA = ActionA +1;
    else
        NoActionA = NoActionA +1;
    end
end

Probabilistic selection (Lipowski and Lipowska 2012) is a key concept in metaheuristic and metaheuristic algorithms, focusing on the process of choosing elements from a set of available options based on their quality. In this approach, elements that exhibit higher quality – typically measured in terms of their fitness or suitability for the problem at hand – are given a greater probability of being selected compared to those of lower quality. This method introduces a bias towards better-performing elements, ensuring that the most promising solutions are more likely to be chosen and retained for future iterations of the algorithm.

The underlying principle of probabilistic selection is to strike a balance between maintaining diversity within the population and converging toward optimal or near-optimal solutions. By preferentially selecting higher-quality elements, the algorithm incrementally improves the overall quality of the population (Yu et al. 2016). However, by allowing elements with lower quality to be chosen with a smaller but non-zero probability, the algorithm retains a degree of diversity. This diversity is crucial for preventing premature convergence to local optima and ensuring that the search explores a broad range of the solution space.

Probabilistic selection can take various forms, such as roulette wheel selection, tournament selection, or rank-based selection, each with its own method of assigning selection probabilities based on quality (Chakraborty and Bhowmik 2015). Regardless of the specific technique, the core idea remains the same: elements that are better suited to solving the problem are more likely to be selected and propagated through the generations of the algorithm. This method of selection is fundamental to the success of many evolutionary algorithms, as it directly influences the trajectory and effectiveness of the search process.

In metaheuristic methods, particularly those involving a population of solutions, a common task is to select a particular solution from the population Pk, where e is an index within the range [1, 2, …, N]. This selection is not arbitrary; it is heavily influenced by the quality or fitness of the solutions in the population, denoted as . The principle guiding this selection process is that solutions with better quality (or higher fitness values) should have a higher probability of being chosen compared to those with lower quality.

Under such a selection process, the probability of choosing the solution from the set of all N solutions is calculated based on its relative fitness compared to the fitness of the other solutions in the population. This probability is typically defined through a specific formula or mechanism which ensures that higher fitness solutions are more likely to be picked. One common approach is to assign selection probabilities proportional to the fitness of each solution. For instance, in a roulette wheel selection mechanism, each solution in the population is given a slice of the wheel, with the size of the slice proportional to its fitness. The higher the fitness, the larger the slice, and thus, the greater the chance of being selected.

This probabilistic selection method plays a crucial role in the dynamics of metaheuristic algorithms, as it directly influences the direction and efficiency of the search process. By preferentially choosing higher-quality solutions, the algorithm can quickly converge toward optimal or near-optimal solutions. However, by maintaining a non-zero probability of selecting lower-quality solutions, the algorithm also retains a degree of exploration and diversity, crucial for avoiding local optima and ensuring a comprehensive search of the solution space.

In metaheuristic algorithms, particularly those that involve a population-based approach, the selection of solutions is often guided by probabilistic methods. Once the selection probabilities {P1, P2, …, PN} for each solution in the population Pk are calculated, along with their cumulative probabilities , the selection process unfolds in the following manner:

  • Generation of a Random Number: The process begins with the generation of a random number rS, uniformly distributed in the interval [0, 1]. This random number serves as a basis for selecting one of the solutions from the population.
  • Iterative Testing Process: Starting with the first solution in the population, a test is conducted to check if the cumulative probability is greater than rS. If this condition is not met, the process continues to the next solution in the population.
  • Continuation of Testing: This testing continues iteratively through the population. For each solution, the algorithm checks if its corresponding cumulative probability meets the condition of being greater than rS.
  • Selection of the Solution: The iterative process concludes when it finds a cumulative probability that satisfies the condition . The solution corresponding to this cumulative probability is then selected as the output of this process.

This approach to selection is widely used in various metaheuristic algorithms, especially in those employing mechanisms like roulette wheel selection. It ensures that solutions with higher probabilities (and typically higher fitness) have a greater chance of being chosen, while still allowing for the possibility of selecting less optimal solutions. This method of selection is key to maintaining a balance between exploration and exploitation, as it allows for both the intensification of the search around promising areas and the diversification of the search to explore new regions of the solution space.

2.7 Random Search

The random search method (Zabinsky 2009), often recognized as one of the earliest optimization strategies grounded in a fully stochastic process, adopts a notably straightforward approach. In this method, the optimization process revolves around the evolution of a single candidate solution, denoted as xk. This method stands out for its simplicity and its reliance on randomness as the primary driver of the search process.

At each iteration of the random search method (Kaelo and Ali 2006), the current candidate solution xk is modified through the addition of a random vector, denoted as Δx. This random vector introduces variability into the solution, enabling the exploration of the search space in a stochastic manner. The process of updating the candidate solution can be expressed mathematically as follows:

(2.13)

In this expression, xk + 1 represents the new candidate solution for the next iteration. The vector Δx is generated randomly, and its addition to the current solution xk results in a new solution that is a random variation of the existing one.

When employing the random search method in a multidimensional context, where the candidate solution xk has d dimensions , each coordinate of the solution is subject to modification. This modification is implemented through a vector of random perturbations, denoted as (Δx = {Δx1, Δx2, …, Δxd}). Each component of this perturbation vector, Δxi (where i ranges from 1 to d), is individually generated and modeled using a Gaussian (or normal) probability distribution as follows:

(2.14)

The Gaussian distribution is characterized by its mean (often denoted as μi) and its standard deviation (σi), and it is a commonly used probability distribution in stochastic processes due to its natural occurrence in many real-world scenarios. In the context of the random search method, the Gaussian distribution is employed to generate each , providing a controlled yet random influence on each dimension of the solution.

In this expression, N(μi, σi) denotes the Gaussian distribution with mean μi and variance σi. The choice of μi and σi can significantly impact the behavior of the random search method. Typically, μi is set to zero, centering the distribution around the current value of xk, while σi controls the spread or variability of the perturbation, influencing the extent of exploration in the search space.

By applying these Gaussian-distributed perturbations to each dimension of the candidate solution, the random search method facilitates a multidimensional exploration of the solution space. This approach allows for a comprehensive and unbiased search, although the randomness of the method may require a large number of iterations to locate optimal or near-optimal solutions, especially in complex, high-dimensional optimization problems.

In the random search method, once the new candidate solution xk + 1 is computed, the subsequent step involves evaluating whether this new position represents an improvement over the previous candidate solution xk. This evaluation is crucial as it determines whether to accept xk + 1 as the new candidate solution or to retain xk for the next iteration.

The improvement test, particularly in the context of a minimization problem, can be defined by comparing the quality or fitness values of xk + 1 and xk. The quality of a solution is typically assessed using an objective function, which quantifies how well the solution meets the criteria of the optimization problem. For a minimization case, the objective is to find the solution with the lowest possible value of this objective function.

The test for whether to accept xk + 1 can be mathematically formulated as follows:

  • If f(xk + 1) < f(xk), then accept xk + 1 as the new candidate solution. This implies that xk + 1 has a lower (and therefore better) value of the objective function compared to xk, signifying an improvement.
  • If f(xk + 1) ≥ f(xk), then retain xk as the current candidate solution. In this scenario, xk + 1 does not offer any improvement over xk in terms of minimizing the objective function.

This process of testing and potentially updating the candidate solution ensures that the random search method progressively moves towards better solutions over successive iterations (Feng and Shen 2015). However, the stochastic nature of the modifications means that improvements are not guaranteed at every step. The algorithm relies on the random generation of new solutions and the systematic evaluation of their quality to gradually find a solution that minimizes the objective function, navigating the solution space in an unbiased and exploratory manner.

The random search method’s reliance on stochasticity means that it does not follow any gradient or specific direction in the search space. Instead, it relies on random sampling to potentially stumble upon optimal or near-optimal solutions. While this method is conceptually simple and easy to implement, it may not be as efficient or effective as other more sophisticated metaheuristic algorithms, especially for complex or high-dimensional problems. However, its significance lies in its foundational role in the evolution of optimization techniques, demonstrating the potential of stochastic processes in searching for solutions.

The criterion used in the random search method for updating the candidate solution is commonly referred to as a “greedy” approach. This term implies that the algorithm only accepts changes to the solution that result in an immediate improvement in its quality. Specifically, in the context of the random search method, this means that a new candidate solution xk + 1 is accepted only if it offers a better (lower for minimization, higher for maximization) objective function value compared to the current solution xk.

However, one challenge inherent to this method, especially due to its stochastic nature, is the possibility of the new solution xk + 1 being generated outside the predefined search space X. Since the objective function f(x). is defined only within the bounds of this search space, a solution lying outside X has no valid objective function value. To manage this situation, the random search algorithm incorporates a safeguard mechanism. If a newly generated solution xk + 1 falls outside the search space X, the algorithm assigns it a very poor quality. This is represented by assigning an extremely large value to the objective function for minimization problems (i.e., f(xk + 1) = ∞) or an extremely low value for maximization problems (i.e., f(xk + 1) = − ∞).

By doing so, the algorithm ensures that any solution generated outside the viable search space is automatically deemed unfavorable and is not accepted as the new candidate solution. This approach effectively keeps the evolution of the solution within the bounds of the defined search space, maintaining the integrity and relevance of the search process. The greedy nature of the substitution criterion, combined with this safeguard against invalid solutions, helps guide the random search method in progressively and efficiently exploring the solution space toward finding an optimal or near-optimal solution.

(2.15)

In this formulation, a two-dimensional function f(x1, x2) with a search space defined in the interval [−3, 3] is considered for each of the decision variables x1 and x2. Figure 2.7 shows a representation of the objective function f(x1, x2).

So, if the quality of xk + 1 is better than xk, the value of xk + 1 is accepted as the new candidate solution, otherwise xk remains unchanged. This process is repeated iteratively until a maximum number of Niter iterations have been reached.

 else

  (ync<=range(4)))
  % If it belongs, it is evaluated
      zn2=f(xnc,ync);
  else
     % If it is not given a very low value
     zn2=-1000;
 end
  % Test whether the newly generated solution is accepted.
  if (zn2>zn1)
      xn=xnc;
      yn=ync;

  k=k+1;
