The PSO algorithm has been executed within the MATLAB environment to demonstrate its search methodology. This specific implementation is showcased in Algorithm 6.1. The primary goal in this process is to minimize an objective function in order to locate the global minimum. The optimization problem selected for this example isn’t representative of an engineering challenge or a real-world application. Rather, it is a mathematical construct known as the peaks function. This function is defined as follows:

(4.33)

The peaks function, defined in a two-dimensional space, is extensively utilized due to its interesting properties. This function is characterized by the presence of both minima and maxima, which include local and global points. These features make it an ideal candidate for swiftly assessing the efficacy of various metaheuristic algorithms. Notably, the peaks function possesses a global minimum, which is approximately −6.54. This distinct landscape of peaks and valleys provides a comprehensive testbed for evaluating the performance and robustness of optimization algorithms like PSO in navigating complex solution spaces.

To visually demonstrate the PSO search process, its implementation has been tailored for the two-dimensional peaks function problem. For those looking to apply this method in higher-dimensional spaces, necessary modifications need to be made. These adjustments include altering key algorithm parameters, such as the number of dimensions (d), the lower (lb), and upper (ub) limits for each dimension, as well as revising the number of particles (N) and the maximum number of iterations (kmax).

It’s important to note that increasing the dimensionality of the problem adds to the complexity of the search. Having more search agents and extended time for conducting the search can significantly enhance the optimization process in such cases. Therefore, modifying the number of particles and iterations is advisable to fine-tune the performance of the optimization.

Algorithm 6.1 details the PSO implementation. Within the algorithm’s code, there are several explanatory comments that assist in understanding how PSO functions. These annotations are particularly helpful in clarifying the adjustments needed for different dimensions and how they influence the overall effectiveness of the PSO in navigating more complex optimization challenges.

Program 4.17 Implementation of the PSO Method by Using MATLAB

%Algorithm 4.17
% Implementation of the PSO algorithm
%% Clear memory and close Matlab Windows
clear all % Clear memory
close all % close Matlab Windows
%% Problem to optimize (minimize), the definition of the objective function
    funObj = @(xi) 3*(1-xi(1))∧2*exp(-(xi(1)∧2)-(xi(2)+1)∧2) ...
                   -10*(xi(1)/5-xi(1)∧3 - xi(2)∧5)*exp(-xi(1)∧2-xi(2)∧2)...
                   -1/3*exp(-(xi(1)+1)∧2 - xi(2)∧2);
%% Parameter configuration
    N = 10;          % Particle number
    d = 2;           % Dimensions
    lb = [-3 -3];    % Lower limit of search the space
    ub = [3 3];      % Upper limit of search the space
    k = 0;           % Current iteration
    kmax = 100;      % Maximum number of iterations
    c1 = 2;          % Cognitive constant
    c2 = 2;          % Social constant
%% Initialization of particles and velocity
    for i = 1:N
        x(i,:) = rand(1,d).*(ub-lb)+lb; % Initialization of particles
        v(i,:) = zeros(1,d);            % Initialization of velocities
    end
%% Evaluation of the initial particles in the objective function
    for i = 1:N
        xi=x(i,:);            % Extraction of the particle xi
        fx(i,:) = funObj(xi); % Evaluation of the particle xi
    end
%% Record of the best global particle and the best local particles
    [gfit, ind] = min(fx); % Fitness of the best global particle 
    g = x(ind,:);          % Position of the best global particle
    fp = fx;               % Fitness of the best local particles
    p = x;                 % Position of the best local particles
%% Calculation of the search space for graphical proposes
    ejex=linspace(min(lb),max(ub),50); % Solutions for vector d = 1
    ejey=ejex;                         % Solutions for vector d = 2
    ejez=[];                           % Fitness matrix 
    for i = 1:length(ejex)
        for j = 1:length(ejey)
            ejez(i,j) = funObj([ejex(i) ejey(j)]); 
        end
    end
    [ejey ejex] = meshgrid(ejex,ejey); % Computation of the meshgrid
%% Iterative process
    while k < kmax % Stop criterion
        k = k + 1; % new iteration
        %% Draw the search space Surface
            figure(1);           % Show Figure 1
            surf(ejex,ejey,ejez) % Draw the function surface
            hold on              % Hold the figures 
        %% Draw the particles 
            % Draw the particles in red color
            plot3(x(:,1),x(:,2),fx,'o','MarkerFaceColor','m','MarkerSize',10)
            % Dibuja las mejores partículas locales en color verde
            plot3(p(:,1),p(:,2),fp,'o','MarkerFaceColor','g','MarkerSize',10)
            % Pause to allow viewing the graph
            pause(0.3)
            % Release figure 1
            hold off   
        %% Draw the function contour
            figure(2)                  % Show figure 2
            contour(ejex,ejey,ejez,20) % The cfunction contour is redraw
            hold on                    % Hold figure 2 for graphical proposes 
        %% Draw the particles in the contour
            % Draw the particles in red color
            plot(x(:,1),x(:,2),'o','MarkerFaceColor','m');
            % Dibuja las mejores partículas locales en color verde
            plot(p(:,1),p(:,2),'o','MarkerFaceColor','g');
            % Pause to allow viewing the graph
            pause(0.3)
            % Release figure 2
            hold off
        %% Computation of the new velocity for each particle
            for i= 1:N
                % Extraction of the particle xi
                xi = x(i,:);
                % Extraction of the local particle pi
                pi = p(i,:);
                % Determination of the new velocity for each particle vi
                v(i,:) = v(i,:)+c1*rand(1,d).*(pi-xi)+c2*rand(1,d).*(g-xi);
            end
        %% Determination of the new position of each particle
            x = x + v;
        %% Verify that the particles do not leave the limits lb and ub
            for i = 1:N                   % For each particle
                for j=1:d                 % For each dimension
                    if x(i,j) < lb(j)     % Check the lower limit
                        x(i,j) = lb(j);   
                    elseif x(i,j)> ub(j) % Check the upper limit
                        x(i,j) = ub(j);
                    end
                end
            end
        %% Evaluation of the new particles with the objective function
            for i = 1:N
                xi = x(i,:);          % Extraction of the particle xi
                fx(i,:) = funObj(xi); % Evaluation of the particle xi
            end
        %% Record of the best global particle and the best local particles
            [gfitkmas1, ind] = min(fx);
            % If a better solution was found, update the global particle
            if gfitkmas1 < gfit
                % Update the fitness of the best global particle
                gfit = gfitkmas1;
                % Update the position of the best global particle
                g = x(ind,:);            
            end
            for i = 1:N
                % If any particle is a better solution than the previous,
                % update your best local particle
                if fx(i,:) < fp(i,:)
                    % Update the fitness of the best local particles
                    fp(i,:) = fx(i,:); 
                    % Update the position of the best local particles
                    p(i,:) = x(i,:);    
                end
            end
%% Historical record of the best solutions found in each generation
            Evolucion(k) = gfit;       
    end 
%% End of the iterative process, display of results
    Figure
    % Graph of the evolutionary process of the PSO
    plot(Evolucion)                            
%% Results of PSO
    disp([The best solution : ', num2str(g)])    
    disp(['The best fitness  : ', num2str(gfit)])

 The particle swarm optimization (PSO) algorithm finds significant utility in machine learning, particularly in optimizing machine learning models and algorithms. PSO can effectively fine-tune hyperparameters, select features, and enhance the performance of various machine learning techniques. Conversely, machine learning methods can also augment PSO. By employing machine learning techniques, such as reinforcement learning or neural networks, the efficiency and accuracy of the PSO algorithm can be significantly improved. These enhancements might include better decision-making in particle movement or more effective adaptation to complex optimization landscapes, leading to a synergistic relationship where both domains benefit from each other’s strengths.

4.4 Differential Evolution (DE) Algorithm

In 1997, Kenneth Price and Rainer Storn introduced the metaheuristic algorithm known as DE, marking a significant advancement in optimization techniques. DE operates as a population-based algorithm, employing a straightforward and direct search strategy. This innovative method generates new parameter vectors by adding the weighted difference between two randomly selected population members, fostering efficient exploration and exploitation of the solution space. This Section considers the operational mechanics of the DE algorithm. It not only elaborates on the mathematical underpinnings of DE’s operators but also discusses its practical implementation in MATLAB, a popular programming environment for algorithmic development. The primary aim of this section is to equip the reader with a thorough understanding of DE’s mathematical framework and its application potential in solving various optimization challenges.

In 1995, Rainer Price tackled the Chebyshev polynomial adjustment problem, as documented by Rozenberg et al. in 2005. Price approached this challenge using the Genetic Annealing algorithm, a method he co-developed with K.V in 1994. Although he successfully resolved the problem, Price recognized that the algorithm fell short of the performance benchmarks essential for a competitive optimization technique. These benchmarks included robust global search capabilities, rapid convergence, and ease of implementation.

In response to these shortcomings, Price, collaborating with Storn in 1997, innovated a new strategy rooted in vector calculus and evolutionary computation principles. This novel approach involved the creation of parameter vectors by adding the weighted difference between two population members to a third member. This operation, known as differential mutation, marked a significant advancement in the field of metaheuristic algorithms.

DE, as this new method was called, demonstrated superior performance compared to other metaheuristic schemes in solving optimization problems. Its key strengths include straightforward implementation, effective convergence properties verified through independent tests, and the ability to parallelize for tackling high-computational-cost problems. The DE algorithm’s most notable feature is its adeptness at finding optimal global solutions for multimodal, non-differentiable, and non-linear functions.

The DE algorithm has showcased its capabilities in prestigious forums such as the IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation (CEC) and has been applied successfully in various real-world optimization scenarios. Like other metaheuristic methods, DE operates iteratively, utilizing exploration-exploitation operators such as mutation and crossover throughout the optimization process to identify the best solution.

In the realm of metaheuristic algorithms, maintaining a balance between exploration and exploitation is crucial. Without this equilibrium, the effectiveness of evolutionary optimization techniques diminishes, especially in practical applications. To circumvent this issue, DE incorporates specific mechanisms to prevent getting trapped in local optima. The mutation operator in DE employs a direct strategy to probe unexplored areas of the search space, while the crossover operator enhances population diversity, increasing the likelihood of locating the global optimum.

Through these thoughtful design choices, DE stands out as a robust and efficient tool in the field of evolutionary optimization, capable of addressing a wide range of complex optimization challenges.

4.4.1 The Search Strategy of DE

DE shares similarities with the PSO method in being a population-based algorithm where each member is represented as a parameter vector. The evolutionary process of DE unfolds through four distinct phases, each critical to the optimization process.

The initial phase involves the creation of a population. Here, parameter vectors are stochastically generated, ensuring a random yet controlled distribution over the search space of the problem at hand. This random generation lays the groundwork for a diverse and robust starting population.

In the second phase, DE employs differential mutation. This process involves recombining elements of the population to foster genetic diversity and enable the exploration of new solution spaces. This mutation is not random but is guided by the differences between the population members, allowing for a more directed and effective search.

The third stage introduces the crossover operator. By combining information from different population elements, this operator significantly enhances the diversity within the population. This increase in diversity is crucial for avoiding local optima and ensuring that the population explores a wide range of potential solutions.

The final, fourth step involves an elitist selection mechanism. This process is designed to ensure that the most promising solutions, or the ‘best’ individuals, are carried over to the next generation. By doing so, DE ensures that each generation improves upon the last, steadily moving toward an optimal solution.

To visualize this process, consider Figure 4.20, which illustrates the distribution of nine solutions on a two-dimensional surface. This figure highlights the operational mechanics of DE by showing how the difference between two randomly selected points (for instance, points 7 and 9, corresponding to vectors and , respectively) is used to guide the evolutionary process. This visual representation helps in understanding how DE navigates the search space, constantly adapting and evolving its population toward the optimal solution.

Following the process described earlier, the DE algorithm takes the next step by scaling the calculated difference between the two randomly chosen vectors and adding it to a third vector, , which is also selected randomly (in this instance, corresponding to point five on the graphical representation). The magnitude of the addition is determined by a scaling factor, denoted as F, which specifies the extent to which the difference between points and is incorporated into the third vector, . The result of this operation is the creation of a new vector, referred to as the mutant vector v1. This entire process, encompassing the scaling and addition to generate the mutant vector, is visually detailed in Figure 4.21. The figure serves to illustrate the systematic approach of the DE algorithm in evolving the vectors within its population, highlighting the methodical progression toward finding an optimal solution.

Figure 4.22 effectively demonstrates a key aspect of the DE algorithm’s process. It shows how the newly created mutant vector v1, derived from the earlier steps, exhibits a better fitness value compared to the original point, labeled as point 1 in the illustration. This superior fitness value is significant because, in the DE algorithm, vectors with better quality – indicated by their fitness – are selected to replace their predecessors in the population. This ensures that the population evolves toward increasingly optimal solutions.

The DE algorithm continues to execute this process of evolution and replacement until it meets a predetermined stopping criterion. This criterion is often based on the maximum number of generations deemed necessary for the optimization process. Essentially, the algorithm iterates through generations, continuously refining its population, until it reaches this set limit.

Upon completing the stipulated number of iterations, the DE algorithm arrives at its final phase. The best solution from the last generation is identified as the optimal solution for the problem at hand, be it a maximization or minimization issue. This solution represents the culmination of the algorithm’s systematic search and optimization process, effectively addressing the formulated optimization problem with the best possible outcome derived from the evolving population.

In the DE algorithm, the population consists of N parameter vectors, each situated within a d-dimensional space of real values. Represented as X, this population comprises vectors , where each denotes a specific position in the d-dimensional space, represented as {x1, x2, … xd}. Throughout each generation (iteration) k, these vectors undergo manipulation through a trio of operators: mutation, crossover, and selection. The aim of these operations is to steer the search strategy toward the global optimum.

Each operator in the DE algorithm plays a crucial role in generating new candidate solutions, striking a balance between exploration and exploitation. This balance is key to enhancing the population’s diversity. After initializing the population positions randomly and uniformly, the DE algorithm iteratively applies the mutation, crossover, and selection operators.

The mutation operation is pivotal for exploring the search space, creating a direct pathway toward the global optimum. Conversely, the crossover operation is tasked with augmenting the diversity of the positions within the parameter vectors. The selection operation then focuses on retaining the best individuals in the population. In each iteration, the fitness value of the vector produced by the mutation and crossover operations is assessed. If this new vector demonstrates better performance than its predecessor, it replaces the latter; if not, the original vector remains.

This selection mechanism ensures that only the most promising solutions are preserved for future generations, facilitating the exchange of information among the best candidates. As a result, the DE algorithm achieves effective convergence toward the global optimum of the optimization problem, continually refining the population toward the most efficient solutions.

Initialization is the initial phase of the DE algorithm. During this phase, it’s crucial to define the boundaries of the search space for the optimization problem. These boundaries are essentially vectors that set the minimum and maximum limits for each dimension of the problem, commonly referred to as box constraints. The lower boundary is denoted by the vector lb = [lb1, lb2, …, lbd], and the upper boundary is represented by ub = [ub1, ub2, …, ubd].

After establishing these boundaries for the search space, the next step is to create a random number generation method. This method relies on a uniform distribution to generate sample values. Utilizing this distribution, the method assigns values to each position in every member of the population. The values are determined within the confines of the lower and upper limits as established, thereby ensuring that each population member is initialized within the specified search space. For this, the following model is employed:

(4.34)

In the context of initializing the DE algorithm’s population, the terms lb and ub refer to the vectors that define the lower and upper limits of the search space, respectively. Each element in these vectors sets the boundaries for the corresponding dimension of the problem. Alongside these, r(0, 1) represents a vector composed of random numbers. These numbers are generated within the range of 0 to 1 and follow a uniform distribution. This mechanism ensures that each member of the population is assigned initial values that are both random and constrained within the defined limits of the search space, providing a diverse and well-distributed starting point for the optimization process.

4.4.2 The Mutation Operation in DE

After completing the initialization phase, the DE algorithm proceeds to employ the mutation operator. This operator plays a crucial role in recombining population elements, thereby creating modified versions of each individual. One of the reasons for the popularity of the DE algorithm is the mathematical simplicity underlying this mutation process. It effectively allows for straightforward yet powerful manipulation of candidate solutions.

In the DE algorithm, the mutation process is specifically termed ‘differential mutation’. This designation reflects the operator’s reliance on the differences between various candidate solutions within the population. By leveraging these differences, the algorithm promotes an exchange of information among all elements, facilitating a more dynamic and effective search process.

The DE algorithm, as covered in existing literature, has seen various adaptations and improvements, particularly in the operation of the mutation operator. These enhancements often involve altering the mutation process to optimize performance in real-world applications. Section 4.6 of the referenced material will delve into the most commonly employed modifications of the mutation operator used in practical scenarios. However, the fundamental mathematical model that underpins the differential mutation in its standard form is outlined in the subsequent discussion. This model lays the foundation for understanding how differential mutation operates within the DE algorithm, setting the stage for exploring its more advanced modifications.

The basic model of differential mutation in the DE algorithm involves merging the randomly scaled difference of two population vectors with a third vector from the same population. This process results in the creation of a new entity, termed the mutant vector. Hence, the mathematical formulation of the differential mutation can be described as follows:

(4.35)

In this context, , and (r1, r2, r3 ∈ {1, 2, …, N} and r1 ≠ r2 ≠ r3 ≠ i) denote randomly chosen candidate solutions from the population. The scaling factor, F, which lies within the range [0, 2], is referred to as the differential weight. This factor plays a critical role in controlling the extent of variation based on the difference (). Essentially, the scaling factor is a numerical value that influences the rate at which the population evolves, thereby aiding in the maintenance of a balanced optimization process. A scaling value close to zero results in faster convergence of the process, whereas a higher value leads to slower convergence. The setting of this parameter is typically predetermined and varies depending on the specific requirements of the application being addressed.

By enabling the generation of a vector in a distinct area, the differential mutation operator significantly contributes to the thorough and effective exploration of the solution space, which is crucial for the overall success of the optimization process in the DE algorithm.

The DE algorithm’s various iterations primarily stem from alterations to the mutation operator. The selection criteria ensure that these solutions are different from each other, adhering to the condition r1 and r2 ∈ {1, 2, …, N} and r1 ≠ r2 ≠ i. Additionally, this strategy incorporates the vector , representing the current individual in the population undergoing the mutation operation, and the vector , which signifies the best-performing member of the population in iteration k.

This mutation strategy, by taking into account two random elements from the population, manages to maintain a certain level of diversity within the population. The differential aspect of the operation, which is the difference between the best individual () and the current individual (), drives the convergence toward the best individual. This approach ensures that the algorithm steadily moves toward an optimal solution.

However, a challenge arises with this strategy when a significant number of individuals cluster around the best individual, potentially leading to a reduction in population diversity. This concentration in the vicinity of the best solution can limit the algorithm’s ability to explore new and diverse areas of the search space. As a result, while this strategy is effective in converging toward the best solution, it needs to be balanced with mechanisms that ensure continued exploration and avoid the risk of stagnation in local optima, thus maintaining the overall health and diversity of the population. This mutation is implemented as follows:

(4.40)

4.4.3 The Crossover Operation in DE

The crossover operation in the DE algorithm serves a pivotal role, primarily aimed at enhancing the diversity of each solution vector. This operation acts as a complement to the mutation strategy, effectively contributing to an increase in the overall diversity of the population. In the crossover process, the mutant vector vk and the individual from the population are subjected to a recombination procedure. This procedure involves an element-to-element exchange between the two vectors. During this exchange, elements from the mutant vector vk and the individual are combined to form a new vector, referred to as the trial vector uk. The creation of this trial vector through crossover ensures that new genetic material is introduced into the population, which helps in exploring new regions of the search space and prevents the population from converging prematurely on local optima. By continuously introducing such variations, the crossover operation plays a crucial role in maintaining a healthy level of genetic diversity within the population, which is essential for the effective search and optimization capabilities of the DE algorithm. This procedure is computed based on the following framework:

(4.41)

In this context, jrand(0,1) ∈ {1, 2, …, d} signifies a specific position within the i-th solution vector. The term rand(0,1) is used to denote a randomly selected number that falls within the uniform distribution range of (0,1). The crossover rate, denoted as CR, is a crucial parameter in this process, governing the extent to which the mutant vector vk influences the formation of the trial vector uk. As a key configuration parameter of the DE algorithm, the crossover rate CR is assigned a value that lies within the range [0, 1]. This parameter plays a significant role in balancing the contribution of the mutant vector to the trial vector, thereby impacting the diversity and exploration capabilities of the DE algorithm.

In the crossover phase of the DE algorithm, there is a random exchange of positions between the individual vector from the population and the mutant vector vk, as formulated in Eq. 4.35. The crossover rate, denoted as CR, acts as a probabilistic factor in this process. It determines which positions from the mutant vector vk are to be incorporated into the creation of the trial vector uk, and which positions will be retained from the individual vector .

The decision of whether to use a parameter from the mutant vector vk or the individual’s vector in forming the trial vector uk is based on the outcome of a random number generator, rand(0,1). If this randomly generated number is less than or equal to the CR value, then the corresponding parameter for the trial vector uk is taken from the mutant vector vk. Conversely, if the random number exceeds the CR value, the parameter for uk is derived from the individual’s vector . This method of selectively combining elements from both the mutant and individual vectors introduces a strategic level of variability and diversity in the population, which is essential for the efficient exploration and optimization capabilities of the DE algorithm.

Figure 4.24 serves as a visual aid to demonstrate the crossover operation involved in the mutation process of the DE algorithm, particularly as outlined in Eq. 4.39. The figure illustrates the interaction between the parameter vector and the mutant vector vk. Notably, both vectors are situated within a 5-dimensional space (d = 5). Each position within these vectors is symbolized by boxes aligned next to the labels corresponding to each vector.

In this depicted example, the creation of the trial vector uk is influenced by both and vk. Specifically, the first (j = 1) and fourth (j = 4) positions of the trial vector uk are derived from the parameter vector , whereas the second (j = 2), third (j = 3), and fifth (j = 5) positions are sourced from the mutant vector vk. The arrows in the figure represent the evaluation process described in Eq. 4.41. During this process, if a randomly generated value falls below the crossover probability CR, the corresponding parameter value for the trial vector uk is taken from the mutant vector vk. If the random value exceeds the CR threshold, the parameter is instead sourced from the individual’s vector .

This graphical representation effectively depicts how the crossover operation blends elements from both the individual and mutant vectors to form the trial vector uk. This process of selective combination and exchange is critical for introducing new genetic material and variations into the population, a key factor in the DE algorithm’s ability to explore and optimize within multidimensional solution spaces.

4.4.4 The Selection Operation in DE

The selection operation in the DE algorithm is crucial for ensuring that the best solutions are retained within the population throughout the optimization process. After the mutation and crossover operations have been performed, the newly formed test vector uk emerges as a potential candidate for inclusion in the population. However, its incorporation is contingent upon meeting a specific quality selection criterion.

This selection process evaluates whether the test vector uk offers an improvement over its predecessor. The criterion for this evaluation involves comparing the fitness values of the test vector uk and the existing individual it is poised to replace. The fitness of each vector is a measure of its solution quality. The decision rule is straightforward: if the fitness value of the test vector f(uk) is superior (which typically means lower in optimization problems) to the fitness of the current individual , then uk will supplant in the population for the subsequent generation. On the other hand, if the test vector does not demonstrate a better fitness value, the existing individual will retain its position in the population for at least another generation.

This selection mechanism plays a pivotal role in the DE algorithm, as it ensures that only improvements or equally competent solutions are carried forward. This approach is essential for the continuous improvement and evolution of the population toward the optimal solution, maintaining the overall quality and efficacy of the population across generations. This selection process is encapsulated in the equation presented below:

(4.42)

In this context, f() denotes the objective function that the algorithm aims to optimize. This selection procedure is methodically repeated in every generation of the algorithm and continues until a predefined stopping criterion is met. Typically, the stopping criterion most frequently employed is the maximum number of generations, Kmax, which is determined by the user at the outset of the optimization process.

4.4.5 Implementation of DE in MATLAB

Code 4.1 showcases the implementation of the DE algorithm in MATLAB®, following the procedural guidelines detailed in Section 4.2. To demonstrate the DE algorithm’s operation, Code 4.1 incorporates a test function commonly utilized in assessing optimization methods, known as the sphere function. This function is characterized by its unimodal, convex, and multidimensional surface. It possesses a singular global minimum at the zero position of each dimension that constitutes the function’s surface. The function’s multidimensional nature serves as a testbed to examine the scaling effects of a metaheuristic algorithm’s operators in high-dimensional environments. Furthermore, the sphere function’s continuous and convex features suggest that nearly all optimization techniques, both classical and evolutionary, can reach the global optimum relatively easily.

The DE algorithm operates with a population size of 50 individuals (N = 50) and the iterative process is designed to cease when it reaches a maximum of 1000 iterations (kmax = 1000). In order to visually demonstrate the behavior of individuals on the sphere function’s surface, the movement of these individuals is plotted in each iteration. This aspect of the implementation is crucial for allowing users to observe the algorithm’s performance in real time. Consequently, the DE algorithm is tested within a two-dimensional search space (d = 2), making it easier to visualize and comprehend the dynamics of the algorithm and the effectiveness of its various operators in navigating and optimizing within the specified search space.

Program 4.18 Implementation of the DE method by Using MATLAB.

%Algorithm 4.18
% Implementation of the DE algorithm
    %% Clearing memory and closing Matlab windows
    clear all 
    close all 
% The function to be optimized, in this case, the sphere
function is considered.
fitness = @(xi) (xi(1)∧2) + (xi(2)∧2);
Kmax = 1000;
N = 50;
F = 0.2;
CR = 0.5;
dim = 2;
lb = -100;
ub = 100;
% Initialization of the population
if size(ub,2)==1
    X=rand(N,dim).*(ub-lb)+lb;
end
if size(ub,2)>1
    for j = 1:N
        for i=1:dim
            high=ub(i);down=lb(i);
            X(j,i)=rand(1,1).*(high-down)+down;
        end
    end
end
% The fitness values of the initial population are obtained.
for i = 1:N
    fitnessX(i,1) = fitness(X(i,:));
end
% The best overall individual is obtained
[fitnessXbest,Index] = min(fitnessX);
xBest = X(Index,:);
% The values are obtained to plot the function
 if dim<=2
        rango=ub-lb;
        figure(1) 
        x1=[lb:rango/100:ub];
        y1=x1;
        [X1,Y1]=meshgrid(x1,y1);
        [row1,col1]=size(X1);
        for q=1:col1
            for hh=1:row1
                zz(hh,q)=fitness([X1(hh,q),Y1(hh,q)]);
            end
        end
 end
 evaluations = 1;
% Iterative process of the algorithm
    while (evaluations <= Kmax)
        for i = 1:N
            
            Indexes = randperm(N);
        a = Indexes(1);        
        b = Indexes(2);        
        c = Indexes(3);        
        %Mutation
        v = X(c,:) + F * (X(a,:) - X(b,:));
               
        if size(ub,2)==1
            for it = 1:dim
                if (v(it) < lb)
                    v(it) = lb;
                end
                if (v(it)> ub)
                    v(it) = ub;
                end
            end
        end
        if size(ub,2)> 1 
            for it = 1:dim
                high=ub(it);down=lb(it);
                if (v(it) < down)
                    v(it) = down;
                end
                if (v(it)> high)
                    v(it) = high;
                end
            end  
        end
             %Crossover
           u=zeros(1,dim);
        j0 = randi([1 dim]);
        for j=1:dim
            if j==j0 || rand<= CR
                u(j)=v(j);
            else
                u(j)=X(i,j);
            end
        end
        % The fitness of the i-th vector is obtained
        fitnessI = fitness(X(i,:));
        % The fitness of the test vector u
        fitnessU = fitness(u);
        % The selection operation is performed
        if fitnessU < fitnessI
            X(i,:) = u;
            if fitnessU < fitnessXbest
                fitnessXbest = fitnessU;
                xBest = u;
            end
        end
    end
    % Current population graph
    if dim <= 2
        surf(X1,Y1,zz);
        hold on
        for iStruct = 1 : N
            plot(X(iStruct,1),X(iStruct,2),...
                'o','markersize',6,'markerfacecolor','r');
        end
        plot(xBest(1),xBest(2),...
        'o','markersize',10,'markerfacecolor','g');
        drawnow;
        hold off
    end
    evaluations = evaluations + 1;
    fprintf('Iteration: %d\n',evaluations);
    end
 fprintf('Best agent: (%d,%d)\n',xBest(1),xBest(2));
 fprintf('Best fitness: %d\n',fitnessXbest);

 The differential evolution (DE) algorithm holds significant potential in the realm of machine learning, primarily as an efficient tool for optimizing complex models, such as neural networks, and fine-tuning hyperparameters. Its ability to navigate multi-dimensional search spaces makes it well-suited for tasks like feature selection and model optimization, which are integral to machine learning workflows. Conversely, machine learning techniques can greatly enhance the DE method itself. For instance, machine learning models can be employed to predict the performance of different parameter combinations in DE, thereby reducing the computational load. They can also be used to adaptively adjust DE’s control parameters in real-time, based on the learning from previous iterations. This symbiotic relationship between DE and machine learning techniques not only amplifies the effectiveness of DE in solving complex optimization problems but also opens up innovative ways to leverage machine learning for algorithmic improvements, leading to more robust and efficient optimization processes.

5
Metaheuristic Techniques for Fine-Tuning Parameter of Complex Systems

5.1 Introduction

The nature of all real problems in engineering and the real world tends to the nonlinearity. Moreover, to analyze and control them is necessary to define the model that represents such a problem or plant. On the other hand, determining the model that represents a specific problem to be treated becomes a titanic task that usually is not feasible. Under such considerations, alternative models can represent the response of several problems and plants which can be highly difficult to approximate (Piroddi et al. 2012). The adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) (Jang 1993) is a suitable type of flexible network for nonlinear systems that has acquired notoriety as a soft computing approach that combines the strengths of two areas of artificial intelligence, the learning capability of adaptive networks through the partial truth reasoning of the Fuzzy system Takagi-Sugeno (Takagi and Sugeno 1985), and the inference employing Fuzzy procedure to obtain an accurate and generalization relationship of input and output pairs.

ANFIS and similar approaches contain in their structure optimizers which are responsible for determining the internal parameters that better fit the system or plant to be approximated. Nevertheless, in many cases, these optimizers cannot perform proper parameter tuning due to their own structure limitations which commonly present different flaws in their search strategy. As an efficient alternative, different authors report in the literature different modifications to the main structures of these approaches in which metaheuristic techniques are considered to improve the fine-tuning of the internal parameters considering their good performance in several complex applications.

5.2 Differential Evolution (DE)

Differential Evolution (DE) is one of the most famous optimization approaches due to its capabilities for determining competitive solutions to complex problems and its relatively simple implementation. DE was proposed by Storn and Price (1997) which is based on the difference between two elements represented as vectors and corresponding to points 7 and 9 as is shown in Figure 5.1a.

Once the distance is determined, it is scaled and added to a third vector randomly selected (in the graphical representation is considered as the element 5) where the scaling factor is represented as F and indicates the magnitude of the difference between elements that is considered to add to the third vector in order to generate a fourth vector known as a mutant vector as can be seen in Figure 5.1b. Finally, in Figure 5.2 the new mutant vector is evaluated using a cost function showing a better quality than element 1 which means that the new element replaces element 1 in the optimization process.

As typical optimization approaches, the population of the DE is represented as a set of N vectors (elements) in which the parameters are defined on the d-dimensional real values search space. Computationally, the population is symbolized by and is formed by a set of vectors where each vector represents a position in the d-dimensional vectoral space . These parameter vectors are manipulated by the DE operators: mutation, crossover, and selection through the optimization process at each iteration k for determining the global solution. The operators employed in the search strategy by the DE are described below.

5.2.1 Mutation

Once the initialization is performed (randomly) the mutation is employed to change the elements into the population to generate a modified population version. This modification is better known as differential mutation because it is based on the difference between vectors promoting the information exchange. The differential mutation is computed as follows:

(5.1)

where , , and (being , , and ) are the vectors randomly selected while is known as the differential weight which adjusts the magnitude regarding the difference between . Equation 5.1 shows the most common combination of three vectors randomly selected from the population to generate a fourth element (vector). Nevertheless, different variations mainly are focused on the operator of the DE that can generate distinct behavior in the mutation stage modifying the search strategy. It is worth mentioning that the mutation Eq. 5.1 is also known as Mutation rand/1. To exemplify the different options of mutation operators, the most used mutation operators are briefly described below.

5.2.1.1 Mutation Best/1

(5.2)

In this strategy, the elements and (, and ) are randomly selected from the population, and is the best element of the iteration k. This mutation increases the convergence rate to the optimal solution but decreases the population diversity which generates that the candidate solutions could be attracted to local solutions.

5.2.1.2 Mutation Rand/2

(5.3)

In this variation on the mutation operator, five vectors are considered to generate a sixth element where and (, and ) are randomly selected from the population. This mutation is appropriate when the dimensionality of the problem to be treated is high due to increases in the diversity by considering more elements for generating the mutant vector.

5.2.1.3 Mutation Best/2

(5.4)

In this strategy, four elements randomly selected are considered under the same restrictions as the last variations. This modification is useful in problems with a nature multimodal in which a fast convergence into the global solution is required maintaining the information between elements increasing the diversity of the population.

5.2.1.4 Mutation Current-to-Best/1

(5.5)

This mutation considers and (, and ) randomly selected from the population, is the current element that is being modified by the operator, and is the best element at iteration k. Considering that just two elements are randomly selected, the diversity remains in a certain grade but as the difference is regarding the best element the convergence is guaranteed in the best current element.

5.2.2 Crossover

The crossover operator has the main objective of increasing the diversity of the population. This operation complements the mutation to balance the exploration and exploitation in the search strategy. In this stage, the elements and combine their information to generate a new element and is described as follows.

(5.6)

where represents one of the positions of the i-th vector and is a normally distributed random number between the interval (0,1). The parameter CR controls the balance between the exploration and exploitation which determines if the operator of mutation or the crossover is performed.

5.2.3 Selection

This stage determines whether a solution can be considered as part of the population, for this purpose an elitist selection is carried out, in this process, it is considered if the last element is replaced by the new mutant vector or remains. To determine which element is replaced, a cost function is employed where the new mutant vector is evaluated as well as the current element , if the fitness value of the new element is better than the current vector is replaced, otherwise remains. To determine the candidate solution to be selected the following expression is employed. For a better understanding of the complete functioning of the DE, the flowchart in the Figure 5.3

For a better understanding of the main functioning of the DE, Algorithm 5.1 presents step-by-step the optimization process over a well-known test function called the sphere function which exhibits unimodal surface, convex, and multidimensional characteristics. Under such conditions, the cost function has just one minimum in zero. In step 1 the function to be optimized is declared, considering that the optimization process is going to be plotted the example must contemplate two dimensions. Step two sets the maximum number of iterations, population size, dimensions number, and DE parameters. In the DE just two parameters are needed, the CR which represents the threshold value between the mutation and crossover, and the F which represents the scaling factor in the mutation stage. In steps 3 and 4 the population is initialized employing a uniform distribution and the fitness value is computed respectively.

After evaluating the population, a memory is generated to store the fitness values and their positions. The best element of each iteration is stored for visualizing the evolution of the optimization process. In step 5 the iterative process of the search strategy where three vectors are randomly selected and the mutation and crossover are performed, at the same time the limits of each particle are verified considering the lower and upper bounds. Step 6 determines by an elitist selection the elements that are able to shape the next population.

 

%Algorithm 5.1

clear all
close all
 
 
%Step 1, The problem to be optimized is defined (Sphere function)
fitness = @(xi) (xi(1)∧2) + (xi(2)∧2);
 
 
% Step 2, DE parameters declaration
Kmax = 100;
N = 50;
F = 0.2;
CR = 0.5;
dim = 2;
 
 
% Stet 3, randomly initialization of the vectors (elements) between

ub = 100;

   X=rand(N,dim).*(ub-lb)+lb;
end
if size(ub,2)>1
   for j = 1:N
       for i=1:dim
           high=ub(i);down=lb(i);
           X(j,i)=rand(1,1).*(high-down)+down;
      end
   end
end
 
 
% Step 4, evaluation of the population using the cost function
for i = 1:N
    fitnessX(i,1) = fitness(X(i,:));
end
 
 
% Save the best element and they fitness in memory
[BestfitnessX,index] = min(fitnessX);
xBest = X(index,:);
 
 
%Plotting the particles in the iteration process
if dim<=2
        rango=ub-lb;
       figure(1) % Plotting current population
       x1=[lb:rango/100:ub];

       [X1,Y1]=meshgrid(x1,y1);
       [row1,col1]=size(X1);
       for q=1:col1
           for hh=1:row1
               zz(hh,q)=fitness([X1(hh,q),Y1(hh,q)]);
           end
       end
end
eval = 1;
  
%Step 5, iterative process of the optimization
while (eval <= Kmax)
     for i = 1:N
% Three vectors randomly selected, mutant vector generation
         index = randperm(N);
         a = index(1);
         b = index(2);
         c = index(3);

               end

                  v(it) = high;
               end
            end
         end
%Crossover

            if j==j0 || rand<= CR
               u(j)=v(j);
            else
               u(j)=X(i,j);
            end
        end
     
%Cost function evaluation to the population and the test vector

%Step 6, Elitist selection is performed
    if fitnessU < fitnessI
            X(i,:) = u;

          BestfitnessX = fitnessU;

end
 
 
%Plotting the current iteration

eval = eval + 1;
fprintf('Iteration: %d\n',eval);
end
 
 
%Step 7, Display the best vector and its fitness value

fprintf('Best fitness: %d\n',BestfitnessX);

(5.17)
(5.18)

In the same scheme, the expression 5.18 is employed for determining the actual premise values and the backpropagation errors, where is the current member function in layer 1 while , , , and are the new premise values for each member function. Under these considerations, the DE is employed in this stage to improve the strategy of determining these values. As mentioned before, to perform the optimization method is necessary to determine a quality metric of solutions achieved by the DE, in this case, the cost function used to measure the feasible solutions is described below (section A3 Figure 5.6).

(5.19)

where and are the previous number of inputs and the number of member functions respectively. The subindexes i and j represent the current node and the parameters of the respective member function and is the backpropagation error while is the value of the cost function. Once the premise parameters of layer 1 are determined, the consequent values of layer 4 are modified considering the backpropagation error and the proposed consequence values from nodes of layers 1 and 4.

Section A4 shows that the backward pass process finishes; and the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) is determined by the current epoch considering the difference between the output of the hybridization of the ANFIS model and the actual sample of the database. Subsequently, the premise values are updated in order to know the evolution of the optimization process at each epoch employing the following expression.

(5.20)

where and represent the current updated and estimated premise parameters, is the step size which is determined by the user in the initialization of the problem, and ℓ is the square root sum of difference from the premise values. In Algorithm 5.2 the hybridization of the ANFIS model and DE approach are performed. In step 1, the initial parameter setting of the ANFIS model, and the dataset used for this experiment are declared. Once the initial parameters are configured by the user, the main structure of the ANFIS model and the network generation is performed in step 2, in this specific example the number of iterations and epochs are considered as 35 and 100 respectively. After step 2 in the function declaration, the complete structure configuration of the ANFIS model is constructed. In step 3, the complete training process where basically two main inter steps are performed; the DE optimization method, and the Kalman filter technique in which the premise and consequent parameters are achieved in the complete process. Finally, in step 4 the test of the trained model is performed, and the process is ended. The approximation test of the trained model is shown in Figure 5.7.

 

%Algorithm 5.2
%Clean data
clear all
close all
 
 
%% Step 1, ANFIS data initialization and dataset uploading
mf=2;
step_size=0.1;
decrease_rate=0.9;
increase_rate=1.1;
 
 
Dataset='datos_prom.xlsx';
data=xlsread(Dataset);
Sdata=data;
aux=[data(:,1:4) data(:,end)];
 
 
data=aux;
 
 
Irun=1;
Frun=35;
 
 
%% Step2, Main ANFIS structure
while Irun<=Frun
    if Irun>1
        fprintf('\n\n')
    end
    disp(['Run
',num2str(Irun),'______________________________________'])
 
 
    epoch_n=100;
 
 
%Step 3, Complete ANFIS training and optimization process
[bestnet,RMSE]=myanfis(data,epoch_n,mf,step_size,...
decrease_rate,increase_rate);
 
 
%Step 4, Evaluation of the training model.
 y_myanfis=evalmyanfis(bestnet,data(:,1:end-1));
 
 
    if Irun==1
        Net.M1_RMSE=zeros(epoch_n,Frun);
        Net.M1_ANFIS=zeros(size(data,1),Frun);
    end
 
 
    Net.M1_RMSE(:,Irun)=RMSE;
    Net.M1_ANFIS(:,Irun)=y_myanfis;
 
 
    if Irun==Frun
        Net.M1_config=bestnet.config;
        Net.M1_mparam=bestnet.mparams;
        Net.M1_kparams=bestnet.kparams;
        Net.M1_Premisa=bestnet.Premisa;
        Net.M1_Consecuente=bestnet.Consecuente;
    end
 
 
    Irun=Irun+1;
end
 
 
% Functions declaration
%% MyANFIS configuration construction.
function [bestnet,RMSE] = 
myanfis(data,epoch_n,mf,step_size,decrease_rate,increase_rate)
inputs=data(:,1:end-1);
output=data(:,end);
ndata=size(data,1);
 
 
mn=min(inputs);
mx=max(inputs);
mm=mx-mn;
ni=size(inputs,2);
nc=mf∧ni;
Node_n = ni + ni*mf + 3*nc + 1;
 
 
min_RMSE=999999999999;
mparams=[];
kparams=zeros(nc,(ni+1));
 
 
for i=1:ni
    tmp=linspace(mn(1),mx(1),mf)';
    mparams=[mparams;repmat([mm(i)/6 2],mf,1) tmp];
end
 
 
mynet.Premisa=mparams;
config=zeros(Node_n);
nodes=zeros(Node_n,1);
 
 
st=ni;
for i=1:ni
    config(i,st+[1:mf])=1;
    st=st+mf;
end
 
 
st=ni+ni*mf+1;
if size(inputs,2)==2
    for i=1:mf
        for j=1:mf
            config(ni+i,st)=1;
            config(ni+mf+j,st)=1;
            st=st+1;
        end
    end
elseif size(inputs,2)==3
    for i=1:mf
        for j=1:mf
            for k=1:mf
                config(ni+i,st)=1;
                config(ni+mf+j,st)=1;
                config(ni+2*mf+k,st)=1;
                st=st+1;
            end
        end
    end
elseif size(inputs,2)==4
    for i=1:mf
        for j=1:mf
            for k=1:mf
                for l=1:mf
                    config(ni+i,st)=1;
                    config(ni+mf+j,st)=1;
                    config(ni+2*mf+k,st)=1;
                    config(ni+3*mf+l,st)=1;
                    st=st+1;
                end
            end
        end
    end
elseif size(inputs,2)==5
    for i=1:mf
        for j=1:mf
            for k=1:mf
                for l=1:mf
                    for m=1:mf
                        config(ni+i,st)=1;
                        config(ni+mf+j,st)=1;
                        config(ni+2*mf+k,st)=1;
                        config(ni+3*mf+l,st)=1;
                        config(ni+4*mf+m,st)=1;
                        st=st+1;
                    end
                end
            end
        end
    end
else
    return;
end
 
 
for i=1:nc
    for j=1:nc
        config(ni+ni*mf+i,ni+ni*mf+nc+j)=1;
    end
end
 
 
for i=1:nc
    config(ni+ni*mf+nc+i,ni+ni*mf+2*nc+i)=1;
end
 
 
for i=1:nc
    config(ni+ni*mf+2*nc+i,end)=1;
end
 
 
for i=1:ni
    for j=1:nc
        config(i,ni+ni*mf+2*nc+j)=1;
    end
end
 
 
mynet.config=config;
mynet.mparams=mparams;
mynet.kparams=kparams;
mynet.nodes=nodes;
mynet.ni=ni;
mynet.mf=mf;
mynet.nc=nc;
mynet.last_decrease_ss=1;
mynet.last_increase_ss=1;
 
 
%% Layer from 1 to 3 construction and the epochs staring
layer_1_to_3_output=zeros(Node_n,ni+1);
for iter=1:epoch_n
    for j=1:ndata
        mynet.nodes(1:mynet.ni)=inputs(j,:)';
 
 
        mynet=calculate_output1(mynet);
        mynet=calculate_output2(mynet);
        mynet=calculate_output3(mynet);
 
 
        layer_1_to_3_output(:,j)=mynet.nodes;
 
 
        kalman_data=get_kalman_data(mynet,output(j));
        mynet=mykalman(mynet,kalman_data,j);
 
 
        if j==1 && iter==1
            mynet.Consecuente=kparams;
        end
    end
 
 
    mynet.mparam_de_do=zeros(mynet.ni*mynet.mf,3);
    mynet.kparam_de_do=zeros(mynet.nc,mynet.ni+1);
 
 
    for j=1:ndata
        mynet.nodes=layer_1_to_3_output(:,j);
 
 
        mynet=calculate_output4(mynet);
        mynet.nodes(end)=sum( mynet.nodes(end-mynet.nc:end-1));
 
 
        anfis_output(j,1)=mynet.nodes(end);
        target=output(j);
        de_dout = -2*(target - anfis_output(j,1));
 
 
        mynet=calculate_de_do(mynet,de_dout);
        mynet=update_de_do(mynet);
    end
 
 
    diff=anfis_output-output;
    [tse]=es_lev(anfis_output,output);
    total_squared_error=tse;
    RMSE(iter,1) = sqrt(total_squared_error/ndata);
 
 
    if rem(iter,10)==0 && rem(iter,50)∼=0
        fprintf('* ')
    elseif rem(iter,10)==0 && rem(iter,50)==0
        fprintf('*\n')
    else
        fprintf('*')
    end
 
 
    if RMSE(iter,1)<min_RMSE
        bestnet=mynet;
        min_RMSE=RMSE(iter,1);
    end
 
 
    tmp=mynet.mparam_de_do;
    tmp=tmp.*tmp;
    len=sqrt(sum(tmp(:)));
    mynet.mparams=mynet.mparams - step_size * ...
        mynet.mparam_de_do/len;
 
 
    [mynet step_size]=update_step_size(mynet,RMSE,iter,... 
         step_size,decrease_rate,increase_rate);
end
end
 
 
%% Calculation of the output 1
function mynet=calculate_output1(mynet)
 
 
mparams=mynet.mparams;
for i=1:mynet.ni
    for j=1:mynet.mf
 
 
        ind=mynet.ni+(i-1)*mynet.mf+j;
 
 
        x = mynet.nodes(i);                   % Input node i
        a = mparams((i-1)*mynet.mf+j,1);
        b = mparams((i-1)*mynet.mf+j,2);
        c = mparams((i-1)*mynet.mf+j,3);
 
 
        tmp1 = (x - c)/a;
        if tmp1 == 0
            tmp2=0;
        else
            tmp2 = (tmp1*tmp1)∧b;
        end
        mynet.nodes(ind)=1/(1+ tmp2);
    end
end
end
 
 
%% Calculation of the output 2
function mynet=calculate_output2(mynet)
 
 
st=mynet.ni+mynet.ni*mynet.mf;
 
 
for i=st+1:st+mynet.nc
    I=find(mynet.config(:,i)==1);         % Find nodes of layer 2
    tmp=cumprod(mynet.nodes(I));
    mynet.nodes(i)=tmp(end);
end
end
 
 
%% Calculation of the output 3
function mynet=calculate_output3(mynet)
 
 
st=mynet.ni+mynet.ni*mynet.mf +mynet.nc ;
 
 
for i=st+1:st+mynet.nc
    I=find(mynet.config(:,i)==1);
    denom=sum(mynet.nodes(I));
    mynet.nodes(i)=mynet.nodes(i-mynet.nc)/denom;
end
end
 
 
%% Calculation of the output 4
function mynet=calculate_output4(mynet)
 
 
st=mynet.ni+mynet.ni*mynet.mf +2*mynet.nc ;
inp=mynet.nodes(1:mynet.ni)';
kparam=mynet.kparams;
 
 
for i=1:mynet.nc
    mynet.nodes(i+st)=wn*...
         (sum(kparam(i,1:end-1).*inp)+ ...
         Kparam(i,end));
end
end
 
 
%% Obtaining the Kalman data (Deterministic approach)
function kalman_data=get_kalman_data(mynet,target)
 
 
kalman_data=zeros((mynet.ni+1)*mynet.nc+1,1);
st=mynet.ni+mynet.ni*mynet.mf +mynet.nc ;
 
 
j=1;
for i=st+1:st+mynet.nc
    for k=1:mynet.ni
        kalman_data(j)=mynet.nodes(i)*mynet.nodes(k);
        j=j+1;
    end
    kalman_data(j)=mynet.nodes(i);
    j=j+1;
end
 
 
kalman_data(j)=target;
end
 
 
%% Performing Kalman method
function mynet=mykalman(mynet,kalman_data,j)
 
 
k_p_n= (mynet.ni+1)*mynet.nc;
alpha = 1000000;
 
 
if j==1
    mynet.P=zeros(k_p_n,1);
    mynet.S=alpha*eye(k_p_n);
end
 
 
x=kalman_data(1:end-1);
y=kalman_data(end);
 
 
tmp1=(x'*mynet.S)';
denom=1+sum(tmp1.*x);
tmp2=(mynet.S*x);
 
 
tmp_m=tmp2*tmp1';
tmp_r=-1/denom*tmp_m;
mynet.S=mynet.S+tmp_r;
 
 
diff=y-sum(x.*mynet.P);
tmp3=diff*(mynet.S*x);
mynet.P=mynet.P+tmp3;
mynet.kparams=reshape(mynet.P,[mynet.ni+1 mynet.nc])';
end
 
 
%% DE optimization approach
function mynet=calculate_de_do(mynet,de_dout)
 
 
mynet.de_do=zeros(size(mynet.nodes));
mynet.de_do(end)=de_dout;
 
 
for i=length(mynet.nodes)-1:-1:mynet.ni+1
    de_do=0;
    II=find(mynet.config(i,:)==1);
    I=find(II>i);
    for j=1:length(I)
        jj=II(I(j));
        tmp1=mynet.de_do(jj);
        tmp2=derivative_o_o(mynet,i, jj);
        de_do = de_do+tmp1*tmp2;
    end
    mynet.de_do(i)=de_do;
end
end
 
 
%% Derivative function of DE
function tmp=derivative_o_o(mynet,i,j)
 
 
if i>mynet.ni+mynet.ni*mynet.mf +2*mynet.nc
    tmp=1;
elseif i>mynet.ni+mynet.ni*mynet.mf +mynet.nc
    tmp=do4_do3(mynet, j);
elseif i>mynet.ni+mynet.ni*mynet.mf
    tmp=do3_do2(mynet,i, j);
elseif i>mynet.ni
    tmp=mynet.nodes(j)/mynet.nodes(i);
end
end
 
 
%% DE operator 1
function tmp=do4_do3(mynet, j)
kparam=mynet.kparams;
inp=mynet.nodes(1:mynet.ni)';
jj=j-mynet.ni-mynet.ni*mynet.mf -2*mynet.nc;
tmp=sum(kparam(jj,1:end-1).*inp)+kparam(jj,end);
end
 
 
%% DE operator 2
function tmp=do3_do2(mynet,i, j)
II=find(mynet.config(:,j)==1);
I=find(II<j);
total=sum(mynet.nodes(II(I)));
if j-i==mynet.nc
    tmp=(total-mynet.nodes(i))/(total*total);
else
    tmp=-mynet.nodes(j-mynet.nc)/(total*total);
end
end
 
 
%% Update DE information
function [mynet] = update_de_do(mynet)
 
 
s=1;
for i=mynet.ni+1:mynet.ni+mynet.ni*mynet.mf
    for j=1:3
        I=find(mynet.config(:,i)==1);
        x=mynet.nodes(I);
        a=mynet.mparams(i-mynet.ni,1);
        b=mynet.mparams(i-mynet.ni,2);
        c=mynet.mparams(i-mynet.ni,3);
        tmp1 = (x - c)/a;
        if tmp1==0
            tmp2=0;
        else
            tmp2 = (tmp1*tmp1)∧b;
        end
        denom = (1 + tmp2)*(1 + tmp2);
        if j==1
            do_dp=(2*b*tmp2/(a*denom));
        elseif j==2 && tmp1==0
            do_dp=0;
        elseif j==2 && tmp1∼=0
            do_dp=(-log(tmp1*tmp1)*tmp2/denom);
        elseif j==3 && x==c
            do_dp=0;
        elseif j==3 && x∼=c
            do_dp=(2*b*tmp2/((x - c)*(denom)));
        end
 
 
        mynet.mparam_de_do(s,j)=...
             mynet.mparam_de_do(s,j)+... 
             mynet.de_do(i)*do_dp;
    end
    s=s+1;
end
 
 
s=1;
 
 
for i=1+mynet.ni+mynet.ni*mynet.mf+2*mynet.nc:size(mynet.config)-1
    for j=1:mynet.ni+1
        wn=mynet.nodes(i-mynet.nc);
        inp=mynet.nodes(1:mynet.ni)';
        inp=[inp 1];
        do_dp=wn*inp(j);
        mynet.kparam_de_do(s,j)=...
             mynet.kparam_de_do(s,j)+...
             mynet.de_do(i)*do_dp;
    end
    s=s+1;
end
end
 
 

 
%% Difference between ANFIS output and current sample
function[tse]=es_lev(anfis_output,output)
step=0.1;
instep=0;
F=0.8;
ngen=100;
cr=1-F;
pop=100;
dim=size(anfis_output,1);
 
 
x=instep+(step-instep).*rand(pop,dim);
x=x';
 
 
for i=1:dim
    for j=1:pop
        if x(i,j)<instep
            x(i,j)=instep;
        elseif x(i,j)>step
            x(i,j)=step;
        end
    end
end
 
 
Diff=zeros(dim,1);
lev=zeros(1,pop);
nlev=lev;
 
 
for i=1:pop
    for j=1:dim
        Diff(j,1)=x(j,i)+anfis_output(j,1);
    end
    diff=Diff-output;
    error=sum(diff.*diff);
    lev(1,i)=error;
end
 
 
x=x';
lev=lev';
gen=1;
 
 
while ngen<=gen
    for i=1:pop
        A=randperm(pop);
        r1=x(A(1),:);
        r2=x(A(2),:);
        r3=x(A(3),:);
 
 
        Pmut=r3+F*(r1-r2);
        for j=1:dim
            if Pmut(1,j)<instep
                Pmut(1,j)=instep;
            elseif Pmut(1,j)>step
                Pmut(1,j)=step;
            end
        end
        Pcros=zeros(1,dim);
 
 
        for j=1:dim
            aux=rand();
            if aux<cr
                Pcros(1,j)=Pmut(1,j);
            else
                Pcros(1,j)=x(i,j);
            end
        end
 
 
        Pcros=Pcros';
        for j=1:dim
            Diff(j,1)=Pcros(j,1)+anfis_output(j,1);
        end
 
 
        diff=Diff-output;
        error=sum(diff.*diff);
        nlev(1,i)=error;
        lev=lev';
        x=x';
        if nlev(i,1)<lev(i,1)
            x(:,i)=Pcros(:,1);
            lev(1,i)=nlev(1,i);
        end
 
 
        x=x';
        lev=lev';
    end
    gen=gen+1;
end
tse=min(lev);
end
 
 
%% Evaluation of the proposed ANFIS_DE
function yhat=evalmyanfis(mynet,inputs)
 
 
ndata=size(inputs,1);
 
 
for j=1:ndata
    mynet.nodes(1:mynet.ni)=inputs(j,:)';
    mynet=calculate_output1(mynet);
    mynet=calculate_output2(mynet);
    mynet=calculate_output3(mynet);
    mynet=calculate_output4(mynet);
    mynet.nodes(end)=sum( mynet.nodes(end-mynet.nc:end-1));
    yhat(j,1)=mynet.nodes(end);
end
end
 
 
%% Update the stepsize of DE
function [mynet step_size]=...
    update_step_size(mynet,error_array,iter,...
    step_size,decrease_rate,increase_rate)
 
 
if check_decrease_ss(error_array, mynet.last_decrease_ss, iter)
    step_size = step_size*decrease_rate;
      mynet.last_decrease_ss = iter;
elseif check_increase_ss(error_array, mynet.last_increase_ss, iter)
    step_size = step_size*increase_rate;
      mynet.last_increase_ss = iter;
end
end
 
 
function sts=check_decrease_ss(error_array, last_change, current)
if (current - last_change < 4)
      sts=false;
elseif ((error_array(current)     < error_array(current - 1)) && ...
         (error_array(current - 1)> error_array(current - 2)) && ...
         (error_array(current - 2) < error_array(current - 3)) && ...
        (error_array(current - 3)> error_array(current - 4)))
    sts=true;
else
    sts=false;
end
end
 
 
function sts=check_increase_ss(error_array, last_change, current)
if (current - last_change < 4)
   sts=false;
elseif ((error_array(current)     < error_array(current - 1)) && ...
         (error_array(current - 1) < error_array(current - 2)) && ...
         (error_array(current - 2) < error_array(current - 3)) && ...
         (error_array(current - 3) < error_array(current - 4)))
    sts=true;
else
    sts=false;
end
end
