  1. Jang, J.S.R. (1993). ANFIS: adaptive-network-based fuzzy inference system. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics 23 (3): 665–685. https://doi.org/10.1109/21.256541.
  2. Piroddi, L., Farina, M., and Lovera, M. (2012). Black box model identification of nonlinear input–output models: a Wiener–Hammerstein benchmark. Control Engineering Practice 20 (11): 1109–1118. https://doi.org/10.1016/J.CONENGPRAC.2012.03.002.
  3. Storn, R. and Price, K. (1997). Differential evolution—a simple and efficient heuristic for global optimization over continuous spaces. Journal of Global Optimization 341–359. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1008202821328.
  4. Takagi, T. and Sugeno, M. (1985). Fuzzy identification of systems and its applications to modeling and control. IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics SMC-15 (1): 116–132. https://doi.org/10.1109/TSMC.1985.6313399.

6
Techniques of Machine Learning for Producing Metaheuristic Operators

6.1 Introduction

Metaheuristic algorithms have been developed to solve minimization/maximization problems. Based on our scientific understanding of biological, ecological, or even social systems, a variety of metaheuristics have been proposed by scientific communities. The performance of metaheuristic method in finding an optimal solution typically depends on its capacity to achieve a suitable balance between its evolutionary stages. The exploration stage and the exploitation stage are two frequent phases of the evolutionary strategy.

Exploration stage entails inspecting new areas in the search space, whereas exploitation entails doing local searches in areas that have already been explored with the goal of enhancing the quality of the solutions. The optimization process loses accuracy when mostly exploratory work is done, but it gains the ability to identify new possible solutions over the search space. On the other hand, if exploitation is privileged, existing solutions are mostly improved. However, adversely, this fact produces that the algorithm can be trapped in local minima due to scarce exploration. Under such circumstances, a balance among these two stages is decisive for the proper functioning of the method.

Since the performance of an evolutionary computation (EC) algorithm highly depends on the balance of exploration and exploitation procedures, different combination of operators may lead to unbalance the optimization process.

To alleviate such issues researchers have suggested the combination of different metaheuristic operators for obtaining new performance levels. Recently, a large variety of approaches that do not entirely adhere to the idea of a single EC approach have been developed. These techniques associate different algorithmic structures, commonly extracted from other computation techniques. These methods have been referred as hybrid EC algorithms (Blum et al. 2008). The main goal of hybridization is to increase the performance of single EC methods by combining complementing computational techniques. The goal of hybridization is to overcome the shortcomings of each individual approach and, via their fusion, produce a synergetic result (Blum et al. 2011). The incorporation of many techniques into hybrid EC approaches enables the blending of the advantages of each method. It has been demonstrated that the appropriate selection of algorithmic elements and fusion strategies, hybrid EC methods can overtake their algorithmic elements because of their synergetic effect (Ma et al. 2014; Niknam and Azad Farsani 2010).

In the last decade, several EC algorithms have been suggested by different scientific communities for enhancing the search capabilities of original EC based on machine learning techniques, fuzzy logic, neural networks and support vector machine (Dash and Dash 2016; Illias et al. 2016). Although most of these approaches are convincing, the study and construction of new hybrid EC methods need further and extensive research.

In this chapter, two different methods are combined to produce a hybrid metaheuristic approach. The produced metaheuristic combines clustering and chaotic sequences. Clustering (Ezugwu et al. 2022) Clustering is the process of grouping together datapoints into clusters that are distinct from one another. Scarcely, the division of the population into different groups has been documented in the literature in order to alter the search mechanism for a metaheuristic algorithm. The proposed metaheuristic method uses a clustering method to divide the population into individual groups at the initial stage of the optimization process. Therefore, the proposed algorithm creates groups based on the spatial associations of datapoints without considering a fixed distance among them or a necessary number of them.

On the other hand, chaotic sequences are increasingly being used to improve existing EC approaches in order to promote population diversity by avoiding premature convergence. Chaos is recognized by its interesting stochastic characteristics (Yang et al. 2007). In order to enhance the performance of an EC approach, chaotic sequences have frequently been utilized rather than random numbers.

In this chapter, a hybrid optimization algorithm for solving optimization problems is presented. The approach, called Cluster-Chaotic-Optimization (CCO), combines the stochastic properties of chaotic sequences with the grouping capabilities of a clustering algorithm to create metaheuristic operators. In the optimization procedure, CCO divides the population into clusters according to spatial associations. Then, two different operations are computed to update the position of each datapoint. The first operation, called intra-cluster, locally explores the search space inside each cluster. This operation modifies the position of all datapoints belonging a cluster. Under such conditions, datapoints belonging to the same cluster are locally modified considering the position of best datapoint inside the cluster. The second operation, called extra-cluster, explores the entire search space among the clusters. This procedure modifies only the best datapoint inside a given cluster whereas the remaining datapoints. Hence, in the extra-cluster procedure, the best datapoint for a given cluster is attracted by the best datapoint of the entire population. In both operations, the position adjustment on each datapoint is generated by using cluster-based operations and chaotic sequences. With such hybridization, the CCO locally and globally examines the entire search space through the optimization process.

In this chapter, we delve into the concept of hierarchical clustering and chaotic sequences. The main aspects of clustering and chaotic sequences will be thoroughly examined, providing a solid foundation for understanding its application in the generation of evolutionary operators. Throughout the chapter, MATLAB will be used to implement these methodologies. This hands-on approach will enable readers to gain practical experience and become proficient in using these techniques to produce metaheuristic operators in their own projects.

6.2 Hierarchical Clustering

Clustering is one of the most used techniques to create homogeneous groups of objects or entities. For a given set of datapoints D = {x1, …, xn}, where xj ∈ Rd grouping the datapoints into X number of clusters so that similar datapoints in the clusters are close to each other. In most of the analytical projects, after the data cleaning process and preparation, clustering methods are often carried out before any analytical modeling.

Clustering falls under the category of unsupervised learning. That means there is no labeled class for a given dataset. We are only interested in grouping similar entities or objects in a cluster. In this chapter, we focus on hierarchical clustering. Hierarchical clustering constructs an association tree over the data, where tree leaves are considered as individual clusters, while the root is a single cluster which contains all the remaining datapoints. Between the tree root and the tree leaves, there are subset of clusters. The goal of hierarchical clustering is to create a series of nested partitions that can be viewed as a tree structure commonly called a dendrogram. The groups within this structure maintain a configuration such that, at the lowest level of the tree, each element represents a group while at the highest level, all points form a single group. Under these conditions, at intermediate levels of the tree, different groupings can be found, depending on the relative distances between elements. There are two schemes under the hierarchical clustering: divisive hierarchical clustering also known as a top-down clustering approach, and agglomerative hierarchical clustering also known as a bottom-up clustering approach.

In divisive clustering, the entire set of datapoints is assigned to a single cluster. Once there is one cluster, the cluster is further divided until there is one cluster for each single datapoint. On the other hand, the agglomerative process operates in the opposite way. At starting point, each single datapoint is treated as a cluster then a pair of clusters are combined until all clusters are merged into a single cluster. In this chapter, it will be focused on the agglomerative clustering for producing metaheuristic operators for exploration and exploitation stages.

6.2.1 Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering Algorithm

In this section, a detailed description of the algorithmic design of the agglomerative hierarchical clustering technique is presented. The design of the agglomerative algorithm considers each single datapoint as a cluster at the starting point then, it will combine a pair of clusters until all clusters are merged into a single big cluster. Since the agglomerative method involves a series of straightforward steps. Here are the steps for designing an agglomerative approach:

  1. Step 1: Set up Initial Clusters:

    Assign each observation as a single point cluster to begin with, so that if there are N observations, there will be N clusters, each containing a single observation.

  2. Step 2: Find Similar Pair of Clusters:

    Find the most similar pair of clusters and merge them into one cluster. (Many similarity and dissimilarity metrics can be used in this step. The metric used in this step can produced different clusters.) In this chapter, Euclidean distance is used for producing metaheuristic operators.

  3. Step 3: Merge Closest Clusters:

    Find the two closest clusters for producing one cluster. (Many linkage techniques can be used in this step. The linkage technique used in this step can produced different clusters). In this chapter, the Ward method is used for merge clusters for producing metaheuristic operators.

  4. Step 4: Repeat Steps 2 and 3 Until all Datapoints are Clustered into a Single Cluster:

 Note

The algorithmic design of an agglomerative clustering is a simple and generic scheme. For that, given a particular clustering application, the algorithm can be adjusted by modifying the Steps 2 and 3. Steps 2 and 3 are computed based on similarity indexes and linkage techniques, respectively. Similarity and dissimilarity indexes commonly refer to the relationship among datapoints by a distance measurement. These indexes indicate a way of measuring how datapoints are related or closed to each other. On the other hand, linkage techniques refers how datapoints are merge between two clusters to produce a new cluster.

In agglomerative clustering, the most used similarity and dissimilarity metrics are:

  • Euclidean distance
  • Manhattan distance
  • Minkowski distance
  • Jaccard similarity coefficient
  • Cosine similarity
  • Gowe’s similarity coefficient
  • Pearson correlation

In agglomerative clustering, the most used linkage techniques are:

  • Single linkage
  • Complete linkage
  • Average linkage
  • Centroid method
  • Ward method

In this chapter the Ward method is used for producing metaheuristic operators. Ward method is computed based on the minimization of the cluster variance. Related literature suggests the use of Ward method as the most suitable method for quantitative variables.

The previously described algorithm generates a dendrogram. A dendrogram is a tree diagram that shows the clusters and levels of similarity that result from the hierarchical clustering process at each step. The individual observations are presented along the horizontal axis, and the similarity level is measured along the vertical axis. Figure 6.1 shows an example of the structure of a dendrogram.

Selecting the final grouping for your data is called cutting the dendrogram. Cutting the dendrogram refers to draw a horizontal line (link) to specify the final grouping, different cuts determine which final grouping makes sense for the data to be clustered. In cluster analysis, to determine the natural cluster divisions the comparison among heights of each link with the heights of neighboring links is used. Commonly, to define a cutting threshold for a dendrogram the height of inconsistent links (links whose height differs noticeably from the height of the links below it is used as cutting criterion.

In Figure 6.1, it is represented an example dendrogram, where each rectangular dashed shape represents different types of cuts to form a cluster. In the figure, the first cluster is obtained by the datapoints 2 and 5. Then, the datapoint 1 is merge into the first cluster to form the second cluster. This process continues until the final cluster which corresponds to the highest hierarchical level.

The MATLAB code (in Algorithm 6.1) is presented by using the built-in functions of MATLAB as follows:

 

%Algorithm 6.1
% Step 1: Set a default random sequence generator to produce
standard random values
rng('default');
 
 
% Step 2: Set 50 datapoints, this will be the dataset
X = [(randn(50,2)*0.75)+1;
    (randn(50,2)*0.25)-1];
 
 
% Step 3: Compute distances among datapoints
Y = pdist(X,"euclidean");
 
 
% Step 4: Merge clusters using Ward method
Z = linkage(X,"ward");
 
 
% Step 5: Plot the dendrogram from the agglomerative process
figure(1)
dendrogram(Z);
 
 
% Step 6: Cut the dendrogram into 2 clusters
T = cluster(Z,'maxclust',2);
 
 
% Step 7: Plot the datapoints clustered by Step 6
figure(2)
gscatter(X(:,1),X(:,2),T)

In Algorithm 6.1, Step 1 indicates which random number generators will be used. The ’default’ instruction from rng function uses a random generator whose output will be the same at each execution of the code. This scheme is used for reproducibility purpose, so the reader can follow a generic output from the clustering process. Step 2, generates 50 datapoints in a random fashion. This datapoints will be the dataset used for clustering process. In the Step 3, all the Euclidean distances among each datapoint is computed. The output from this step, will be the input to the linkage scheme from Step 4 where the ward’s method is used to merge clusters. The plot from de dendrogram is then produced by using the built-in function dendrogram(). In Step 6, the dendrogram is cut considering a maximum number of clusters set to 2. Finally, Step 7 plots a scatterplot based on the cutting scheme from Step 6. The output of the Algorithm 6.1 can be seen in Figure 6.2.

In Figure 6.2a, the produced dendrogram from the dataset of Step 2 in the Algorithm 6.1 is shown. As it can be shown, the dendrogram associate natural associations among each datapoint, then it will merge pair of clusters until one single cluster is produced at the root of the tree. Since the Step 6 cuts the dendrogram to produced two clusters from the datapoints, Figure 6.2b shows the result scatter plot.

The agglomerative clustering process is simple to implement but powerful technique since user can define the natural division of groups. According to the characteristics of a given dataset, the user can use a cutting scheme to better model the datapoint divisions.

6.3 Chaotic Sequences

Chaos is a type of characteristic nonlinear dynamic system, which presents interesting properties such as ergodicity, pseudo-randomness, and sensibility of initial values in its control parameters. In the last decade, chaotic sequences are increasingly considered rather than random numbers in several engineering applications. Recently, many researchers have adopted the use of chaotic sequences for producing metaheuristic operators. In engineering optimization methods, the use of randomness can be replaced by a chaotic sequence to improve their performance. Related literature reveals that the experimental analysis of several metaheuristic methods performs better chaotic sequences rather than random numbers (Huang et al. 2016; Snaselova and Zboril 2015).

The simplest systems that can generate chaotic values are one-dimensional, non-invertible sequences. In related literature, several chaotic sequences have been proposed. However, most of them hold a randomness behavior considering specific configurations. An exception to those is the Iterative Chaotic Map with Infinite Collapses (ICMIC) due to ICMIC behaves chaotically throughout a wider configuration range. Under such configurations, The ICMIC sequence regulates the bias and dispersion of the generated random numbers. Due of these properties, the ICMIC sequence was used in this chapter to create random perturbations in the optimization process. The following mathematical model is used to compute the ICMIC sequence:

(6.1)

Figure 6.3 illustrates the pseudo-random behavior produced by the chaotic map of Eq. 6.1. The figure shows a portion of the time period from within the interval [3.5–4.4]. In this chapter, the chaotic parameter ϕ has been set to ϕ = 4. The dynamic reaction produced by ICMIC is represented by this value. With this value, ICMIC produces pseudo-random values around zero with a deviation in the interval [−1 –1]. These characteristics describe the primary behavior of a random number generator.

The MATLAB code (in Algorithm 6.2) presents the simulation of one-dimensional chaotic sequence. The chaotic sequence is given by the following mathematical description:

(6.2)

 

%Algorithm 6.2
%% INITIAL CONFIGURATION
%Clear memory and Close Matlab windows
clear all
close all
 
 
%% Step 1 Definition of initial conditions
x = 0.400000;
y = 0.399999;
x1 = x;
x2 = x;
x3 = x;
y1 = y;
y2 = y;
y3 = y;
lambda1 = 2.0;
lambda2 = 1 + sqrt(5);
lambda3 = 4.0;
 
 
%% Step 2 Chaotic sequence emulation
for i = 1:20
     fprintf('%f %f %f %f %f %f\n',x1,x2,x3,y1,y2,y3);
     x1 = lambda1 * x1 * (1-x1);
     y1 = lambda1 * y1 * (1-y1);
     x2 = lambda2 * x2 * (1-x2);
     y2 = lambda2 * y2 * (1-y2);
     x3 = lambda3 * x3 * (1-x3);
     y3 = lambda3 * y3 * (1-y3);
end

The Algorithm 6.2, represents the simulation of one-dimensional chaotic sequence considering three different lambda values to show the chaotic behavior given from initial conditions. The output of the code clearly indicates that the values from the first and fourth columns represents an attraction point, while the second and fifth columns represents a limit cycle.

6.4 Cluster-Chaotic-Optimization (CCO)

Clustering using population is assumed as the main goal of the CCO. With the clustering procedure, the goal is to determine which search regions should receive more attention during the evolution process. This idea establishes an alternative methodology to produced metaheuristic operators to conduct a search mechanism where spatial associations guide the optimization process. The majority of EC algorithms employ techniques that take into account each individual without taking into account their spatial relationship among the rest of elements in the population. Under such conditions, Traditional metaheuristic operators struggle to locate promising search areas, and even when they do, they hardly exploit such areas. On the other hand, On the other hand, employing chaotic sequences to carry out random perturbations is another essential feature of the presented hybrid strategy. It has been shown that using chaotic sequences instead of random numbers can significantly improve the effectiveness of optimization techniques. With its inclusion, EC algorithms improve its convergence by avoiding local minima stagnation.

CCO has been designed to locate the global solution of a nonlinear optimization problem in the following form:

(6.3)

where J : Rn → R is a nonlinear optimization problem whereas S = {x ɛ Rn ∣ lj ≤ xj ≤ uj, j = 1, …, n } is a bounded search space, restricted by the lower (lj) and upper (uj) bounds. Additionally, x is a solution within the set of possible solutions.

In order to solve an optimization problem using the CCO, it considers a population of datapoints containing ND number of possible solutions. These solutions will evolve from initial iteration (k = 0) until a total number of iterations is reached (k = Max _Iter). Each datapoint represents an n-dimensional decision variable vector. After a random initialization for the population, each datapoint is modified by two metaheuristic operators based on a hierarchical clustering scheme: intra-cluster and extra-cluster.

Since CCO method involves a series of straightforward steps. Here are the steps:

  1. Step 1: Initialization:

    Initialize a population D containing ND datapoints. Each datapoint corresponds to a candidate solution for a given optimization problem.

  2. Step 2: Clustering:

    Compute an agglomerative clustering approach using the population D of datapoints as the input data to generate a dendrogram. Then, use a cutting method to generate clusters that will be evolved.

  3. Step 3: Intra-Cluster Procedure:

    Explores the search space within each formed cluster from Step 2. This procedure adjusts the position of all datapoints inside each cluster. This metaheuristic operators can be considered as the exploitation stage in the optimization process.

  4. Step 4: Extra-Cluster Procedure:

    Explores the search space outside among clusters from Step 3. This procedure adjusts the best datapoint in term of fitness value to be attracted to the best datapoint in the entire population. This metaheuristic operator can be considered as the exploitation stage in the optimization process.

  5. Step 5: Repeat Steps 2–4 until the Maximum Number of Iterations is Reached.

    In the following subsections, a detailed description of each main procedure for the CCO method is described.

6.4.1 Initialization

At this stage the population D of ND datapoints is randomly and uniformly initialized. The values of each decision variable are randomly and uniformly distributed among a predefined the lower (lj) and upper (uj) bounds. The initialization procedure is defined as:

(6.4)

where represents to the j-th decision variable of the i-th datapoint at the k-th iteration.

6.4.2 Clustering

The primary method of data analysis employed by CCO is clustering. The goal of the clustering is to determine which search areas should receive more attention throughout the evolution process. With this idea, a new approach for conducting search strategies is established, one in which each unique association conducts the optimization process.

The Ward linkage method has been employed as a clustering approach for producing metaheuristic operators: intra-cluster and extra-cluster evolutionary operators. The generation of the dendrogram from the population D is computed at each iteration before the inter-cluster and extra-cluster procedures. After the execution of the Ward method at k-th iteration, the complete population Dk is divided into g clusters, where each cluster contains number of datapoints.

For producing g clusters, a cutting scheme based on the inconsistency links is considered. Commonly, in cluster analysis, the final grouping is achieved by considering the maximum number of inconstant links. That means, in the proposed methodology, there are considered the maximum number of links whose height differs noticeably from the height of the links below it.

6.4.3 Intra-Cluster Procedure

Under this procedure, each cluster produced by the Ward linkage technique is independently treated. The Intra-Cluster operator involves two different phases: the local attraction movement and a local perturbation process. Both phases are executed over each datapoint, except for the best element inside the cluster. This process increases the search capabilities by exploiting the search space within the cluster.

6.4.3.1 Local Attraction Movement

Assuming that the cluster is integrated by a set of datapoints, each datapoint is attracted to the best datapoint (solution) inside the cluster. The best datapoint inside the cluster is computed based on fitness value. In this chapter, it is considered a minimization problem, which can be expressed as follows:

The local attraction metaheuristic operator updates the position of the datapoint in terms of the j-th decision variable as follows:

The density cluster term can be considered as a velocity factor. This term emulates small movements to clusters containing few datapoints. On the other hand, clusters containing larger number of datapoints produce high movements of its datapoints. Figure 6.4 illustrates the effect of the local attraction movement considering two study cases. Figure 6.4a shows the velocity vectors as small arrows to represent small movements inside the cluster since it contains high number of datapoints. On the other hand, Figure 6.4b illustrates the velocity vectors as large arrows to represent larger movements inside the cluster. This process contributes to the exploration inside the cluster induced by larger movements.

6.4.3.2 Local Perturbation Strategy

The local perturbation strategy is executed after the movements produced by the local attraction procedure. This mechanism is applied to each datapoint for each cluster. The goal of this procedure is to increase the search capabilities inside each cluster promoting population diversity. Under this operation, new datapoints are locally modified following a circular path to produce two new different solutions (datapoints) and . Both solutions are generated following the model:

6.4.3.3 Extra-Cluster Procedure

Under this metaheuristic operation, the best datapoints of the set clusters (b ∈ 1, …, g) are evolved based on the best global solution (datapoint) being so far in the entire current population. The best global solution is defined as:

6.4.3.4 Global Attraction Movement

The global attraction operator adjusts the position of each best datapoint among all clusters. This procedure reorganized the best elements for each cluster, to explore into a wider zone within the search space. The attraction model can be described as follows:

6.5 Computational Procedure

The algorithmic structure of the CCO follows an iterative process, in which intra-cluster and extra-cluster metaheuristic operators are executed. Such procedures can be summarized in the Pseudo-code 6.1.

Pseudo-code 6.1 Computational Procedure of the Cluster Chaotic Optimization (CCO) Method

In the Pseudo-code 6.1, the Step 1 initialize the population of datapoints. Then, the Ward’s method is computed to produce clusters using the current population. Step 3 and 4 executes the intra-cluster and extra-cluster procedures respectively. Finally, the Step 5 repeats Steps 2–4 until a maximum number of iterations is reached.

6.6 Implementation of the CCO Algorithm in MATLAB

In Algorithm 6.3, it is described the MATLAB code for the CCO algorithm. To observe the functionality of the algorithm, the code encodes a benchmark function commonly used in performance testing related to the optimization of continuous functions. In this example, the Ackley function is implemented, so that the reader can observe the functionality of the CCO algorithm considering a minimization process.

The Ackley function exhibits a non-convex unimodal surface in a 2-dimensional space, and has a single global minimum located at position 0 of each of the decision variables used in the search space. The non-convex feature is used to test the scaling of the metaheuristic operators of the CCO algorithm when operates over surfaces that contain multiple local optima. On the other hand, the Ackley function is continuous and non-convex, which indicates that not any optimization technique either classical or metaheuristic can reach the global optimum. The mathematical model of the Ackley function is as follows:

(6.15)

Finally, so that the reader can see the behavior of the datapoints on the Ackley surface, at each iteration the movement of the solutions (datapoints) on the Ackley surface is plotted.

 

%Algorithm 6.3
%% INITIAL CONFIGURATION FOR THE OPTIMIZATION PROCESS
%Clear memory and Close Matlab windows
clear all;
close all;
%The maximum number of iterations is established
Max_Iter = 1000;
%The size of the population is established
Np = 50;
%The number of decision variables is established
dim = 2;
%The limits of the search space are defined.
lb = -32;
ub = 32;
%Adaptive parameters are calculated to control
%the optimization process in terms of iterations
sum = 0;
if size(ub,2)==1
    for i = 1:dim
        sum = sum + (ub - lb);
    end  
end
if size(ub,2)> 1
    for i = 1:dim
        high=ub(i); down=lb(i);
        sum = sum + (high-down);
    end  
end
%Initial alpha term is computed
alphaTotal = (sum/dim);
if alphaTotal> min(ub)
    alphaTotal = alphaTotal-ub;
    alphaTotal = alphaTotal / norm(alphaTotal);
end
%The maximum number of iterations is divided into three phases
%Phase 1 considers the 70%, Phase 2 considers the 20% and
%Phase 3 considers the last 10%.
EP = [70, 20, 10];
IT = zeros(1,3);
i = EP(1);
IT(1) = round((Max_Iter * i) / 100);
i = EP(1) + EP(2);
IT(2) = round(((Max_Iter * i) / 100));
IT(3) = round(Max_Iter);
 
 
%% Step 1 INITIALIZATION
%Initialization of the initial population,
%X is the variable representing the population of N elements
if size(ub,2)==1
    X=rand(Np,dim).*(ub-lb)+lb;
end
if size(ub,2)>1
    for i=1:dim
        high=ub(i);down=lb(i);
        X(:,i)=rand(Np,1).*(high-down)+down;
    end
end
%The fitness values of the initial population are obtained
fitness=ObjectiveFunction(X,dim);
 
 
%The population is sorted in ascending order
[Lightn,Index]=sort(fitness,'ascend');
sortedPop = X(Index, :);
%The best solution is obtained from the population
xbest = sortedPop(1,:);
fobj=Lightn(1);
fitness=ObjectiveFunction(sortedPop,dim);
[LightnBest,IndexBest]=sort(fitness,'ascend');
sortedPop = sortedPop(IndexBest, :);
%The plot the function to be optimized is computed
if dim<=2 
    rangeUpLb=ub-lb;
    figure(1)
    x=[lb:rangeUpLb/100:ub];
    y=x;
    [xg,yg]=meshgrid(x,y);
    [row,col]=size(xg);
    for l=1:col
        for h=1:row
            z(h,l)=ObjectiveFunction([xg(h,l),yg(h,l)],dim);
        end
    end
end
cutmean = 1;
count = 0;
phase = 1;
div = 100;
%Iterative process of the algorithm
while count <= Max_Iter
    %The adaptive alpha term is computed according to the actual
    %in the optimization process based on the number of
    %phase iterations
    alfAdaptive =  alphaTotal * (EP(phase) / div);
 
 
    %% Step 2 CLUSTERING
    Z = linkage(sortedPop,'ward',{'euclidean'});
    %Dendrogram cutting process
    I = inconsistent(Z);
    cutAux = cutmean;
    cutmean = max(I(:,4));
    cutmean = cutmean - (cutmean* 0.001);
    if cutmean <= 0
        cutmean = cutAux;
    end
    clust = cluster(Z,'cutoff',cutmean);
    aux_clust = max(clust);
    %The computation of each cluster centroid is performed
    [n,m] = size(sortedPop);
    aux_clust = max(clust);
    for k = 1: m
        for j = 1: aux_clust
            centroid(j,k) = mean(sortedPop(j==clust,k));
        end
    end
    %The density term for each cluster is computed
    for i = 1: aux_clust
        sum = 0;
        index = find(clust==i);
        xAux = sortedPop(index,:);
        for j = 1: size(xAux,1)
            d(j) = (norm(xAux(j,:) - centroid(i)));
            sum = d(j) + sum;
        end
        maxDist = max(max(d));
        minDist = min(min(d));
        dis(i) = (sum/aux_clust) ;
        if maxDist == 0 
            density(i) = size(xAux,1) / 50;
        else
            density(i) = (size(xAux,1)/50) *  aux_clust;
        end   
    end
    density = sort(density,'ascend');
    
    %% Step 3 INTRA-CLUSTER PROCEDURE
    for k = 1:aux_clust
        f = find(clust==k,1);
        bestCluster(k,:) = sortedPop(f,:);
        index = find(clust==k);
        index = index(2:end);
        if ∼isempty(index)
            for i = 1 : size(index,1)
                xAux = sortedPop(index(i),:);
                %Local Attraction movement
                sortedPop(index(i),:) = xAux + ...
((bestCluster(k,:) - xAux).* ...
chaosVector(lb,ub,dim).*...
(density(k)));
                sortedPop(index(i),:) =
findrange(sortedPop(index(i),:),lb,ub,dim,1);
                fitnessO = ...
ObjectiveFunction(sortedPop(in ex(i),:), dim);
                LightnBest(1,index(i)) = fitnessO;
                %Local Perturbation Strategy
                vT = vTransform(dim,alfAdaptive,lb,ub);
                left =  sortedPop(index(i),:) -
(sortedPop(index(i),:).*(chaosVector(lb,ub,dim))).*vT;
                left = findrange(left,lb,ub,dim,1);
                vT = vTransform(dim,alfAdaptive,lb,ub);         
                right = sortedPop(index(i),:) +
(sortedPop(index(i),:).*(chaosVector(lb,ub,dim))).*vT;
                right = findrange(right,lb,ub,dim,1);
                fitnessLR=ObjectiveFunction([left;right],dim);
                if fitnessLR(1) < fitnessO
                    sortedPop(index(i),:) = left;
                    LightnBest(1,index(i))  = fitnessLR(1,1);
                end
                if fitnessLR(2) < fitnessO
                    sortedPop(index(i),:) = right;
                    LightnBest(1,index(i))   = fitnessLR(1,2);
                end                       
            end
        end
        %% Step 4 EXTRA-CLUSTER PROCEDURE
        vT = vTransform(dim,alfAdaptive,lb,ub);
        %Global Attraction movement
        bestCluster(k,:) =  bestCluster(k,:)  + (xbest -
bestCluster(k,:)).* vT.*(chaosVector(lb,ub,dim));  
        bestCluster(k,:) = findrange(bestCluster(k,:),lb,ub,dim,1);
        fitnessOBC =     ObjectiveFunction(bestCluster(k,:),dim);
        sortedPop(f,:) = bestCluster(k,:);
        LightnBest(1,f) = fitnessOBC;
        %Global Perturbation Strategy
        vT = vTransform(dim,alfAdaptive,lb,ub);
        left =   bestCluster(k,:) -
(bestCluster(k,:).*(chaosVector(lb,ub,dim))).*vT;
        left = findrange(left,lb,ub,dim,1);
        vT = vTransform(dim,alfAdaptive,lb,ub);            
        right =  bestCluster(k,:) + 
(bestCluster(k,:).*(chaosVector(lb,ub,dim))).*vT;
        right = findrange(right,lb,ub,dim,1);
        fitnessLR= ObjectiveFunction([left;right],dim);
        if fitnessLR(1) < fitnessOBC
            sortedPop(f,:)  = left;
            LightnBest(1,f) = fitnessLR(1,1);
        end
        if fitnessLR(2) < fitnessOBC
            sortedPop(f,:) = right;
            LightnBest(1,f) = fitnessLR(1,2);
        end
    end
    [LightnBest,IndexBest]=sort(LightnBest,'ascend');
    sortedPop = sortedPop(IndexBest, :);
    %Selection of the best solution so far
    if LightnBest(1)  < fobj
        xbest = sortedPop(1,:);
        fobj = LightnBest(1);
    end
    %Iteration and phase counters
    count = count + 1;
    if count> IT(phase)
        phase = phase + 1;
        div = div * Max_Iter;
    end
    %The plot the population is generated
    if dim<=2
        surf(xg,yg,z);
        title('Ackley function')
        hold on
        plot3(sortedPop(:,1),sortedPop(:,2),LightnBest(1,:),'o',
'markersize',6,'markerfacecolor','r');
        plot3(xbest(1,1),xbest(1,2),fobj,'o','markersize',10,
'markerfacecolor','g');
        drawnow;
        hold off                        
    end
    fprintf('Iteration: %d\n',count);
    fprintf('Best solution: (%d,%d)\n',xbest(1,1),xbest(1,2));
    fprintf('Best fitness: %d\n',fobj);
end
 
 
%%OBJECTIVE FUNCTION
%Ackley function implementation
function fit = ObjectiveFunction(L,dim)
    [N,∼]=size(L);
    for i=1:N 
        fit(i)= -20*exp(-.2*sqrt(sum( L(i,:).∧2)/dim))-
exp(sum(cos(2*pi.* L(i,:)))/dim)+20+exp(1);
    end
end
 
 
%Circular perturbation strategy
function vT = vTransform(dim,r,lb,ub)
    vT = ones(1,dim);
    [∼,col]=size(lb);
    for i = 1: dim
        if col> 1
            vT(1,i) = 1*cos(r(i)*rand);
        else
            vT(1,i) = 1*cos(r*rand);
        end
    end
end
 
 
%Iterative Chaotic Map with Infinite Collapses function
function y = chaosVector(low,up,dim)
     
    if size(up,2)==1
        for i = 1:dim
            aux = rand;
            for j =1:50
                aux = sin((pi*4)/aux);
            end
            y(1,i) = aux;
        end  
    end
    if size(up,2)> 1
        for i = 1:dim
            high=up(i);down=low(i);
            aux = rand;
            for j =1:50
                aux =  sin((pi*4)/aux);
            end
            y(1,i) = aux;
        end  
    end
end
 
 
%Find range function
function X = findrange(X,low,up,dim,N)
    if size(up,2)==1
        for j = 1 : N
            for i = 1:dim   
                if (X(j,i) < low) 
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(up-low)+low;
                end
                if (X(j,i)> up)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(up-low)+low;
                end
            end     
        end   
    end
    if size(up,2)> 1   
         for j = 1 : N
             for i = 1:dim
                high=up(i);down=low(i);
                if (X(j,i) < down)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(high-down)+down;
                end
                if (X(j,i)> high)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(high-down)+down;
                end          
             end
         end
    end
end

The Algorithm 6.3 graphically shows the evolution of the population using the iterative structure of the CCO method. The plotted graph is shown in Figure 6.7.

In Algorithm 6.3, the first stage indicates the initial parameters configuration required by the optimization process. Such configuration relies on setting the maximum number of iterations, the population size, the number of decision variables involved in the optimization process and the definition of the limits of the search space. During the optimization process of the CCO it is also introduced an adaptive mechanism to regulate the balance between exploration and exploitation operators. Under this scheme, the maximum number of iterations is divided into three phases: Phase 1 considers the 70%, Phase 2 considers the 20% and Phase 3 considers the last 10% of iterations. This mechanism cannot be considered as a metaheuristic operator since it only regulates the optimization procedure.

The algorithm describes the Step 1, in this step the initialization of the population is achieved. Each datapoint is randomly generated within the limits of the search space. Additionally, the fitness value for each datapoint is then obtained. The main loop of the algorithm begins to the Step 2 that means to compute the dendrogram of the population followed by the Ward’s method. Once the dendrogram is generated, a cutting scheme is applied based on the maximum number of inconsistencies of the dendrogram. Step 3 implements the Intra-cluster procedure, where the local attraction movement and local perturbation strategy explores the space inside each cluster. Step 4 implements the Extra-cluster procedure, where the global attraction movement and global perturbation strategy is explores the space outside each cluster to promote exploration into wider search zones. In the algorithm, the objective function to be optimized is implemented above the main loop. The objective function considered in this chapter is the well-known Ackley function. Also it is implemented the circular perturbation mechanism and the iterative chaotic map with infinite collapses to produce chaotic sequence values.

6.7 Spring Design Optimization Problem Using the CCO Algorithm in MATLAB

Optimization problems involve finding an optimal solution within a possible set of solutions that pose maximization or minimization problems. Most areas in engineering can present optimization problems to find the optimal solution to planning problems, operations research, or even engineering design problems, among others. From this perspective, the need to develop optimization techniques that solve these problems is of great interest within the scientific and engineering community. In Section 6.5, the code related to the implementation of the CCO algorithm using a synthetic benchmark function that exhibits a unimodal and convexities was presented. However, in such example the CCO is tested using a mathematical function that is part of a set of test functions that do not represent a real application. Under this circumstance, this section analyzes an engineering design problem and describes how the CCO method can be used to solve real world applications.

The simple spring design problem is a complex engineering problem where the objective is to design a spring for tension or compression. For this problem, a set of specific design requirements (also called constraints) must be addressed to include the minimum deflection and frequency, as well as the maximum diameter and shear stress of the spring.

The main objective of simple spring design is to minimize the weight of the tension or compression spring. To do this, the mathematical description of the model is formulated as an optimization problem taking the following form:

(6.16)

where x1, x2 and x3 represent the thickness of the rod (W), the average diameter of the coil (D), and the number of active coils (L), respectively. These values are distributed in a three-dimensional space (d = 3) and define the decision variables of the problem. In turn, g1(x),…, g4(x), correspond to the four non-linear restrictions that must be met for the spring design to be optimal. The limits of the search space corresponding to each dimension of the problem are defined as: 0.05 ≤ x1 ≤ 2, 0.25 ≤ x2 ≤ 1.3 and 2 ≤ x3 ≤ 15. The design parameters for the spring problem are graphically illustrated in Figure 6.8, where D corresponds to the average diameter of the coil, L represents the number of active coils, and W the thickness of the rod. The optimization process of this engineering problem using the CCO algorithm is shown in Algorithm 6.4.

 

%Algorithm 6.4
%% INITIAL CONFIGURATION FOR THE OPTIMIZATION PROCESS
%Clear memory and Close Matlab windows
clear all;
close all;
%The maximum number of iterations is established
Max_Iter = 1000;
%The size of the population is established
Np = 50;
%The number of decision variables is established
dim = 3;
%The limits of the search space are defined.
lb = [0.05 0.25 2];
ub = [2 1.3 15];
%The penalization parameters are defined.
rg = 100;
cg = 2;
%Adaptive parameters are calculated to control
%the optimization process in terms of iterations
sum = 0;
if size(ub,2)==1
    for i = 1:dim
        sum = sum + (ub - lb);
    end  
end
if size(ub,2)> 1
    for i = 1:dim
        high=ub(i); down=lb(i);
        sum = sum + (high-down);
    end  
end
%Initial alpha term is computed
alphaTotal = (sum/dim);
if alphaTotal> min(ub)
    alphaTotal = alphaTotal-ub;
    alphaTotal = alphaTotal / norm(alphaTotal);
end
%The maximum number of iterations is divided into three phases
%Phase 1 considers the 70%, Phase 2 considers the 20% and
%Phase 3 considers the last 10%.
EP = [70, 20, 10];
IT = zeros(1,3);
i = EP(1);
IT(1) = round((Max_Iter * i) / 100);
i = EP(1) + EP(2);
IT(2) = round(((Max_Iter * i) / 100));
IT(3) = round(Max_Iter);
 
 
%% Step 1 INITIALIZATION
%Initialization of the initial population,
%X is the variable representing the population of N elements
if size(ub,2)==1
    X=rand(Np,dim).*(ub-lb)+lb;
end
if size(ub,2)>1
    for i=1:dim
        high=ub(i);down=lb(i);
        X(:,i)=rand(Np,1).*(high-down)+down;
    end
end
%The fitness values of the initial population are obtained
fitness=ObjectiveFunction(X,dim,rg,cg);
 
 
%The population is sorted in ascending order
[Lightn,Index]=sort(fitness,'ascend');
sortedPop = X(Index, :);
%The best solution is obtained from the population
xbest = sortedPop(1,:);
fobj=Lightn(1);
fitness=ObjectiveFunction(sortedPop,dim,rg,cg);
[LightnBest,IndexBest]=sort(fitness,'ascend');
sortedPop = sortedPop(IndexBest, :);
%The plot the function to be optimized is computed
if dim<=2 
    rangeUpLb=ub-lb;
    figure(1)
    x=[lb:rangeUpLb/100:ub];
    y=x;
    [xg,yg]=meshgrid(x,y);
    [row,col]=size(xg);
    for l=1:col
        for h=1:row
            z(h,l)=ObjectiveFunction([xg(h,l),yg(h,l)],dim,rg,cg);
        end
    end
end
cutmean = 1;
count = 0;
phase = 1;
div = 100;
%Iterative process of the algorithm
while count <= Max_Iter
    %The adaptive alpha term is computed according to the actual
    %phase in the optimization process based on the number of
    %iterations
    alfAdaptive =  alphaTotal * (EP(phase) / div);
 
 
    %% Step 2 CLUSTERING
    Z = linkage(sortedPop,'ward',{'euclidean'});
    %Dendrogram cutting process
    I = inconsistent(Z);
    cutAux = cutmean;
    cutmean = max(I(:,4));
    cutmean = cutmean - (cutmean* 0.001);
    if cutmean <= 0
        cutmean = cutAux;
    end
    clust = cluster(Z,'cutoff',cutmean);
    aux_clust = max(clust);
    %The computation of each cluster centroid is performed
    [n,m] = size(sortedPop);
    aux_clust = max(clust);
    for k = 1: m
        for j = 1: aux_clust
            centroid(j,k) = mean(sortedPop(j==clust,k));
        end
    end
    %The density term for each cluster is computed
    for i = 1: aux_clust
        sum = 0;
        index = find(clust==i);
        xAux = sortedPop(index,:);
        for j = 1: size(xAux,1)
            d(j) = (norm(xAux(j,:) - centroid(i)));
            sum = d(j) + sum;
        end
        maxDist = max(max(d));
        minDist = min(min(d));
        dis(i) = (sum/aux_clust) ;
        if maxDist == 0 
            density(i) = size(xAux,1) / 50;
        else
            density(i) = (size(xAux,1)/50) *  aux_clust;
        end   
    end
    density = sort(density,'ascend');
    
    %% Step 3 INTRA-CLUSTER PROCEDURE
    for k = 1:aux_clust
        f = find(clust==k,1);
        bestCluster(k,:) = sortedPop(f,:);
        index = find(clust==k);
        index = index(2:end);
        if ∼isempty(index)
            for i = 1 : size(index,1)
                xAux = sortedPop(index(i),:);
                %Local Attraction movement
                sortedPop(index(i),:) = xAux +  ((bestCluster(k,:) -
xAux) .* chaosVector(lb,ub,dim) .*(density(k)));
                sortedPop(index(i),:) =
findrange(sortedPop(index(i),:),lb,ub,dim,1);
                fitnessO =
ObjectiveFunction(sortedPop(index(i),:),dim,rg,cg);
                LightnBest(1,index(i)) = fitnessO;
                %Local Perturbation Strategy
                vT = vTransform(dim,alfAdaptive,lb,ub);
                left =  sortedPop(index(i),:) -
(sortedPop(index(i),:).*(chaosVector(lb,ub,dim))).*vT;
                left = findrange(left,lb,ub,dim,1);
                vT = vTransform(dim,alfAdaptive,lb,ub);         
                right = sortedPop(index(i),:) +
(sortedPop(index(i),:).*(chaosVector(lb,ub,dim))).*vT;
                right = findrange(right,lb,ub,dim,1);
                fitnessLR=ObjectiveFunction([left;right],dim,rg,cg);
                if fitnessLR(1) < fitnessO
                    sortedPop(index(i),:) = left;
                    LightnBest(1,index(i))  = fitnessLR(1,1);
                end
                if fitnessLR(2) < fitnessO
                    sortedPop(index(i),:) = right;
                    LightnBest(1,index(i))   = fitnessLR(1,2);
                end                       
            end
        end
        %% Step 4 EXTRA-CLUSTER PROCEDURE
        vT = vTransform(dim,alfAdaptive,lb,ub);
        %Global Attraction movement
        bestCluster(k,:) =  bestCluster(k,:)  + (xbest -
bestCluster(k,:)).* vT.*(chaosVector(lb,ub,dim));  
        bestCluster(k,:) = findrange(bestCluster(k,:),lb,ub,dim,1);
        fitnessOBC = ...
ObjectiveFunction(bestCluster(k,:), dim,rg,cg);
        sortedPop(f,:) = bestCluster(k,:);
        LightnBest(1,f) = fitnessOBC;
        %Global Perturbation Strategy
        vT = vTransform(dim,alfAdaptive,lb,ub);
        left =   bestCluster(k,:) -
(bestCluster(k,:).*(chaosVector(lb,ub,dim))).*vT;
        left = findrange(left,lb,ub,dim,1);
        vT = vTransform(dim,alfAdaptive,lb,ub);            
        right =  bestCluster(k,:) + 
(bestCluster(k,:).*(chaosVector(lb,ub,dim))).*vT;
        right = findrange(right,lb,ub,dim,1);
        fitnessLR= ObjectiveFunction([left;right],dim,rg,cg);
        if fitnessLR(1) < fitnessOBC
            sortedPop(f,:)  = left;
            LightnBest(1,f) = fitnessLR(1,1);
        end
        if fitnessLR(2) < fitnessOBC
            sortedPop(f,:) = right;
            LightnBest(1,f) = fitnessLR(1,2);
        end
    end
    [LightnBest,IndexBest]=sort(LightnBest,'ascend');
    sortedPop = sortedPop(IndexBest, :);
    %Selection of the best solution so far
    if LightnBest(1)  < fobj
        xbest = sortedPop(1,:);
        fobj = LightnBest(1);
    end
    %Iteration and phase counters
    count = count + 1;
    if count> IT(phase)
        phase = phase + 1;
        div = div * Max_Iter;
    end
    %The plot the population is generated
    if dim<=2
        surf(xg,yg,z);
        title('Ackley function')
        hold on

        plot3(sortedPop(:,1),sortedPop(:,2),...
LightnBest(1,:),'o','markersize',6,...
'markerfacecolor','r');
        plot3(xbest(1,1),xbest(1,2),fobj,...
'o','markersize',10,...
'markerfacecolor','g');
        drawnow;
        hold off                        
    end
    fprintf('Iteration: %d\n',count);
    fprintf('Best solution: (%d,%d)\n',xbest(1,1),xbest(1,2));
    fprintf('Best fitness: %d\n',fobj);
end
 
 
%%OBJECTIVE FUNCTION
%Implementation of the Spring design optimization problem
function fit = ObjectiveFunction(L,dim,rg,cg)
    [N,∼]=size(L);
    for i=1:N
        fitnessX = (L(3) + 2) * L(2)* (L(1)∧2);
        g1= 1-((L(i,2)∧3*L(i,3))/(71785*L(i,1)∧4) );
        p1=4*L(i,2)∧2-L(i,1)*L(i,2)/12566*(L(i,2)*L(i,1)∧3-L(i,1)∧4);
          p2=1/(5108*L(i,1)∧2);
        g2=(p1+p2-1) ;
          g3=(1-( (140.45*L(i,1))/(L(i,2)∧2*L(i,3)) ) );
          g4=(((L(i,2)+L(i,1))/1.5)-1);
        P = (rg * min(0,g1)∧2) +...
(rg * min(0,g2)∧2) +...
(rg * min(0,g3)∧2) +...
(rg * min(0,g4)∧2);
        fitnessX = fitnessX + P;
        rg = rg * cg;
        fit(i)= fitnessX;
    end
end
 
 
%Circular perturbation strategy
function vT = vTransform(dim,r,lb,ub)
    vT = ones(1,dim);
    [∼,col]=size(lb);
    for i = 1: dim
        if col> 1
            vT(1,i) = 1*cos(r(i)*rand);
        else
            vT(1,i) = 1*cos(r*rand);
        end
    end
end
 
 
%Iterative Chaotic Map with Infinite Collapses function
function y = chaosVector(low,up,dim)
     
    if size(up,2)==1
        for i = 1:dim
            aux = rand;
            for j =1:50
                aux = sin((pi*4)/aux);
            end
            y(1,i) = aux;
        end  
    end
    if size(up,2)> 1
        for i = 1:dim
            high=up(i);down=low(i);
            aux = rand;
            for j =1:50
                aux =  sin((pi*4)/aux);
            end
            y(1,i) = aux;
        end  
    end
end
 
 
%Find range function
function X = findrange(X,low,up,dim,N)
    if size(up,2)==1
        for j = 1 : N
            for i = 1:dim   
                if (X(j,i) < low) 
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(up-low)+low;
                end
                if (X(j,i)> up)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(up-low)+low;
                end
            end     
        end   
    end
    if size(up,2)> 1   
         for j = 1 : N
             for i = 1:dim
                high=up(i);down=low(i);
                if (X(j,i) < down)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(high-down)+down;
                end
                if (X(j,i)> high)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(high-down)+down;
                end          
             end
         end
    end
end

In Algorithm 6.4, the initial configuration declares the dimensionality and the limits of the search space according to the spring design problem. The spring design optimization problem contains 4 constraints. These constraints refer to physical requirements for designing a spring. Commonly in metaheuristics a penalization term is added to the fitness value. For that the variables rg and cg are defined to control the penalization for the objective function. The objective function implements each of the constraints in Eq. 6.16. The penalization term is added to the actual fitness value. The penalized fitness value incorporates information in future iterations of the optimization process.

7
Techniques of Machine Learning for Modifying the Search Strategy

7.1 Introduction

Extracting knowledge is the process of finding new information in data. For extracting significant information, a set of multiple techniques can be applied. Some techniques include neural networks, decision trees, and clustering. Knowledge extraction is the main part of building artificial intelligence applications since it allows machines to learn the intrinsic characteristics of the data and make predictions or recommendations. One of the most interesting techniques is based on the Self-Organization Maps (SOMs) introduced by Teuvo Kohonen (1982).

A SOM is an unsupervised neural network which has been extensively employed in fields including information extraction and machine learning. In SOM, vector quantization is used to condense a large number of data vectors into a manageable subset of representative vectors grouped in a fixed lattice. SOM has several advantages over other methods for extracting knowledge. SOMs enable for the discovery of unexpected patterns in input data by mapping complicated, high-dimensional data onto a predefined lattice (topology). In order to keep the lattice map’s spatial relationships between neighboring items in the original data and the neural units, SOM preserves the data organization. The visualization of complicated data structures is thus made intuitive by the association of numerous input data with a single neural unit (Akinduko et al. 2016). These properties make it possible to identify unexpected data structures, determine if groups of vectors are similar or dissimilar, and examine their intrinsic patterns.

The learning process of the SOM involves the concept of competitive learning. In competitive learning, a set of neural units compete with each other to produce a winning neuron, which is often the neuron that best matches the input data. Then, the weights of each neuron are updated according to their activation response. The importance of this kind of learning relies on its capacity to automatically group similar data inputs into clusters in input data when no prior information or labels are provided. The main goal of the competitive learning strategy of SOMs is to classify input data without the use of input-labeled data.

The inherent characteristics of the competitive learning mechanism of the SOMs can be employed to produce interesting search strategies for developing metaheuristic algorithms.

Most of the metaheuristic algorithms are proposed as metaphors of natural, biological, or even social phenomena as a source of inspiration to construct search strategies into computational algorithms for finding optimal solutions in complex optimization problems. Recently, the scientific community has focused their attention on how to improve the existing search strategies by introducing some kind of knowledge in their metaheuristic operators. Under such circumstances, the metaheuristic approaches can be categorized into two groups. The first class incorporates knowledge before the beginning of the optimization process. These methods are known as Evolutionary Methods with a Prior Information (EMAI). Under these techniques, the incorporated information remains fixed during the entire optimization process (Deveci and Demirel 2018; Kobeaga et al. 2018). On the other hand, the second class incorporates knowledge of each iteration of the optimization process. These methods are known as Evolutionary Techniques with Dynamic Information (ETDI) (Mobin et al. 2018; Nobile et al. 2018; Yeguas et al. 2014).

ETDI methods extract information from the optimization process using some techniques such as: statistical analysis methods, regression trees, and genetic programming (Hong et al. 2018; Hu et al. 2017). The extracted information of these methods modifies the search strategy of the metaheuristic algorithm. Most of these approaches use straightforward machine learning techniques that only take into account a few population members as well as the best current element as complete representations of the optimization process. Under such circumstances, the development of novel metaheuristic algorithms where the knowledge extraction is not based only on the population but on the entire search strategy is an emerging research topic.

This chapter describes the EA-SOM metaheuristic optimization algorithm, which uses information gained from the optimization process at each generation to control its search strategy. The proposed method employs a SOM as an extracting knowledge method to identify potential locations. The proposed strategy trains the SOM using a subset of the entire group of produced solutions seen thus far for each generation. The neural unit from lattice that corresponds to the best solution is found after the training stage. Then, a full population of potential solutions is generated using a local knowledge mechanism.

In this chapter, we delve into the concept of competitive learning. Competitive learning model is the mechanism employed by the structure of SOMs for training a lattice of neural units. The main aspect of involving the concept of competitive learning during the optimization process relies on extracting information of the optimization process at each generation. This methodology produces evolutionary strategies for improving the search mechanism of metaheuristic algorithms by guiding the search process through the gained information by the optimization process iteratively. Throughout the chapter, MATLAB will be used to implement this methodology. This hands-on approach will enable readers to gain practical experience and become proficient in using SOM structure to produce metaheuristic operators in their own projects.

7.2 Self-Organization Map (SOM)

The SOMs, also called Kohonen’s maps, were introduced by Teuvo Kohonen. A SOM is a technique that analyzes data in many dimensions with complex relationships between them and reduces them to represent them in, usually, one, two, or three dimensions. SOMs are mathematical models based on the abstraction process of the topographic mapping between the human visual system to the cerebral cortex. Analyzing and modeling the topographic mapping are important to understand how the human brain recognizes and processes the pattern it receives from the human visual system to make decisions. A SOM is an unsupervised neural network which is an extensively used technique for extracting knowledge in machine learning tasks. This kind of neural networks are effective methods for analyzing complex multidimensional data.

SOMs have several significant advantages over other methods for extracting knowledge, one of which is that the processed data keeps the original elements’ topology (data organization) intact. SOMs are frequently used as data reduction or clustering methods due to this property. Vector quantization is used by SOM to condense a large number of data vectors into a manageable subset of representative vectors arranged in a predetermined lattice. SOMs allow for the discovery of unexpected patterns in input data by mapping complex, high-dimensional data into a fixed lattice. SOM maintains the data organization so that similar elements in the original data remain close to neural units in the output layer. In order to facilitate the visualization of complex data structures, SOMs link multiple input data to a single prototype neural unit. These characteristics make it possible to identify unexpected data structures, determine whether groups of vectors are similar or dissimilar, and examine their natural patterns.

A SOM can be illustrated as a two-layer neural network that only contains input layer and output layer. The input layer contains the input (training data), while the output layer represents a rectangular grid of neural units called lattice (Figure 7.1).

The objective of SOMs is to find a mapping between input data and the lattice through a competitive learning model. SOMs perform unsupervised learning model, where labels and prior classifications are not necessary for the input data. Due to this approach, SOMs can operate under unlabeled or sparsely labeled data to form clusters from input data. The learning process of SOMs is based on the concept of competitive learning model, where a set of neural units competes with each other to produce a winning neuron that best matches the input data. The importance of this kind of learning model relies on its capacity to automatically group similar input data without the necessity of prior labels for each input data.

The competitive learning strategy used in SOMs can be defined into three main procedures: Competition, cooperation, and synaptic adaptation. In the competition phase, the SOM structure finds the correspondence among input data and each neural unit in the output layer, producing a winning neuron in the lattice. The winning neuron is the neural unit in the lattice that best matches the input data. The cooperation phase determines the spatial relationship also called neighborhood relation, so adjacent neural units to the winning neuron share knowledge locally. Finally, the synaptic adaptation phase updated the weights of the neural units according to their importance in the neighborhood. Closer neurons to the winning neuron will share more information than distant neurons. This fact follows the neurobiological studies which indicate that biological neurons are excited following a local and decreasing interaction over time.

In the following sections, the network architecture, and the competitive learning model of a SOM are detailed.

7.2.1 Network Architecture

The SOM is composed by a set of neurons, commonly arranged in a 2-D rectangular or hexagonal grid, to form a discrete topological map (lattice) where the input data will be mapped. A SOM integrates two different layers: an input layer and a competitive layer (output layer). The network architecture of a SOM networks can be shown in Figure 7.2.

The network is made by the input layer which represents the training data set, and the output layer which corresponds to the mapping learned through the competitive learning strategy. In this structure, SOM considers as input data an n-dimensional vector x. Each node (neural unit) in the lattice is fully connected to each node in the input layer. The output lattice involves Z = z z competitive neural units. Associated with each neural unit in the lattice, there is a weight vector which is equal in size to an input vector x. The weight vector of each neural unit represents the input data to which it is associated.

The learning model of SOMs consists of finding the best neural unit in the lattice (topology) that best matches an input data vector. Once the winning neuron is obtained, a definition of a neighborhood relation can be computed for the cooperative phase in the learning model. The importance of obtaining the winning neuron is the representation of the best knowledge from the input data, and the importance of the neighborhood is that closer neural units to the winning neuron will represent important knowledge, rather than distant neurons.

The topology of a SOM is dictated by the adjacent neurons by a neighborhood relation. This relationship affects the way data is associated. Complex neighborhood relationships result in more complex extensions of the neighborhood. Commonly, the topology employed in SOMs is a rectangular or hexagonal grid to maintain simple neighborhood relations over the entire lattice. Since SOMs are based on the abstraction process of how the human visual system maps into the cerebral cortex, the neurobiological field suggests that the neighborhood relationship among biological neurons can be modeled as a decreasing function of time. Under such circumstances, the neighborhood relation in SOMs should be a symmetric and monotonically decreasing function of time considering the spatial relation of the winning neuron. In Figure 7.3a, a rectangular topology of a SOM is presented. In Figure 7.3b, a hexagonal topology of an SOM is described.

7.2.2 Competitive Learning Model

Unsupervised learning model learns the intrinsic nature of the input data without prior knowledge from the input dataset. These techniques learn by their own without external assumptions. In SOMs, the unsupervised learning process produces clusters formed for the input data, which allows data compression from the input space. This process is achieved by introducing the concept of competitive learning in which the neurons from the output layer compete with each other to be activated, as a result, only one neuron (winning neuron) is activated through each generation. The aim of SOMs is to transform input data in n-dimensional space into a discrete lattice. This mechanism compresses input data into low-dimensional feature space. For that, SOMs are considered neural networks that selectively transform data into a low-dimensional representation of the entire input data.

The competitive learning model from SOMs is considered as the training stage of the algorithm. The objective of the training stage is to find the final topology of the lattice, which will represent the main features of the input data into a low-dimensional representation. In order to train a SOM, three important processes must be executed. Competition procedure, cooperation procedure, and synaptic adaptation.

7.2.2.1 Competition Procedure

In this procedure, each input data vector computes its correspondence to each neural unit in the output layer. The correspondence value is computed by a discriminant function. Commonly, SOMs employ the Euclidean distance between input vectors with the weights of each neural unit in the lattice. The neural unit with the smallest discriminant value is declared as the winning neuron.

 Note

In competitive learning, the most commonly used discriminant functions are:

  • Euclidean distance.
  • Manhattan distance.
  • Minkowski distance.
  • Cosine similarity

In this chapter, the Euclidean distance is employed as a discriminant function. Euclidean distance is the most common measurement to implement the competition mechanism of SOMs. However, readers can implement any discriminant function for their own applications. One important aspect to consider is the fact that different discriminant functions can obtain different clusters in the output layer in SOMs. We encourage readers to experiment with different discriminant functions considering the input dataset.

7.2.2.2 Cooperation Procedure

Under this procedure, the winning neuron determines its spatial associations in terms of neighborhood relation. That is, neighbor neurons around the winner are also excited. This mechanism mimics the basis of knowledge cooperation since closer neurons respect the winner and will share important information rather than distant neurons from the winner. This mechanism is also called as lateral interaction. According to neurobiological studies, biological neurons are excited following a local and decreasing interaction over time among neighbor neurons. Under such circumstances, in the cooperation procedure neurons will share information following a symmetric and monotonically decreasing function of time around the winner.

 Note

In competitive learning, the most common topological neighborhood relations for producing cooperative behavior among the lattice are:

  • Exponential decay.
  • Average rate.
  • Gaussian curve.
  • Mexican-hat curve.

In this chapter, the combination of Gaussian curve and exponential decay is employed to obtain the cooperative behavior of the competitive learning model. Gaussian curve defines the neighborhood in terms of a Gaussian function, where the winning neuron is the highest value of the Gaussian shape function. Additionally, an exponential decay is also employed to mimic a monotonically decreasing function to indicate that neighbor neurons closer to the winner will share more important information than distant neurons.

7.2.2.3 Synaptic Adaptation Procedure

Under this procedure, the weight vectors of the winning neuron and its neighbors are updated following the Hebbian learning rule. The effect of employing this weight adaptation strategy is to move the weight vectors of both the winning neuron and its neighbors toward the input vector to construct a final lattice representation of the entire dataset.

 Note

In neural networks, the most common rule used for updating weights is the Hebbian rule based on the studies of the neuroscientific Donald Heeb in his publication in 1949, “The Organization of Behaviour.” The idea behind the theory is that when human brains learn something new, neurons become activated and linked together to form neural networks. These connections are initially weak, but as the stimulus is repeated, they become increasingly strong, making the action more intuitive.

7.2.3 Self-Organization Map (SOM) Algorithm

The algorithmic design to implement a SOM involves a series of straightforward steps. Here are the steps:

  1. Step 1: Initialization:

    In this step, the weight vectors for each neural unit of the output layer are randomly initialized with small values. For this stage, it is required the definition of a lattice. The lattice used in this chapter is a rectangular grid representation.

  2. Step 2: Competition Procedure:

    In this step, the Euclidean distance between the input data vector with the weight vector associated with each neural unit is computed. Afterward, the neural unit representing the smallest distance in the lattice is selected and considered as the winning neuron.

  3. Step 3: Cooperation Procedure:

    In this step, the neighborhood of the winning neuron is computed. The neighborhood is defined based on a gaussian function. Also, an exponential decay function is computed.

  4. Step 4: Synaptic Adaptation Procedure:

    In this step, the weight vectors of the winning neuron, and its neighbors are updated. The adaptation process follows the Hebbian learning rule.

  5. Step 5: Repeat Steps 2–4 until the Stop Criterion is Reached:

    The complete algorithm for SOMs can be summarized as follows:

    1. Define the initial topological structure.
    2. Initialize all weight vectors from the lattice.
    3. Set the number of generations Max_Gen.
    4. Set the initial generation counter k = 0.
    5. From the dataset, select an input data vector x.

    6. Perform the competition procedure.

      Compute the Euclidean distances among x and each weight vector of a neural unit wj. Obtain the winning neuron according to the following scheme:

      Where i(x) represents the index of the neural unit from the lattice which is the closest element to the input vector.

    7. Perform cooperative procedure.

      Compute the neighborhood function hj,i(x) following equations:

      where is the distance between the winning neuron and each neighbor neuron. And σ is the neighborhood radius at k-th iteration.

    8. Perform synaptic adaptation procedure

      Adjust the weights of both the winner unit and its neighbor elements considering this model:
