7.2.4 Application of Self-Organization Map (SOM)

The MATLAB code (in Algorithm 7.1) is presented by using the built-in functions of MATLAB as follows:

 

%Algorithm 7.1
%% INITIAL CONFIGURATION
%Clear memory and Close Matlab windows
clear all
close all
 
 
%% Step 1 Load Sample Dataset from Matlab
load simplecluster_dataset;
%Obtain the input data from the previous
x = simpleclusterInputs;
 
 
%% Step 2 Create the Self-Organization Map
%Create a 10x10 lattice
dim1 = 10;
dim2 = 10;
net = selforgmap([dim1 dim2]);
 
 
%% Step 3 Train the Network
[net,tr] = train(net,x);
 
 
%% Step 4 Plot the network lattice and hits
figure(1)
plotsompos(net,x)
figure(2)
plotsomhits(net,x)

In Algorithm 7.1, Step 1 loads a synthetic dataset from Matlab. The simplecluster_dataset contains 1000 sample datapoints. In Step 2, the architecture of the SOM is defined. In this example, it is considered a lattice containing 10 × 10 neurons. The built-in function selforgmap creates the lattice. Then, in Step 3 the training stage from the SOM is defined in Step 2. Finally, after the training stage, Step 4 plots the network final lattice and the network hints. The output of Algorithm 7.1 can be seen in Figure 7.4.

From Figure 7.4a, it can be shown that synthetic data is grouped by the SOM lattice. The built-in function plotsompos represents the weight positions from the trained SOM. The built-in function plotsomhits represents a layer in which each neuron counts the number of input vectors it classifies. This can be shown in Figure 7.4b.

7.3 Evolutionary-SOM (EA-SOM)

The competitive learning model in SOMs allows data input to be clustered into low-dimensional space. This characteristic categorizes SOMs as data reduction techniques. SOMs are considered as exploratory data analysis method, where no prior information of the input data is required. Under such circumstances, the structure of SOMs can be reformulated to create metaheuristic operators to propose interesting search strategies to contribute to the optimization process.

Most of the metaheuristic algorithms published in the literature contemplate the iterative nature of evolutionary principles. One of the pillars of metaheuristic algorithms is based on sampling the search space by using exploration and exploitation operations through generations. The sampling scheme in metaheuristic algorithms is one of the most critical aspects to solve any optimization problem since there is no guarantee that the evolutionary operators are reevaluating solutions from past generations. In this section, it is presented a strategy search scheme which combines the most important features of the competitive learning model in SOMs to learn information related to previous solutions from past generations to improve the search capabilities in future generations. Utilizing previous data from a process reduces the need to acquire new data in order to infer its internal properties and relationships. In metaheuristic methods, using knowledge to conduct the search strategy is an intriguing idea that has the potential to improve the effectiveness of optimization techniques.

In this section, a proposed metaheuristic called Evolutionary-SOM (EA-SOM) is presented. This metaheuristic algorithm has been developed to locate the global solution (global minimum/maximum) of a nonlinear optimization problem. A nonlinear optimization problem can be mathematically described as follows:

(7.5)

where J : ℝn → ℝ is a nonlinear objective function whereas S = {x ɛ ℝn ∣ lj ≤ xj ≤ uj, j = 1, …, n } represents the entire set of solution vectors x within a search space bounded by the lower (lj) and upper (uj) limits. The objective of the optimization process is achieved once the optimization method finds the g-th solution which represents the best global solution within the set of possible solutions.

In order to solve an optimization problem using the EA-SOM, it considers a population of datapoints containing ND number of possible solutions. These solutions will evolve from initial iteration (k = 0) until a total number of iterations is reached (k = Max _Iter). Each datapoint represents an n-dimensional decision variable vector. After a random initialization for the population, promising areas are found by the extracted information by the SOM. As a result, to train the SOM, the proposed method uses a portion of the past solutions observed thus far in each iteration. After training, the winning neuron of the output layer that best matches the best solution is identified. Then, by using neighborhood information, the SOM produces new population members for the next generation.

To get an intuition of the EA-SOM, Figure 7.5a shows a benchmark optimization function, containing several datapoints. These datapoints are considered as the input data for the input layer of a SOM. Once the SOM is trained, promising areas within the search space can be located in Figure 7.5b. The internal mechanism of the competitive learning of the SOM generates the lattice from Figure 7.5c. In this figure, it is shown the mapping from the input data to the data reduction of the search space. This mechanism provides information to the metaheuristic operators to guide the search strategy into the promising areas of the search space.

Since EA-SOM method involves a series of straightforward steps. Here are the steps:

  1. Step 1: Initialization:

    Initialize a population D containing ND datapoints. Each datapoint corresponds to a candidate solution x for a given optimization problem. Also, all the initial datapoints of D are stored in two different memory structures: Historical memory H, and initial training set memory T(0). An important aspect in the T(0) is that each initial input data vector is built combining the candidate solution and its respective initial fitness value . During the optimization process, the memory structures H and T will be updated according to the following steps.

  2. Step 2: Training:

    In this stage, the SOM is trained to identify promising areas by compressing the search space of the objective function. Therefore, a lattice of [z, z] neural units is defined. By using the competitive learning model, the SOM is trained considering a set T datapoints. During the training process, each input data vector is built combining the candidate solution and its respective fitness value .

  3. Step 3: Knowledge Extraction:

    In this step, the knowledge extraction mechanism is based on the data organization features of SOMs. That is, elements in the original data remain close to neural units in the output layer. For that, once trained the promising regions are mapped in the competitive layer of (z · z) lattice. This process represents the data reduction scheme for the search space.

  4. Step 4: Solution Production:

    Once the promising regions of the output layer are obtained, new solutions are generated considering the winning neuron and its neighborhood. These generated solutions will be part of the next population for the optimization process.

  5. Step 5: New Training set Construction:

    Once the generated solutions from Step 4 were generated, the new training set T(k + 1) is created incorporating the produced solutions. Also, the generated solutions will be stored in the historical memory structure H(k + 1).

  6. Step 6: Repeat Steps 2–5 until the Maximum Number of Iterations is Reached:

    In the following subsections, a detailed description of each main procedure for the EA-SOM method is described.

7.3.1 Initialization

At this stage, the population D of ND datapoints is randomly and uniformly initialized. The values of each decision variable are randomly and uniformly distributed among a predefined lower (lj) and upper (uj) bounds. The initialization procedure is defined as:

(7.6)

where represents the j-th decision variable of the i-th datapoint at the k-th iteration.

All the initial datapoints (where k = 0) in the population D(k) are also stored in the historical memory H(k), and the training set memory structure T(k). The historical memory structure H(k) will store solutions since the initial population through the last iteration. The training set memory structure T(k) will store training data to feed the SOM model. The elements in T(k) will change considering the information of actual k-th iteration.

At the beginning, the T(0) contemplates that each initial input data vector is built combining the candidate solution and its respective initial fitness value .

7.3.2 Training

In this step, a lattice composed by [z, z] neural units is defined (z, corresponds to the number of neurons, since rectangular lattice is considered in this chapter, the total number of neural units is z * z).

Following the competitive learning model in SOMs, in this procedure, the SOM is trained considering the competition, cooperative, and synaptic adaptation procedures (Section 7.2.3). For the training scheme, each input data vector is built combining the candidate solution and its respective fitness value .

 Note

An important aspect in the training stage is that the number of training samples that are used in the learning process affects the quality of the reduced search space. The use of all available historical data would produce the best approximation. However, the use of this big amount of data increases the computational effort. For that, depending on the application, the reader must consider using a reasonable number of samples, and neurons to avoid computational overload.

7.3.3 Knowledge Extraction

Once trained, several information can be extracted from the previous step such as: The promising areas by the output layer of the SOM, the winning neuron, and the information about its neighborhood.

To summarize, at the end of the training step, it is assumed the following model:

(7.7)

where w represents the w-th winning neuron from the [z, z] lattice. And g represents the best datapoint solution in the optimization problem for the k-th iteration (Eq. 7.5). That means, that the index of the winning neuron is obtained and therefore its neighborhood information.

In this step, to extract more information codified in the output layer of the trained SOM, neighborhood information around the winning neuron ww is also obtained. In EA-SOM, the two closest neurons from the winning neuron are also identified wA and wB. These close neurons also represent competitive neurons that contain minimal distances around the best solution g without considering the existence of unit ww. Along with the neurons ww, wA, and wB, their respective distances to g are also preserved due to the data organization feature of the SOM.

The distances of the neurons ww, wA, and wB can be computed as:

With the information obtained by Eqs. 7.7 and 7.8, the idea is to relate the position of the original input data with the information mapped in the output layer. The relation to this case, is defined as a rank function which is calculated as:

where m corresponds to the central unit of the lattice (m = (z * z)/2). The objective of the rank function is to keep a value near to one in the middle of the lattice, whereas in the border of the lattice a value near to zero.

The extracted information from Eqs. 7.7 to 7.9 will be used in the production of new solutions by the next step.

7.3.4 Solution Production

The main idea in the EA-SOM is that extracted information during the optimization process can be employed to guide the search strategy based on past information not only keeping the population elements through iterations but also maintaining local information of the output layer to improve the entire optimization process. For that, extracted information in the previous step is used to generate new solutions based on the detection of the promising regions in the output layer.

In this step, a set N of new solutions is generated. Since SOM maintains relationships between input data with the mapping of the lattice, new solutions can be produced considering that the original positions of the input data contain a high probability to be inside of the influence neighborhood by the winning neuron ww. This influence neighborhood acts as a radius among the neurons ww, wA, and wB which corresponds to promising search zones in the search space. The influence radius δ, is computed as:

Figure 7.6 graphically presents the intuition of the influence radius δ.

Finally, to produce N new solutions, the following model computed each:

where r represents a uniformly distributed random number in [0, 1].

 Note

An important aspect of the solution production scheme is that all the functionality of the proposed methodology relies on the relationship between the best solution in the optimization problem and the winning neuron as well as its neighborhood. The reader can design another search strategy contemplating different aspects of the extracted information. In this chapter, authors keep the simplest strategy in order to show the potential of extracting information during the optimization process.

7.3.5 New Training Set Construction

The produced N solutions from Eq. 7.11 contain solutions generated by the extracted information of the competitive learning model in SOM. The final step is to construct the new training set T(k + 1) for the next iteration of the EA-SOM. At each iteration, a new set containing N solutions will be produced. After a certain number of iterations, a large number of solutions will be generated. Under such circumstances, it is impractical to add the N generated solutions to the new training set. Therefore, considering that the size of the T(k + 1) will be the same as the population size, that is ND elements. It is assumed that N must be much less than ND. Under this scheme, only the first N elements will be part of T(k + 1). The rest of the elements will be randomly selected from the historical data H.

After the construction of T(k + 1), the historic memory will be updated as follows:

7.4 Computational Procedure

The algorithmic structure of the EA-SOM follows an iterative process, in which the steps from the previous are executed. Such procedures can be summarized in the Pseudo-code 7.1.

Pseudo-code 7.1 Computational Procedure of the Evolutionary-SOM (EA-SOM) Method

In Pseudo-code 7.1, Step 1 initializes the population of datapoints, as well as the historic memory, and the training set memory structure. Then, the competitive learning is executed in Step 2. Step 3 extracts information from the training stage. Step 4 generates new solutions. Finally, Step 5 constructs the new training set and updates the historical memory. This process repeats until a maximum number of iterations is reached.

7.5 Implementation of the EA-SOM Algorithm in MATLAB

In Algorithm 7.2, it is described the MATLAB code for the EA-SOM algorithm. To observe the functionality of the algorithm, the code encodes a benchmark function commonly used in performance testing related to the optimization of continuous functions. In this example, the Bird function is implemented, so that the reader can observe the functionality of the EA-SOM algorithm considering a minimization process.

The Bird function exhibits a non-convex unimodal surface in a 2-dimensional space and contains six global minima. The non-convex feature is used to test the scaling of the search strategy of the EA-SOM method when operates over surfaces that contain multiple global optima. On the other hand, the Bird function is continuous and non-convex, which indicates that no optimization technique either classical or metaheuristic can reach the global optimum. The mathematical model of the Bird function is as follows:

(7.13)

Finally, so that the reader can see the behavior of the datapoints on the Bird function surface, at each iteration the movement of the solutions (datapoints) on the Bird surface is plotted.

 

%Algorithm 7.2
%% INITIAL CONFIGURATION FOR THE OPTIMIZATION PROCESS
%Clear memory and Close Matlab windows
clear all;
close all;
 
 
%% Step 1 INITIALIZATION
%The maximum number of iterations is established
Max_Iter = 1000;
%The size of the population is established
Np = 50;
%The number of decision variables is established
dim = 2;
%The limits of the search space are defined
lb = -2*pi;
ub = 2*pi;
%Initialization of the initial population,
%X is the variable representing the population of Np elements
if size(ub,2)==1
    X=rand(Np,dim).*(ub-lb)+lb;
end
if size(ub,2)>1
    for i=1:dim
        high=ub(i);down=lb(i);
        X(:,i)=rand(Np,1).*(high-down)+down;
    end
end
%The fitness values of the initial population are obtained
fitness = ObjectiveFunction(X,dim);
%The population is sorted in ascending order
[fitnessA, indexSorted] = sort(fitness,'ascend');
%The best solution is obtained from the initial population
bestX = X(indexSorted(1),:);
bestFitness = fitnessA(1);
count = 0;
%Initialization of the SOM, in this example a lattice is composed by
% 20 * 20 neurons
dimM = 20;
rSampling = 20;
%The topology of the SOM is created
net = selforgmap([dimM dimM]);
%The plot the function to be optimized is computed
if dim<=2
    rangeUpLb=ub-lb;
    figure(1)
    x=[lb:rangeUpLb/100:ub];
    y=x;
    [xg,yg]=meshgrid(x,y);
    [row,col]=size(xg);
    for l=1:col
        for h=1:row
            z(h,l)=ObjectiveFunction([xg(h,l),yg(h,l)],dim);
        end
    end
end
%Iterative process of the algorithm
while count < Max_Iter
 
 
    %% Step 2 TRAINING
    P = [X';fitness];
    net = configure(net,P);
    %The number of epochs is established
    net.trainParam.epochs = 25;
    %This instruction disables the convergence
    %graph of the learning process
    net.trainParam.showWindow = 0;
    %The train is achieved by the MATLAB function train
    net = train(net,P);
    %The fitness values are sorted
    [fitness, indexSorted] = sort(fitness,'ascend');
    XTemp = X(indexSorted(1),:);
    FTemp = fitness(1);
    %Selection of the best solution so far
    if FTemp < bestFitness
        bestX = XTemp;
        bestFitness = FTemp;
    end
    data = [XTemp';FTemp];
    %SOM output
    out= net(data);
    %The index of the winning neuron is obtained
    neuron_aux=find(out==1);
    %The weight vector of the winning neuron is obtained
    Mat=net.IW{1,1};
    %The Euclidean distance among the winning neuron respect the
    %remaining neural units from the lattice is obtained. This
    %mechanism will be used in order to find the two closest neurons
    %around the winning neuron
    for Idx = 1 : dimM*dimM
        dis(Idx)= pdist2(Mat(Idx,1:end), Mat(neuron_aux,1:end));
    end
    [disS, ID]=sort(dis,'ascend');
    aux = find(disS,1);
    sd1 = (ID(aux))/(dimM*dimM);
    sd = mean(disS(aux:aux+2))/(max(disS(aux:end))-min(disS(aux:end)));
    sd = ((disS(aux)∧2)/(sd1))*sd;
    sd = sd∧(exp(-count/(1000-count)));
    %The weight vector of the winning neuron is perturb (this mechanism,
    %will promote solution diversity)
    Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim) = ...
(XTemp - Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim)) + ...
sd.*rand(1,dim);
    Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim) = ...
findrange( Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim),...
lb,ub,dim,1);
    Mat(neuron_aux,end) = ObjectiveFunction(Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim),dim);
 
 
    %% Step 3 KNOWLEDGE EXTRACTION
    %Based on the extracted information, a subset of neurons around the
    %winning neuron is created
    XNew = Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim);
    fitnessNew = Mat(neuron_aux,end);
    xSub = repmat(Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim),...
rSampling,1) + sd .* ...
rand(rSampling,dim);
    xSub = findrange(xSub,lb,ub,dim,size(xSub,1));
    fitnessSub = ObjectiveFunction(xSub,dim);
    XNew = [XNew;xSub];
    fitnessNew = [fitnessNew, fitnessSub];
 
 
    %% Step 4 SOLUTION PRODUCTION
    %The two closest neurons around the winning neuron are obtained
    T = ID(aux:aux+3);
    xSubNeurons = Mat(T,1:dim);
    xSubNeurons = findrange(xSubNeurons(:,1:dim), ...
lb,ub,dim,size(xSubNeurons,1));
    fitnessSubNeuronas = ObjectiveFunction(xSubNeurons,dim);
 
 
    %% Step 5 NEW TRAINING SET CONSTRUCTION
    XNew = [XNew;xSubNeurons];
    fitnessNew = [fitnessNew, fitnessSubNeuronas];
    %Since EA-SOM tend to produce several solutions at each generation,
    %a cleaning process is applied to avoid overfitting
    remaining = Np - size(XNew,1);
    if size(ub,2)==1
        XAux=rand(remaining,dim).*(ub-lb)+lb;
    end
    if size(ub,2)>1
        for i=1:dim
            high=ub(i);down=lb(i);
            XAux(:,i)=rand(remaining,1).*(high-down)+down;
        end
    end
    FAux = ObjectiveFunction(XAux,dim);
    X = [XNew;XAux];
    fitness = [fitnessNew,FAux];
    %The plot the population is generated
    if dim<=2
        surf(xg,yg,z);
        title('Bird function')
        hold on
        plot3(X(:,1),X(:,2),fitness(1,:),'o',...
             'markersize',6,'markerfacecolor','r');
        plot3(bestX(1,1),bestX(1,2),bestFitness,'o',...
             'markersize',10,'markerfacecolor','g');
        drawnow;
        hold off
    end
    %Iteration counters
    count = count + 1;
    fprintf('Iteration: %d\n',count);
    fprintf('Best solution: (%d,%d)\n',bestX(1,1),bestX(1,2));
    fprintf('Best fitness: %d\n',bestFitness);
end
 
 
%%OBJECTIVE FUNCTION
%Bird function implementation
function fit = ObjectiveFunction(L,dim)
    [N,∼]=size(L);
    for i=1:N
        fit(i) = sin(L(i,1))*exp((1-cos(L(i,2)))∧2) + ...
             cos(L(i,2))*exp((1-sin(L(i,1)))∧2) + ...
             (L(i,1)-L(i,2))∧2;
    end
end
 
 
%Find range function
function X = findrange(X,low,ub,dim,N)
    if size(ub,2)==1
        for j = 1 : N
            for i = 1:dim
                if (X(j,i) < low)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(ub-low)+low;
                end
                if (X(j,i)> ub)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(ub-low)+low;
                end
            end
        end
    end
    if size(ub,2)> 1
         for j = 1 : N
             for i = 1:dim
                high=ub(i);lb=low(i);
                if (X(j,i) < lb)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(high-lb)+lb;
                end
                if (X(j,i)> high)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(high-lb)+lb;
                end
             end
         end
    end
end

The Algorithm 7.2 graphically shows the evolution of the population using the iterative structure of the EA-SOM method. The plotted graph is shown in Figure 7.7.

In Algorithm 7.2, the Step 1 configures the initial parameters required by the optimization process. Such configuration relies on setting the maximum number of iterations, the population size, the number of decision variables involved in the optimization process, and the definition of the limits of the search space. Additionally, in this step, the structure of a SOM is defined. In the code, the built-in function selforgmap creates a lattice containing 20 * 20 neurons. The Step 2 defines the training phase of the EA-SOM. In this step, the competitive learning method is implemented to obtain the winning neuron. Then, in Step 3 the knowledge extraction mechanism is employed considering the algorithmic structure in Section 7.3.3. Step 4 defines the procedure for solution production which by the definition of the three closest neighbor neurons to the winning neuron. Finally, in Step 5 the new training set is built considering past solutions and produced solutions of Step 4. In the algorithm, the objective function to be optimized is implemented after the definition of the main loop. The objective function considered in this chapter is the well-known Bird function. Also, it is implemented a findrage function as an auxiliary function to limit the produced solutions maintained inside the limits of the search space.

7.6 Gear Design Optimization Problem Using the EA-SOM Algorithm in MATLAB

Most areas in engineering can present optimization problems to find the optimal solution to complex problems. From this perspective, the extensive necessity to apply an optimization algorithm to find the optimal solution is a required step for defining a solution. In Section 7.5, the code related to the implementation of the EA-SOM algorithm using a benchmark function that exhibits a multimodal complexity was presented. However, in such example, the EA-SOM performs over synthetic functions that do not represent a real application. Under this circumstance, this section analyzes an engineering design problem and describes how the EA-SOM method can be used to solve real-world applications. In this section, a gear design optimization problem is defined in order to be solved by the EA-SOM algorithm.

The design problem of a gear train is considered as a complex engineering problem where the objective is to design a gear train that can transmit maximum power. The mathematical description of the model is formulated as an optimization problem taking the following form:

(7.14)

where x1, x2, x3 and x4 represent the number of teeth for each of the gears. These values are distributed in a four-dimensional space (d = 4) and define the decision variables of the problem. Also, the limits of the search space corresponding to each dimension of the problem are defined as: 12 ≤ xi ≤ 60, i = 1, … 4. Figure 7.8 illustrates the design parameters for the assembly train. In the figure, the A corresponds to x1, B represents x2, D is represented by x3, and finally, F corresponds to x4.

The optimization process of this engineering problem using the EA-SOM algorithm is shown in Algorithm 7.3.

 

%Algorithm 7.3
%% INITIAL CONFIGURATION FOR THE OPTIMIZATION PROCESS
%Clear memory and Close Matlab windows
clear all;
close all;
 
 
%% Step 1 INITIALIZATION
%The maximum number of iterations is established
Max_Iter = 1000;
%The size of the population is established
Np = 50;
%The number of decision variables is established
dim = 4;
%The limits of the search space are defined
lb = 12;
ub = 60;
%Initialization of the initial population,
%X is the variable representing the population of Np elements
if size(ub,2)==1
    X=rand(Np,dim).*(ub-lb)+lb;
end
if size(ub,2)>1
    for i=1:dim
        high=ub(i);down=lb(i);
        X(:,i)=rand(Np,1).*(high-down)+down;
    end
end
%The fitness values of the initial population are obtained
fitness = ObjectiveFunction(X,dim);
%The population is sorted in ascending order
[fitnessA, indexSorted] = sort(fitness,'ascend');
%The best solution is obtained from the initial population
bestX = X(indexSorted(1),:);
bestFitness = fitnessA(1);
count = 0;
%Initialization of the SOM, in this example a lattice is composed by
% 20 * 20 neurons
dimM = 20;
rSampling = 20;
%The topology of the SOM is created
net = selforgmap([dimM dimM]);
%The plot the function to be optimized is computed
if dim<=2
    rangeUpLb=ub-lb;
    figure(1)
    x=[lb:rangeUpLb/100:ub];
    y=x;
    [xg,yg]=meshgrid(x,y);
    [row,col]=size(xg);
    for l=1:col
        for h=1:row
            z(h,l)=ObjectiveFunction([xg(h,l),yg(h,l)],dim);
        end
    end
end
%Iterative process of the algorithm
while count < Max_Iter
 
 
    %% Step 2 TRAINING
    P = [X';fitness];
    net = configure(net,P);
    %The number of epochs is established
    net.trainParam.epochs = 25;
    %This instruction disable the convergence graph of the learning
    %process
    net.trainParam.showWindow = 0;
    %The train is achieved by the MATLAB function train
    net = train(net,P);
    %The fitness values are sorted
    [fitness, indexSorted] = sort(fitness,'ascend');
    XTemp = X(indexSorted(1),:);
    FTemp = fitness(1);
    %Selection of the best solution so far
    if FTemp < bestFitness
        bestX = XTemp;
        bestFitness = FTemp;
    end
    data = [XTemp';FTemp];
    %SOM output
    out= net(data);
    %The index of the winning neuron is obtained
    neuron_aux=find(out==1);
    %The weight vector of the winning neuron is obtained
    Mat=net.IW{1,1};
    %The Euclidean distance among the winning neuron respect the
    %remaining neural units from the lattice is obtained. This
    %mechanism will be used in order to find the two closest
    %neurons around the winning neuron
    for Idx = 1 : dimM*dimM
        dis(Idx)= pdist2(Mat(Idx,1:end), Mat(neuron_aux,1:end));
    end
    [disS, ID]=sort(dis,'ascend');
    aux = find(disS,1);
    sd1 = (ID(aux))/(dimM*dimM);
    sd = mean(disS(aux:aux+2))/...
(max(disS(aux:end))-min(disS(aux:end)));
    sd = ((disS(aux)∧2)/(sd1))*sd;
    sd = sd∧(exp(-count/(1000-count)));
    %The weight vector of the winning neuron is perturb (this
    %mechanism, will promote solution diversity)
    Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim) = (XTemp - Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim)) + sd.*
rand(1,dim);
    Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim) = ...
findrange( Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim),lb,ub,dim,1);
    Mat(neuron_aux,end) = ...
ObjectiveFunction(Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim),dim);
 
 
    %% Step 3 KNOWLEDGE EXTRACTION
    %Based on the extracted information, a subset of neurons around
    %the winning neuron is created
    XNew = Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim);
    fitnessNew = Mat(neuron_aux,end);
    xSub = repmat(Mat(neuron_aux,1:dim),rSampling,1) + sd .*
rand(rSampling,dim);
    xSub = findrange(xSub,lb,ub,dim,size(xSub,1));
    fitnessSub = ObjectiveFunction(xSub,dim);
    XNew = [XNew;xSub];
    fitnessNew = [fitnessNew, fitnessSub];
 
 
    %% Step 4 SOLUTION PRODUCTION
    %The two closest neurons around the winning neuron are obtained
    T = ID(aux:aux+3);
    xSubNeurons = Mat(T,1:dim);
    xSubNeurons =
findrange(xSubNeurons(:,1:dim),lb,ub,dim,size(xSubNeurons,1));
    fitnessSubNeuronas = ObjectiveFunction(xSubNeurons,dim);
 
 
    %% Step 5 NEW TRAINING SET CONSTRUCTION
    XNew = [XNew;xSubNeurons];
    fitnessNew = [fitnessNew, fitnessSubNeuronas];
    %Since EA-SOM tend to produce several solutions at each
    %generation, a cleanning process is applied to avoid overfitting
    remaining = Np - size(XNew,1);
    if size(ub,2)==1
        XAux=rand(remaining,dim).*(ub-lb)+lb;
    end
    if size(ub,2)>1
        for i=1:dim
            high=ub(i);down=lb(i);
            XAux(:,i)=rand(remaining,1).*(high-down)+down;
        end
    end
    FAux = ObjectiveFunction(XAux,dim);
    X = [XNew;XAux];
    fitness = [fitnessNew,FAux];
    %The plot the population is generated
    if dim<=2
        surf(xg,yg,z);
        title('Bird function')
        hold on
        plot3(X(:,1),X(:,2),fitness(1,:),'o',...
             'markersize',6,'markerfacecolor','r');
        plot3(bestX(1,1),bestX(1,2),bestFitness,'o',...
             'markersize',10,'markerfacecolor','g');
        drawnow;
        hold off
    end
    %Iteration counters
    count = count + 1;
    fprintf('Iteration: %d\n',count);
    fprintf('Best solution: (%d,%d)\n',bestX(1,1),bestX(1,2));
    fprintf('Best fitness: %d\n',bestFitness);
end
 
 
%%OBJECTIVE FUNCTION
%Bird function implementation
function fit = ObjectiveFunction(L,dim)
    [N,∼]=size(L);
    for i=1:N
        fit(i) = ((1/6.931) - (L(3)*L(2)/L(1)*L(4))∧2);
    end
end
%Find range function
function X = findrange(X,low,ub,dim,N)
    if size(ub,2)==1
        for j = 1 : N
            for i = 1:dim
                if (X(j,i) < low)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(ub-low)+low;
                end
                if (X(j,i)> ub)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(ub-low)+low;
                end
            end
        end
    end
    if size(ub,2)> 1
         for j = 1 : N
             for i = 1:dim
                high=ub(i);lb=low(i);
                if (X(j,i) < lb)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(high-lb)+lb;
                end
                if (X(j,i)> high)
                    X(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(high-lb)+lb;
                end
             end
         end
    end
end

In Algorithm 7.3, the initial configuration declares the dimensionality and the limits of the search space according to the gear train design problem. The objective function implements the constraints mathematical formulation of Eq. 7.14.

8
Techniques of Machine Learning Mixed with Metaheuristic Methods

8.1 Introduction

Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are, arguably, the most popular machine learning (ML) technique among nonspecialists. This popularity is significantly due to recent developments in Deep Neural Networks (DNN), in particular Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Large Language Models (LLMs). The success of text and image generators based on DNNs has been such that artificial intelligence (AI) and ANNs have practically become interchangeable terms in the popular vocabulary. Although ANNs are perceived as a relatively new technique for this population sector, this is not the case. ANNs, as a branch of ML, can be dated back to the 1950s, particularly to the work of Frank Rosenblatt (1958), who invented the perceptron, the first implemented ANN.

The perceptron consists of only one layer of input nodes that send weighted inputs to a receiving node, generating an output value based on the activation function of choice. Although the ANNs currently in use are significantly more complex than the perceptron, the general functioning remains the same, where the efficacy of the network relies on choosing an appropriate architecture and finding the combination of weights that allows the network to generate the expected output for each presented input. Although significant efforts have been made to solve these two tasks, these are still open problems. Choosing the correct network architecture has proven difficult to automate, remaining primarily a craft where the designer’s expertise plays a central role in the network’s success. On the other hand, training the network, which is adjusting its weights, has well-established methods, such as backpropagation. During the training phase, the network is presented with labeled training data, and the weights are iteratively updated to minimize a defined loss function, ultimately allowing the network to generalize to unseen data.

Metaheuristic methods have been used to solve the network’s architecture automatic selection and the training process. To illustrate the hybridization of machine learning techniques and metaheuristic methods, this chapter presents the training of an ANN using a metaheuristic method. Namely, a Feedforward Neural Network (FNN), also known as a multilayer perceptron, is trained using the Flower Pollination Algorithm (FPA). We begin by presenting the FPA algorithm and its computational procedure. Then, we explain the generalities of ANNs and their training process. Finally, we explain how an ANN can be trained using a metaheuristic method, namely the FPA.

8.2 Flower Pollination Algorithm (FPA)

FPA, initially proposed by Yang (2012), takes inspiration from the pollination process of flowering plants as it occurs in natural environments. In general, flower pollination refers to the transferring of pollen between flowers of the same or different plants, a process so effective that it has allowed flowering plants to dominate the landscape. Pollination can be carried out in two ways: abiotic and biotic. Abiotic pollination refers to those cases where environmental agents such as wind or water carry the pollen from one flower to another. About 10% of the pollination processes fall into the abiotic case. The remaining 90% of pollination processes are of the biotic type; this is, the pollen is transported between flowers by living organisms like insects, bats, and birds. At the same time, pollination is divided into two groups according to their source: self-pollination and cross-pollination. These classifications are summarized in Table 8.1. In the context of FPA, while abiotic and self-pollination are associated with local search, biotic processes and cross-pollination are related to global search. One interesting phenomenon observed in biotic pollinators, and essential to the FPA, is the called flower constancy, a tendency of some pollinators to visit flowers of the same species.

Idealizing the above characteristics of the different types of pollination and pollinators and incorporating the flower consistency phenomenon, the FPA proposes the following rules:

  1. Global Rule: Biotics and cross-pollination are considered global pollination processes. Pollen-carrying pollinators performing Lévy flights.
  2. Local Rule: Abiotics and self-pollination are considered local pollination processes.
  3. Reproduction Rule: Flower constancy is considered as the reproduction probability proportional to the similarity of the two flowers involved.
  4. Switch Rule: The transition between local pollination and global pollination is controlled by a switch probability p ∈ [0, 1].

8.2.1 Global Rule and Lévy Flight

When the global rule is selected, the pollen is considered to be carried out by biotic pollinators such as insects and birds. Under this rule, the pollinators’ capacity to travel long distances and cover longer ranges ensures the reproduction of the fittest. To portray the behavior of biotic pollinators, taking pollen from one flower to the next and eventually flying over long distances, it is a common practice to resort to the Levy flight, mathematically defined in Eq. 8.1.

8.2.2 Local Rule

The local rule aims to mimic self-pollination and the process carried out by abiotic pollinators. This rule, including flower constancy, is given by Eq. 8.6.

where and represent different flowers from the same species and ∈ is a local random walk in the range [0, 1].

The switching rule is controlled by the parameter p. Usually, a parametric study must be conducted to find the most appropriate p-value to the problem at hand. The search begins with p = 0.5 for a balanced search. As p approaches 1, the probability of selecting the global rule increases. Otherwise, p values below 0.5 result on more frequent selection of the local rule.

8.2.3 Elitist Selection Procedure

The elitist selection procedure updates the solution population, one at a time, based on their fitness. This rule guarantees that the evolution of all solutions is always toward better performance. Under such circumstances, this operation indicates that only reasonable solutions will be stored through future generations. To accomplish elitist selection, a simple rule is applied. If the fitness value of the produced solution by the Eq. 8.5 or Eq. 8.6 is better than the current solution; the former replaces the latter. This mechanism is resumed in the following rules:

(8.7)

The overall functioning of the FPA algorithm is shown in the flowchart in Figure 8.1.

The implementation in MATLAB of the FPA algorithm to find the minimum of the Rosenbrock’s test function is presented in Algorithm 8.1. The code is divided into six steps that can also be found in the FPA flowchart (see Figure 8.1).

 

%Algorithm 8.1
%Clean data
close all
clear all
 
 
% Step 1, problem, and FPA parameters declaration
% problem parameters
dim = 2;                     % dimensionality
l_bound = -2*ones(1,dim);    % lower boundary
u_bound =  2*ones(1,dim);    % upper boundary
 
 
% FPA parameters
max_it = 3000;         % Maximum number of iterations
n = 20;                % Population size
p = 0.8;               % Switching probability
 
 
% Create aux structure
aux_ant.Position = [];
aux_ant.Cost = [];
 
 
% Step 2, 3 randomly initialization of the solutions set
% within the search space bounds and cost function evaluation
for i=1:n
    % Random solution
    POL(i).Position = unifrnd(l_bound, u_bound, [1,dim]);
    % Evaluation
    POL(i).Cost = fitness_function(POL(i).Position);
end
 
 
% 
S = POL;
 
 
% Init fitness history
fitness_history = zeros(max_it,1);
 
 
% FPA main loop
for k=1: max_it
    % Step 4, get best solution so far
    [fmin, I]= min([POL.Cost]);
    best = POL(I);
    fitness_history(k) = best.Cost;
 
 
    % Step 5, update solutions set
    for i=1:n
    % select between global and local rule
    if rand> p
        % Global rule case
        % Get Levy step for number of dimensions
        L = Levy(dim);
        dS = L.*(POL(i).Position – best.Position);
        S(i).Position = POL(i).Position + dS;
    else
        % Local rule case
        epsilon = rand;
        % Find two random flowers
        JK = randperm(n);
        ds = epsilon*(POL(JK(1)).Position - POL(JK(2)).Position);
        S(i).Position = POL(i).Position + ds;
    end
    % Check if within bounds
    S(i).Position = simplebounds(S(i).Position, l_bound, u_bound);
    % Step 6, Elitist selection
    % Cost function evaluation
    S(i).Cost = fitness_function(S(i).Position);
    if S(i).Cost <= POL(i).Cost,
        POL(i) = S(i);
    end
end
 
 
% Update fitness history
[fmin, I]= min([POL.Cost]);
best = POL(I);
fitness_history(k) = best.Cost;
 
 
%*******************************************************************
% PLOT COST FUNCTION AND BEST SOLUTION
%*******************************************************************
% Graphic representation Rosenbrock 
range=u_bound - l_bound; 
figure(1)
x1=[l_bound:range/100:u_bound];
y1=x1;
[X1,Y1]=meshgrid(x1,y1);
[row1,col1]=size(X1);
for q=1:col1
    for hh=1:row1
        vector = [X1(hh,q),Y1(hh,q)];
        zz(hh,q)=(1-vector(1))∧2+100*(vector(2)-vector(1)∧2)∧2;
    end
end
mesh(X1,Y1,zz, 'edgecolor', [0.5,0.5,0.5]);
hold on
 
 
% Add best solution
plot(best.Position(1),best.Position(2),'o', . . .
     'markersize',6,'markerfacecolor','r');
 
 
%*******************************************************************
% FUNCTIONS
%*******************************************************************
 
 
%*******************************************************************
% Lévy function
%*******************************************************************
function L=Levy(d)
   beta=3/2;
   sig_num = gamma(1+beta)*sin(pi*beta/2);
   sig_den = gamma((1+beta)/2)*beta*2∧((beta-1)/2)
   sigma=(sig_num/ sig_den)∧(1/beta);
    u=randn(1,d)*sigma;
    v=randn(1,d);
    step=u./abs(v).∧(1/beta);
    L=0.01*step;
end
 
 
%*******************************************************************
% Rosenbrock’s cost function
%*******************************************************************
function ft = fitness_function(xn)
   ft = (1-xn(1))∧2+100*(xn(2)-xn(1)∧2)∧2;
end

In Step 1 of the algorithm, the parameters of the problem and the FPA algorithm are defined, including the problem’s dimensionality, lower and upper boundaries, maximum number of iterations, population size, and switching probability (p). In Step 2, the solutions are randomly initiated, considering a uniform probability distribution across the entire search space. In Step 3, the fitness values are computed. The main loop takes place from Steps 4 to 6. First, the best solution so far is updated in Step 4. In Steps 5 and 6, the solutions are updated either by global or local rules and following an elitist selection principle. The algorithm iterates over Steps 4 to 6 till the stop criteria are met. Figure 8.2 shows the function and the best solution found by the FPA optimization.

8.3 Feedforward Neural Networks (FNNs)

Although certainly not a new type of machine learning algorithm, ANNs have gained popularity in recent years, mainly since the introduction of DNNs. ANNs are loosely based on the operation of biological neural systems. An ANN consists of an interconnected group of units called artificial neurons. In an ANN, neurons are aggregated into layers, and signals travel from the input layer to the output layer, passing through as many intermediate layers (hidden layers) as the model considers. The connections between artificial neurons aim to mimic synapses and have associated weights that increase or decrease the strength of the signal flowing through. Each artificial neuron receives input signals from one or multiple connected neurons; these signals are summed and internally processed by some nonlinear function (activation function) to generate an output signal, which is sent to other connected neurons.

ANNs are, in most cases, feedforward networks; this is, connections only allow signals to flow in one direction without any type of loops. However, it is also possible to find Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), a type of ANN with connections that allow signals to flow in both directions. These types of connections render RNNs with memory and make them ideal for applications such as speech and handwriting recognition.

For an ANN to produce the expected output, both architecture and weights must be optimized according to the problem at hand. Neither selecting the optimal architecture nor finding its weights are trivial tasks. Selecting the optimal architecture for an ANN; this is the number of layers, number of neurons per layer, type of connections, and activation function of each network is generally a trial-and-error process in which the designer’s expertise plays a central role. On the other hand, finding the weights to optimize the network’s performance is done through training, a process during which weights are adjusted iteratively. Undoubtedly, backpropagation is among the most popular training algorithms. The effectiveness of backpropagation depends on a series of decisions such as weights’ initialization, number of iterations, and learning rate.

Significant efforts have been made to optimize the ANN’s parameters, both related to its architecture and its weights. As a representative case, this chapter presents the optimization of an FNN’s weights using an FPA. A series of concepts must first be further covered to understand this process operation better.

8.3.1 Perceptron

In the early 1940s, Warren McCullochs and Walter Pitts, neurophysiologist and mathematician, respectively, proposed for the first time a model that aimed to describe how neurons interact with each other to classify an input into two different classes (McCulloch and Pitts 1943). Later, this model was improved by Rosenblatt (1958), who was also responsible for its first hardware implementation.

In the context of machine learning, the perceptron is a linear classifier that maps its input X (a vector of real values) to an output value f(X) (a single binary value) (Figure 8.3). Hence, the perceptron’s output can be represented using Eq. 8.8.

(8.8)

where H is the Heaviside step function and W is the vector of weights. The dot product , where n is the number of inputs to the perceptron, including the bias, which is used to shift the decision boundary and it is independent of any other input.

8.3.2 Feedforward Neural Networks (FNNs)

The perceptron’s limitation to exclusively solve linear classification problems (Minsky and Papert 1969) led to an eventual loss of interest in the topic of artificial neural networks among researchers. It was not until several years later, when it was proved that networks with two or more layers of neurons (FNNs) were significantly more potent than single (layer) perceptrons, that the field of NN experienced a resurgence. The extra layers of perceptrons, conferred FNNs the ability to classify nonlinearly separable data groups, being the first to report on it Shun’ichi Amari (1967). The general structure of an FNN (Figure 8.4) consists of:

  • An input layer.
  • At least one hidden layer.
  • An output layer.
  • Connections between consecutive layers.

Instead of the Heaviside function found on the perceptron, FNNs mainly rely on two sigmoidal activation functions:

(8.9)
(8.10)

where is the weighted input to the neuron. The hyperbolic tangent (Eq. 8.9) ranges from −1 to 1, while the logistic function (Eq. 8.10) ranges from 0 to 1. To reduce the computational cost of the training procedure and overcome numerical problems related to the saturation in sigmoids, these have been frequently substituted with the rectified linear unit (ReLU), particularly in the context of deep learning, where the number of layers and neurons has increased significantly with every new development.

 Note

It is worth noting the difference between the terms feedforward neural network (FNN) and multilayer perceptron (MLP), which, although sometimes used interchangeably, are not equivalent. The FFN is one of two broad groups in which ANNs are classified and refers to any artificial neural network consisting of three or more successive layers, where the signals flow unidirectionally, from input to output, and through the hidden layers. An MLP, on the other hand, is a type of FNN consisting of fully connected neurons with the Heaviside step function as an activation function. More modern FNN architectures include not-fully connected layers and use nonlinear activation functions. The other broad group in which ANNs are classified is recursive neural networks (RNNs), whose connections allow signals to flow in both directions.

8.4 Training an FNN Using FPA

Although ANNs can be trained following any of the three main learning paradigms in machine learning (supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning), the supervised learning approach allows for a straightforward understanding of how learning occurs in ANNs.

Under supervised learning, ANNs aim to minimize empirical risk, reducing the difference between the desired outputs and the actual outputs delivered by the model. During the training phase, ANNs are presented with a large number of labeled data, known as training set. The value of a defined loss function is obtained for each input–output pair. The ANN’s weights are updated at each turn to minimize the loss function. Usually, gradient-based methods are used to estimate the network’s weights update, with backpropagation being the most popular (Rumelhart et al. 1986).

As an alternative to backpropagation, the use of metaheuristic algorithms to train ANN has gained traction in the last decades. In specialized literature, it is possible to find examples of particle swarm optimization (PSO) (Yu et al. 2008), differential evolution (DE) (Ilonen et al. 2003), artificial bee colony (ABC) (Taheri et al. 2017), genetic algorithms (GA) (Harpham et al. 2004), and FPA (Kaya and Kaya 2021; Wang et al. 2019).

The learning process when using a metaheuristic algorithm instead of backpropagation remains the same overall. The major change resides in how the network’s weights are iteratively updated. In the particular case of the FPA, illustrated in Figure 8.5, each of the solutions in the FPA population represents a candidate set of weights for the NN. At each iteration, all candidate solutions are put to the test with a training set and its corresponding fitness value is obtained. Based on the solutions’ performance, the population is updated, keeping record of the best global solution. As with any implementation of the FPA, the optimization procedure ends when a fitness threshold is surpassed or the maximum number of iterations is met.

 Note

It is common to assume that ANNs can only be trained under a supervised learning approach. This might be because many texts only cover this case when explaining how ANNs learn, which is an understandable decision since supervised learning might be the most straightforward paradigm associated with ANNs’ training procedure. However, ANNs can also be trained following an unsupervised or reinforcement learning approach. As always, the type of learning paradigm of choice will depend on the task at hand. Maybe the most common case for unsupervised learning on ANN is clustering, standing out the Self-organized maps (SOM), an ANN type of architecture designed explicitly for clustering (Kohonen 1982).

With mixing machine learning and metaheuristic methods, it is crucial to keep in mind the advantages and limitations of both in order to make the most out of their hybridization. Training an ANN using a metaheuristic algorithm can be particularly beneficial when approaches based on gradient descent get stuck in local minima or plateaus of the loss function. However, metaheuristic algorithms are, in the rule, more computationally expensive than their gradient-based counterparts; hence, it is also important to consider the number of parameters (weights to adjust) when deciding for one of the approaches.

It is important to remember that, as mentioned in the introduction to this chapter, the hybridization of machine learning and metaheuristic methods is not limited to the training of ANNs using metaheuristic algorithms. Thanks to the large availability of training data, modern ANNs have become larger, and although in these scenarios of high-dimensional parameter space, the gradient descent might struggle to find the loss function’s global minimum, this might be preferred over the high cost of implementing an alternative methodology. However, adjusting hyperparameters to avoid overfitting can still be solved using metaheuristic algorithms or, even more critical, finding the right topology for the network (Stanley and Miikkulainen 2002).
