9
Metaheuristic Methods for Classification

9.1 Introduction

Classification is one of the most important topics in machine learning. In the classification task, the main goal is to label the inputs to a respective output such as , where C determines the number of classes. If the problem involves two classes the classification becomes a binary classification, otherwise, if the task considers more than two classes the problem becomes a multiclass classification. The classification can be determined into two different types: parametric models, which can be described employing statistical models with a fixed number of parameters, while the nonparametric models can change the number of parameters regarding the amount of training parameters.

On the other hand, metaheuristic approaches have been widely used in several areas because they employ different search strategies to determine optimal solutions to complex problems. Most metaheuristic techniques are based on the behavior of some species considering that they must overcome several difficulties over millions of years to survive developing the strategies for success. Under such considerations, computationally we emulate these behaviors to determine the best solution to different problems. In this chapter, we focus on the most employed techniques for classification and the Crow Search Algorithm (CSA) to improve the accuracy of classification techniques.

9.2 Crow Search Algorithm (CSA)

The CSA is a metaheuristic approach based on the intelligent conduct of crows and was presented by Askarzadeh (2016). Despite being a recent technique, the CSA has drawn the research community’s attention and has been employed and adjusted for solving comprehensive engineering problems (dos Santos Coelho et al. 2018; Meraihi et al. 2021). In the CSA, the goal is to emulate specific intelligent conducts of crows that have been considered one of the most brilliant birds in nature (Buniyaadi et al. 2020). Four principal conducts stand out in CSA: the ability to live in a flock, the capacity to hide food and remember the place of the hiding position, the capability to steal other crows’ food, and the self-awareness of being robbed.

Computationally, the CSA is conformed for a flock with N search particles (crows) where each of them is an n-dimensional vector, which n is related to the problem dimension. Each agent (crow) has a related memory for remembering the best position (hidden place) known until the current iteration. The position and the memory of the crow i at iteration k are described in Eqs. 9.1 and 9.2.

(9.1)
(9.2)

where maxIter is the stop criteria in the evolutionary process.

The new position for crow i on iteration k + 1 is carried out by either tracking or evasion. In both conducts, a crow i follows a crow j to discover its hidden place. In tracking, the crow i reaches its target and approaches the hiding location. In evasion, crow j detects the tracking crow i and assumes a random position. Equation 9.3 computationally describes these conducts.

(9.3)

where is the awareness probability parameter that manipulates the crow conducts if a random number (uniformly distributed between 0 and 1) is higher or equal than , then the pursuit is performed; otherwise, evasion is executed. In the pursuit stage, is the flight distance parameter which indicates the closeness degree toward the best position of crow j, is the best location of crow j, and is uniformly distributed in the range [0, 1]. The new crow location is computed in the objective function and its memory is calculated by Eq. 9.4.

(9.4)

The required stages of CSA are shown in the flowchart of Figure 9.1. In the first stage the problem is initialized (dimensions and limits) and the parameters of the CSA (fl, AP, stop criterion) are defined. In the next stage, the position of the population (crows) is initialized randomly through the search space and then each solution is evaluated employing the cost function of the problem. Then, new positions are calculated using Eq. 9.3 and their feasibility is proved. Once the new positions are generated, they are evaluated by the cost function, and the memory is updated. Finally, the stop criterion is verified to determine if the algorithm terminates or continues with the iterative process. The stop criterion is related directly to the application of the CSA, but two typical rules are employed: (1) the use of a maximum number of iterations, and (2) when the objective function value of the best particle converges and there are no changes along the iterations.

 

%Algorithm 9.1
%Clean data
close all
clear all
 
 
% Step 1, problem, and CSA parameters declaration
pd=2;
N=20;
AP=0.1;
fl=2;
l=-5.12;
u=5.12;
 
 
% Step 2, randomly initialization of the particles (crows)
% between lower and upper bounds
for i=1:N
    for j=1:pd
        x(i,j)=l-(l-u)*rand;
    end
end
 
 
% Step 3, evaluation of the population using the cost function
xn=x;
ft=fitness(xn,N);
 
 
% Save the population and they fitness in memory
mem=x;
fit_mem=ft;
 
 
% Step 4, the CSA generates new solutions where crows chase other
% crows and flying randomly through the search space
tmax=500;
for k=1:tmax
    num=ceil(N*rand(1,N));
    for i=1:N
        if rand>AP
            xnew(i,:)= x(i,:)+fl*rand*(mem(num(i),:)-x(i,:));
        else
            for j=1:pd
                xnew(i,j)=l-(l-u)*rand;
            end
        end
    end
 
 
% Step 5, evaluation of the new population using the cost function
xn=xnew;
ft=fitness(xn,N);
 
 
% Update position and memory
    for i=1:N
        if xnew(i,:)>=l & xnew(i,:)<=u
            x(i,:)=xnew(i,:);
            if ft(i)<fit_mem(i)
                mem(i,:)=xnew(i,:);
                fit_mem(i)=ft(i);
            end
        end
    end
end
 
 
% Step 6, display the best particle and its fitness value
[a, b] = min(fit_mem); respf = ['Best fitness:'];
respp = ['Best particle (crow):'];
disp (respf); min(fit_mem)
disp (respp); mem(b,:)
 
 
% Cost function
function ft=fitness(xn,N)
   for i=1:N
       ft(i)=sum(xn(i,:).∧2); % Sphere function
   end
end

In order to represent the main functioning of the CSA, Algorithm 9.1 shows the implementation in MATLAB and the Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox. As we mentioned in the flow chart, the first step is determining the problem parameters (number of variables), lower and upper bounds (physics or design limitations in the parameters of certain applications), and the algorithm parameters setting (each metaheuristic approach has its own parameter setting). In Step 2, the population (crows) is generated using random numbers drawn from a uniform distribution. In Step 3 each element (crow) of the population must be evaluated, this evaluation indicates the quality of the solution, to determine this evaluation is necessary a metric better known as cost function or objective function. Once the particles have been evaluated, they are saved into a memory where the best solutions are collected.

In Step 4, the operators of the CSA are employed to generate the chasing behavior of crows or flying randomly through the search space to determine feasible solutions. To carry out this step, an awareness probability (AP) and flight length (fl) are set previously, if a number randomly generated is higher than the AP the chasing behavior is performed, otherwise, the random flight is conducted. In Step 5, the new population is evaluated employing the cost function and is compared with the population previously stored in the memory, if the new position of the particle j + 1 has a better quality than the same particle at iteration j then is replaced, otherwise, remains.

In this case, the test function known as the sphere function is employed. To perform this experiment, the number of dimensions (variables of the problem) and the upper and lower bounds must be set by the user considering the characteristics of the problem to be treated. For this experimental example, the upper and lower bounds are 5.12 and −5.12 respectively, and the dimensions are set in 2 for a good appreciation of the reader. Under such circumstances, the CSA employs its search strategy to determine the values between these ranges that better results provide considering that the goal is the minimization of the cost function (in this case the optimal solution is zero). Figure 9.2 shows the graphical representation of the sphere function, Figure 9.2a is the 3D representation while Figure 9.2b is the same representation but in a view of 2D from the bottom.

9.3 CSA for Nearest-Neighbor Method (k-NN)

The Nearest-Neighbor Method is one of the most straightforward techniques for classification in machine learning, and due to its easy implementation, it is widely employed in several applications. In this approach, the data from different groups are labeled during the training stage while once a new observation is acquired, the distance between the closest N samples regarding the new data is determined. Under such an approach, this new observation is labeled to a group by considering the consensus of the closest neighbors (Biau and Devroye 2015).

In this example, the CSA is employed to improve the classification task of the k-NN approach using the operators to perform a search in the space of feasible solutions. As we mentioned before, k-NN is the simplest classification technique where some parameters can be determined by the user in order to obtain a better outcome. Under such considerations, the main element is the number of the k-elements that better train the model for a specific dataset. In this case, the employed data is the Iris dataset which is widely used for academic tasks. This is a small dataset that MATLAB already includes within its software distribution in which the elements are easily distinguished between them.

This database considers 150 samples that include four characteristics of different flowers, to get this database, we use the follow command:

>> load fisheriris

After the database is loaded, the information is separated into a matrix that contains the four characteristics of the flowers, and a vector that labels the types of flowers with such traits.

>> X = meas;
>> Y = species;

When the matrix X and vector Y are defined, 70% of the data contained are used in the training stage of the k-NN method, and the left 30% in the test stage (Xtrain, SpeciesTrain, Xtest, Speciestest) as is shown in Step 1. Under such circumstances, the CSA must be modified in terms of this new application where the number of dimensions is set in 1 considering that the number of neighbors must be determined by the optimization approach, lower and upper bounds are set in 1 and 20 respectively as is indicated in Step 2, here the initialization remains as in Algorithm 9.1.

To perform the k-NN classification with the CSA, the main structure of Algorithm 9.1 remains but the cost function (objective function) must be replaced by one that considers the specifications of the problem, in this case, the cost function is replaced by Algorithm 9.2.

 

%Algorithm 9.2
%Clean data
close all
clear all
 
 
% Step 1, problem, and CSA parameters declaration
pd=1;
N=1;
AP=0.1;
fl=1.5;
load fisheriris
X = meas;
a1 = X(1:35,:);  a11 = X(36:50,:);
a2 = X(51:85,:);   a22 = X(86:100,:);
a3 = X(101:135,:);   a33 = X(136:150,:);
Xtrain = [a1; a2; a3];  Xtest= [a11; a22; a33];
b1 = species (1:35,:);  b11 = species (36:50,:);
b2 = species (51:85,:);   b22 = species (86:100,:);
b3 = species (101:135,:);   b33 = species (136:150,:);
SpeciesTrain = [b1; b2; b3];   Speciestest= [b11; b22; b33];
 
 
% Step 2, randomly initialization of the particles (crows)
% between lower and upper bounds
 
 
% Step 3, evaluation of the population using the cost function
 
 
% Save the population and they fitness in memory
 
 
% Step 4, the CSA generates new solutions where crows chase other
% crows and flying randomly through the search space
 
 
% Step 5, evaluation of the new population using the cost function
 
 
% Update position and memory
 
 
% Step 6, display the best particle and its fitness value
gscatter(Xtrain(:,1), Xtrain(:,2), SpeciesTrain,'rgb','osd');
xlabel('Sepal length');
ylabel('Sepal width');
hold on
plot(Xtest(1:15,1), Xtest(1:15,2), '*', 'markersize',...
10, 'markerfacecolor','r');
hold on
plot(Xtest(16:30,1), Xtest(16:30,2), '+', 'markersize',...
10, 'markerfacecolor', 'g');
hold on
plot(Xtest(31:45,1), Xtest(31:45,2), '.', 'markersize',...
10, 'markerfacecolor','g');
legend ('Setosa', 'Vericolor', 'Virginica', 'SetosaTest',...
'VericolorTest', 'VirginicaTest')
 
 

 
% Cost function
function ft=fitness(xn, N, Xtrain, YTrain, Xtest, Ytest)
   for i=1:N
      Mdl = fitcknn(Xtrain, YTrain,'NumNeighbors', xn(i));
      ypredict = predict(Mdl, Xtest);
      T = strcmp (ypredict, Ytest); incorrect = find (T == 0);
      ft (i) = (length(Ytest) - length (incorrect))/length(Ytest);
   end
end

For this example, we use the MATLAB software distribution k-NN technique which can be employed by the following command.

>> Mdl = fitcknn (Features, Labels, 'NumNeighbors', k)

This command needs at least two input arguments that represent the characteristics of the elements to be classified, the labels of the objects, and optionally the k elements to train the technique, otherwise, the technique determines a fixed number of elements. In Algorithm 9.2, the k-NN train is determined by Mdl where the features (4 features available in the database) and labels are introduced from the database previously loaded, and the number of k elements is determined by the CSA for each particle (crow). Once the data is complete and the model trained, we employ the left 30% of the data to test the k-NN model using the predict command. When the trained model is tested, the metric employed as the new cost function is the accuracy of the model determined in Eq. 9.5.

(9.5)

where trp expresses the true prediction determined by the model, and tp is the total of predictions. Under this consideration, the CSA has a metric that helps to determine the next step in the search strategy. For this example, the CSA is able to determine the necessary number of k elements that better perform the classification set in 5 to get the 100% of true classification. Figure 9.3 shows the result of the training and test classification in the case of the Iris database, where the circle, square, and rhomb represent the training data while star, plus sign, and dot represent the test data.

 Note

When a specific application is performed employing a metaheuristic approach, the user must be careful of the specification, constrains, and specifications of the problem. In this example, the particles (crows) must be integers positives due to the number of k neighbors cannot be decimal.

9.4 CSA for Logistic Regression

Logistic regression is an example of a parametric approach, this technique is similar to linear regression, but the main difference is laid out in the binary outcome [0, 1] as well as in the parametric model and the hypothesis (Hosmer et al. 1989). This regression employs the expression also known as the logistic function or sigmoidal due to its peculiar “S” shape shown in Figure 9.4. As we mentioned before, this function can map all real numbers scale into the interval [0, 1] and can be described as in the following expression.

(9.6)

In this example as well as in the k-NN, the CSA approach is employed to determine the best classification process in a binary dataset that describes the score of two tests on the scale of [0, 100] and in a binary result [0, 1] which represents if the participants were or not accepted for a certain job. The dataset employed in this example is presented in Table 9.1 and the implementation is presented in Algorithm 9.3.

 

%Algorithm 9.3
%Clean data
close all
clear all
 
 
% Step 1, problem, and CSA parameters declaration
pd=3;
N=10;
AP=0.1;
fl=1.5;
x1 = readmatrix('logitdata.xlsx');
X = x1(:, [1,2]); X = zscore(X);
Y = x1(:, 3);
in = find (Y ==1); out = find(Y==0);
[m,n] = size(X);
X =  [ones(m,1) X];
 
 
% Step 2, evaluation of the population using the cost function
x=zeros(N,pd);
xn=x;
[ft, S]=fitness(xn, X, Y, N);
 
 
% Save the population and they fitness in memory
mem=x;
fit_mem=ft;
 
 
% Step 4, the CSA generates new solutions where crows chase other
% crows and flying randomly through the search space
 
 
% Step 5, evaluation of the new population using the cost function
 
 
% Step 6, display the best particle and its fitness value
[a, b] = min(fit_mem); respf = ['Best fitness:'];
respp = ['Best particle (crow):'];
disp (respf); min(fit_mem)
disp (respp); mem(b,:)
 
 
syms x1 x2
fnn=mem(b,1)+mem(b,2)*x1+mem(b,3)*x2-0.5;
plot (X(in, 2), X(in, 3),'*k'); hold on
plot (X(out, 2), X(out, 3),'+b');
fimplicit (fnn);
legend('Accepted','Rejected','Decision boundary')
 
 
% Cost function
function [ft, S]=fitness(xn, X, Y, N)
    for i=1:N
      m = length (Y);
      S = sigm(X*xn');
      ft  = (-1/m) * sum (Y.* log(S) + (1-Y).*log(1-S));
    end
end
 
 
% Logistic function
function S = sigm(z)
    S = zeros (size(z) );
    [m , n] = size(z) ;
    for i = 1:m
        for j = 1:n
            S (i,j) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z(i,j)) );
        end
    end
end

In Step 1 all parameters of the CSA are initialized, and the database is loaded from an xlsx file which is located in the same directory of the script. Once the data is loaded, two different sets are generated in order to train our model the information data and the labels, as the classification task involves two possible results, true or false, the labels are in a binary format [0, 1]. For simplicity, after the data separation, the training data are standardized and identify the true and false cases. In Step 2, for simplicity, the initial parameters are set to zero and evaluated using the cost function described in Eq. 9.7. After that, the fitness value is stored in the memory.

(9.7)

Steps 4 and 5 remain with no modifications, the algorithm iterates until the stop criteria is reached. Step 6 plots the elements that are rejected and the accepted considering the qualification obtained in the two tests while the line represents the decision boundary due to the logistic classification. The graphical representation is presented in Figure 9.5.

9.5 CSA for Fisher Linear Discriminant

The Fisher linear discriminant is a classification approach that has been widely employed in two-dimensional problems for simple applications, on the other hand, as the difficulty of the problem increases the computational complexity considerably increases. Fisher linear discriminant (FLDA) is a supervised parametric classification that employs dimensionality reduction approaches to perform the classification task. For this example, the simplest case where two classes are considered, after the analysis, the study can be generalized into N different classes (Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David 2013).

Suppose that we have a set of data which are conformed for two classes, the main objective is determine the vector defined by such that the N-dimensional space better separate the defined classes projected in (Figure 9.6).

 Note

As we mentioned before, the FLDA is an approach that can be used for dimensionality reduction and classification approaches. The FLDA shares some features regarding the Principal Component Analysis (PCA) in which the dimensions are reduced by considering the elements (dimensions) that more variations contribute to the study. On the other hand, the most variation of data is not crucial in the FLDA approach, instead, the variation of data in this technique focuses on maximizing the separability between two groups in order to make the best decision when new data is considered in such an analysis.

To clarify the functioning of the FLDA employing the CSA, we are required to generate a dataset, for simplicity, the number of characteristics is 2 and we consider 25 samples. In Step 1 of Algorithm 9.4, the CSA initial parameters and the dataset are generated and separated into two groups that are labeled with [1, 0].

Step 2 generates the initial population; in this specific application, a single particle is used for simplicity. However, the population can be increased as the user considers appropriate where the upper and lower bounds are set in 1 and −1, respectively. After the initialization, the population is evaluated using the cost function which must be generated by considering the application’s specific requirements. In the case of the FLDA, the main goal is to determine the line that better separates the classes. Under such circumstances, the cost function maximizes the distance between classes. The cost function is represented in Eq. 9.8, where m1 and m2 are the means of groups 1 and 2, respectively.

(9.8)

 

%Algorithm 9.4
%Clean data
clear all
close all
% Step 1, problem, and CSA parameters declaration
pd=2;
N=2;
AP=0.1;
fl=1.5;
 
 
% Generate the database
 
 
X = [randn(10,2); randn(15,2) + 1.5];  Y = [zeros(10,1); ones(15,1)];
Xaux1 = find (Y==1); X1 = (X(Xaux1,:));
Xaux2 = find (Y==0); X2 = (X(Xaux2,:));
 
 
% Step 2, randomly initialization of the particles (crows) between
% lower and upper bounds
[-1,1]
l= -1;
u= 1;
for i=1:N
    for j=1:pd
        x(i,j)=l-(l-u)*rand;
    end
end
 
 
% Step 3, evaluation of the population using the cost function
 
 
% Save the population and they fitness in memory
 
 
% Step 4, the CSA generates new solutions where crows chase other
% crows and flying randomly through the search space
 
 
% Step 5, evaluation of the new population using the cost function
 
 
% Update position and memory
 
 
% Step 6, display the best particle and its fitness value
 
 
[a, b] = min(fit_mem); respf = ['Best fitness:'];
respp = ['Best particle (crow):'];
disp (respf); min(fit_mem)
disp (respp); mem(b,:)
 
 
xaux = [xn(1,1:2); xn(1,3:4)];
a1=X1 * xaux; a2=X2 * xaux;
plot (X2(:, 1), X2(:, 2),'*r');
hold on
plot (X1(:, 1), X1(:, 2),'+b');
legend ('Group 1', 'Group 2');
figure
plot (a2(:, 1), a2(:, 2),'*r');
hold on
plot (a1(:, 1), a1(:, 2),'+b');
legend ('Group 1', 'Group 2');
 
 
% Cost function
function [ft]=fitness(xn, X1, X2)
 
 
    x = [xn(1,1:2); xn(1,3:4)];
    G1 = X1 * x; G2 = X2 * x;
    m1 = mean (G1); m2 = mean (G2);
    ft = (norm (m1-m2));
 
 
end

Once the CSA determines the best elements of the matrix w, the data is plotted in two graphics, Figure 9.7a shows the original database where the groups are represented with ‘*’ and ‘+’ while Figure 9.7b shows the data representation after the FLDA analysis. Under such circumstances, the experimental results generate new positions of the data where the distance between means is bigger.

9.6 CSA for Naïve Bayes Classification

Naïve Bayes (NB) classification approach is a classification technique based on the likelihood of belonging to a certain group due to the features of an element. The NB technique classifies the k values of a N number of features . This approach does not consider the possible correlation between elements, or in other words, NB considers that the data are conditionally independent (Wickramasinghe and Kalutarage 2021). In order to perform an example of NB employing the CSA to improve the performance of the classification approach, the command of the MATLAB software distribution employed is described below.

Mdl = fitcnb(Tbl,ResponseVarName)

As the NB approach is based on probabilities, the optimization technique must be employed for a different consideration. In Algorithm 9.5 the complete optimization process is presented, nevertheless as in the last examples, the steps that change regarding the original CSA are shown while the steps that are the same as the original CSA are omitted but are mentioned in the code.

In this example, a dataset of 1200 samples randomly generated is employed. Step 1 shows the data generation where 80% are used for training while the last 20% are employed to test the trained model. Under the characteristics of the NB technique, the CSA is employed to determine the number of elements that better classify the train data considering the lower quantity of elements. In the data generation, the 480 elements are considered for training and 120 for testing, the data are separated into two groups labeled with [0, 1] as seen in Figure 9.7.

 

%Algorithm 9.5
%Clean data
clear all
close all
 
 
% Step 1, problem, and CSA parameters declaration
pd=480;
N=10;
AP=0.1;
fl=1.5;
 
 
% Generate database
 
 
X = [randn(600,2); randn(600,2) + 1.5];
Y1test = [zeros(120,1)]; Y2test = [ones(120,1)];
X1train = X((1:480),:); X1test = X((481:600),:);
X2train = X((601:1080),:); X2test = X((1081:1200),:);
Xtest = [X1test; X2test];
Y1train = [zeros(480,1)]; Y2train = [ones(480,1)];
Ytest = [zeros(120,1); ones(120,1)];
 
 
% Step 2, Randomly initialization of the particles (crows) between
% lower and upper bounds
l= 1;
u= 480;
for i=1:N
    for j=1:pd
        x(i,j)=l-(l-u)*rand;
    end
end
 
 
% Step 3, Evaluation of the population using the cost function
 
 
xn=x;
[X, Mdl, ft, Tind] = fitness(xn, X1train, X2train, N,...
Xtest, Y1train, Y2train, Ytest);
 
 
% Save the population and they fitness in memory
 
 
% Step 4, the CSA generates new solutions where crows chase other
% crows and flying randomly through the search space
 
 
% Step 5, evaluation of the new population using the cost function
 
 
% Update position and memory
 
 
% Step 6, Display the best particle and its fitness value
[a, b] = min(fit_mem); respf = ['Best fitness:'];
respp = ['Best particle (crow):'];
disp (respf); min(fit_mem)
disp (respp); resp = mem(b,:);
best = resp(ind_mem(:,b))
 
 
% Cost function
function [X, Mdl, ft, Tind]=fitness(xn, X1train, X2train, ...
N, Xtest, Y1train, Y2train, Ytest)
 
 
    xn1 = round(xn);
    for i=1:N
        for j=1: length(xn1)
    if (0<=xn1(i,j)) & (xn1(i,j)>= 480)
       xn1 (i,j)=479;
   else
       xn1 (i,j) =  xn1 (i,j);
    end
        end
    end
    mi = min(min(xn1(:,1)));
    ma = max(max(xn1(:,1)));
 
 
    for i=1:N
        indx = randi ([mi ma],1, xn1(N,1) ); %indx = round(indx)';
        tr1 = X1train(indx,:); tr2 = X2train(indx,:);
        y1 = Y1train(indx); y2 = Y2train(indx);
        Y = [y1 ; y2];
        X = [tr1; tr2];
        Mdl = fitcnb(X,Y);
        pred = predict(Mdl, Xtest);
        good = 0; bad = 0;
        for j = 1 : length (pred)
            if pred (j) == Ytest(j)
                good = good + 1;
            else
                bad = bad + 1;
            end
        end
        ft(i) = (1 / (good / length (pred)));
        Tind (:,i) = indx;
    end
end

In Step 2 the CSA and problem parameters are configured, where the population size is 10 and the number of dimensions is considered the same number of elements that are included in the study (480) that represent the number of elements of each group as is shown in Figure 9.8. Step 3 evaluates the objective function in which the model is trained considering the number of elements that the CSA determines optimal for the classification task. In Steps 4 and 5, the optimization process is performed employing the search strategy of the CSA until the stop criterion is reached. In the cost function, a validation step is included to guarantee that all particles are within the bounds of the problem. Once the best solution is determined by the CSA, the result is displayed where the final elements employed to determine the best classification as well as the fitness value are shown.

9.7 CSA for Support Vector Machine

The support vector machine (SVM) is an unsupervised classification technique which generates a hyperplane that maximizes the distance between groups for a better generalization. Originally the SVM was generated to solve binary problems, nevertheless, can be extended for multiclass classification (Farhat 1992; Shalev-Shwartz and Srebro 2008). Considering a pair of training data which are considered as linearly separable labeled into two different groups [1, −1] in the case of binary classification where the separation class maximizes the distance between them as can be shown in Figure 9.9.

In order to perform the example considering that the CSA improves the model’s internal parameters, the data and main structure of the CSA_NN employed is reported in the literature by Mousavi (2017). Under such circumstances, the functioning algorithm is shown in Algorithm 9.6. Due to this example’s characteristics, the algorithm’s corresponding steps are considered in the generation of the network and for the result display instead of the main CSA functioning.

In Step 1, training data is loaded from a previously generated data file containing 40 elements with 300 features each. The elements are labeled with their respective groups (6 groups for this example) and the dimensions of the problem to generate the network are defined. Once the number of hidden layers is set, the construction of the network is performed in Step 2 employing the MATLAB command described below.

net = newff(P,T,S)

where P represents the features of the elements, T is the target or the labels of each element, and S is the data of the network such as the parameters number and hidden layers.

 

%Algorithm 9.6
%Clean data
clear all
close all
 
 
% Step 1, Generate the data for the training and test.
netdata=load('Test.mat');
netdata=netdata.FinalReady;
% Data, groups, and variable change
network=netdata(:,1:end-1); netlbl=netdata(:,end);
inputs = network; targets = netlbl;
% Dimension of the problem
InputNum = size(inputs,2);
OutputNum = size(targets,2);
pr = [-1 1];
PR = repmat(pr,InputNum,1);
 
 
% Number of Hidden Layers
NH=5;
 
 
% Step 2, Generation of the first Network
Network1 = newff(PR,[NH OutputNum],{'tansig' 'tansig'});
 
 
% Step 3, CSA for improving the network training
Network1 = CSA_NN(Network1,inputs,targets);
 
 
% Step 4, Obtain the Outputs of the CSA_NN model
outputs = Network1(inputs');
outputs=outputs';
sizenet=size(network);
sizenet=sizenet(1,1);
 
 
% Computing the error in of the CSA_NN
MSE=mse(outputs);
% Bias Output for Confusion Matrix
outputs=outputs-(MSE*0.1)/2;
 
 
% Detecting Mislabeled Data
for i=1 : 50
            if outputs(i) <= 0.9
               out(i)=0;
        elseif outputs(i)>= 0.9
               out(i)=1;            end;end;
for i=51 : 100
            if outputs(i) <= 0.9
               out(i)=0;
        elseif outputs(i)>= 0.9
               out(i)=2;            end;end;
for i=101 : 150
            if outputs(i) <= 0.9
               out(i)=0;
        elseif outputs(i)>= 0.9
               out(i)=3;            end;end;
for i=151 : 200
            if outputs(i) <= 0.9
               out(i)=0;
        elseif outputs(i)>= 0.9
               out(i)=4;            end;end;
for i=201 : 250
            if outputs(i) <= 0.9
               out(i)=0;
        elseif outputs(i)>= 0.9
               out(i)=5;            end;end;
for i=251 : 300
            if outputs(i) <= 0.9
               out(i)=0;
        elseif outputs(i)>= 0.9
               out(i)=6;            end;end;
       out1=single(out');
% CSA Final Accuracy
       psomse=mse(out1,targets);
       MSEError=abs(mse(targets)-mse(out1));
       cnt=0;
       for i=1:sizenet
           if out1(i)∼= targets(i)
               cnt=cnt+1;
           end;
       end;
      fin=cnt*100/ sizenet;
      psoacc=(100-fin)-psomse;
 
 
%% Step 5, Display the classification result
 
 
figure
set(gcf, 'Position',  [50, 100, 1300, 300])
cmpso = confusionchart(out1,targets);
cmpso.Title = (['CSA NN Classification =  ' num2str(psoacc) '%']);
 
 
%%%%%% Functions description %%%%%%%%%%%
 
 
%% Crow Search Algorithm NN training
 
 
function [Network2  BestCost] = NBCSA(Network,Xtr,Ytr)
 
 
IW = Network.IW{1,1}; IW_Num = numel(IW);
LW = Network.LW{2,1}; LW_Num = numel(LW);
b1 = Network.b{1,1}; b1_Num = numel(b1);
b2 = Network.b{2,1}; b2_Num = numel(b2);
TotalNum = IW_Num + LW_Num + b1_Num + b2_Num;
NPar = TotalNum;
 
 
% Problem, and CSA parameters declaration
pd=NPar;
N=20;
AP=0.1;
fl=1.5;
 
 
% Randomly initialization of the particles (crows) between lower and
% upper bounds
l= -1;
u= 1;
for i=1:N
    for j=1:pd
        x(i,j)=l-(l-u)*rand;
    end
end
 
 
% Evaluation of the population using the cost function
 
 
xn=x';
ft = fitness(xn,Xtr,Ytr,Network, N);
 
 
% Save the population and they fitness in memory
mem=x;
fit_mem=ft;
 
 
% The CSA generates new solutions where crows chase other crows and
% lying randomly through the search space
tmax=100;
for t=1:tmax
    num=ceil(N*rand(1,N));
    for i=1:N
        if rand>AP
            xnew(i,:)= x(i,:)+fl*rand*(mem(num(i),:)-x(i,:));
        else
            for j=1:pd
                xnew(i,j)=l-(l-u)*rand;
            end
        end
    end
% Evaluation of the new population using the cost function
xn=xnew';
ft = fitness(xn,Xtr,Ytr,Network, N);
 
 
% Update position and memory
    for i=1:N
        if xnew(i,:)>=l & xnew(i,:)<=u
            x(i,:)=xnew(i,:);
            if ft(i)<fit_mem(i)
                mem(i,:)=xnew(i,:);
                fit_mem(i)=ft(i);
            end
        end
    end
end
 
 
% Display the best particle and its fitness value
[a, b] = min(fit_mem); respf = ['Best fitness:'];
respp = ['Best particle (crow):'];
disp (respf); min(fit_mem)
disp (respp); resp = mem(b,:);
% best = resp(ind_me2m(:,b))
Network2 = NetConstruct(Network,mem(b,:));
BestCost = min(fit_mem);
 
 
end
 
 
%% fitness function
function ft = fitness(xn,Xtr,Ytr,Network, N)
    ft = zeros(N,1);
        for ii = 1:N
            X = xn(:,ii);
            Network = NetConstruct(Network,X);
            YtrNet = sim(Network,Xtr')';
            C = mse(YtrNet - Ytr);
            ft(ii,1) = C;
        end
end
 
 
%% Network construction
function Network2 = NetConstruct(Network,X)
    IW = Network.IW{1,1}; IW_Num = numel(IW);
    LW = Network.LW{2,1}; LW_Num = numel(LW);
    b1 = Network.b{1,1}; b1_Num = numel(b1);
    b2 = Network.b{2,1}; b2_Num = numel(b2);
    IWs = X(1:IW_Num); IW = reshape(IWs,size(IW,1),size(IW,2));
    LWs = X(IW_Num+1:IW_Num+LW_Num);
    LW = reshape(LWs,size(LW,1),size(LW,2));
    b1s = X(IW_Num+LW_Num+1:IW_Num+LW_Num+b1_Num);
    b1 = reshape(b1s,size(b1,1),size(b1,2));
    b2s = X(IW_Num+LW_Num+b1_Num+1:IW_Num+LW_Num+b1_Num+b2_Num);
    b2 = reshape(b2s,size(b2,1),size(b2,2));
    Network2 = Network;
    Network2.IW{1,1} = IW;
    Network2.LW{2,1} = LW;
    Network2.b{1,1} = b1;
    Network2.b{2,1} = b2;
end

When the network is generated, the CSA is employed to improve the internal parameters of the NN to perform a better classification of the data. In this case, the optimization technique (CSA) is called a function which is described in the section of functions description, in this section the CSA employs its search strategy for determining the best solution considering the classification data as is shown in Step 3. Once the result of the CSA is performed the parameters are used for generating the final NN trained for the specific task. Step 4 determines the error and the mislabeled data to show the classification result using a confusion matrix. Finally, in Step 5 the result is displayed showing the right and worn classification as is shown in Figure 9.10.

10
Metaheuristic Methods for Clustering

10.1 Introduction

Clustering is one of the most important tasks in machine learning projects. Clustering is a set of techniques which aim to create homogeneous groups of objects or entities called clusters. Each group of objects share similarities among their elements. Different clusters yield to different categorization or classes among data. In most of the data science projects, after the data cleaning process and preparation, clustering methods are often carried out before any analytical modeling.

Clustering falls under the category of unsupervised learning (Ezugwu et al. 2022). That means there is no labeled class for a given dataset. The objective of each clustering algorithm is to form groups of elements without prior knowledge of each input data vector. Each clustering algorithm assigns membership values to all data linked to each cluster center. However, even when clustering algorithms are essential techniques for data analysis process, they contain some limitation such as initialization, false positive response, and sensitivity to data outliers.

On the other hand, metaheuristic methods have been widely used in several disciplines since they employ different search mechanisms to determine optimal solutions in complex optimization tasks. Recently, metaheuristic approaches have been applied to overcome some difficulties of clustering. The flexibility of metaheuristics can reformulate the clustering task by improving the performance of the clustered outcomes (Dhaenens and Jourdan 2022).

In the year 2009, Xin-She Yang and Suash Deb proposed an evolutionary algorithm based on the phenomenon of nest parasitism which is present in some kind of birds, fish, or insects. Within nature, there is a kind of bird called a cuckoo bird, which represents a species that uses the phenomenon of parasitism to lay eggs in the nests of other species. The Cuckoo Search Method (CSM) has been proposed as a model that mimics the natural behavior of cuckoo birds that computationally solves optimization problems.

This chapter describes the CSM as a metaheuristic optimization algorithm for improving the clustering process of K-Means (KM) clustering algorithm widely used in several applications (Wilkin and Huang 2008). Throughout the chapter, MATLAB will be used to implement CSM to reformulate some widely used clustering algorithms. This hands-on approach will enable readers to gain practical experience and become proficient in using metaheuristic methods to improve the clustering process.

10.2 Cuckoo Search Method (CSM)

In the year 2005, Robert Payne describes in his book entitled, "The Cuckoos" the bird class of cuckoos (Payne and Sorenson 2005). In his work, Payne describes that this class of organisms promotes what is known as nest parasitism. This consists of the female depositing her eggs in the nests of other species, where the host parents feed and raise the cuckoos. This natural mechanism of selection of nests foreign to the biological parents of a cuckoo bird generates a controversy, since when the cuckoo egg opens, the new individual will do its best to throw the other eggs, so that this is the only one that can receive food from the host parents.

The phenomenon of nest parasitism consists of the female cuckoo depositing her eggs in nests belonging to other bird species, because the female cuckoo is not in charge of caring for and feeding her young. However, the controversy begins when the hatchling breaks her egg and begins to throw the other eggs or hatchlings out of the nest. This mechanism promotes the criterion of natural selection, which indicates that only the strongest individual is able to survive.

In 2009, Yang and Deb (2009) proposed an evolutionary algorithm based on the nest parasitism behavior of some bird, fish, and insect species. The CSM algorithm uses nest parasitism behavior as a search operator and at the same time uses Lévy flights (Pavlyukevich 2007) to mimic the flight of the cuckoo bird. The combination of these two operators makes the CSM algorithm an interesting proposal since, thanks to the combination of its operators, the optimal solution of an optimization problem is obtained in an efficient way.

In the CSM, the metaphor of nest parasitism behavior in cuckoo birds is used to formulate a search operator, where the candidate solution (cuckoo egg) is the particle that explores in a certain search space (nest). Likewise, the flight performed by these birds to deposit eggs in host nests can be emulated based on what is known as a Lévy flight. The Lévy flight describes a random behavior, which shares similarities with the trajectories commonly used by birds, insects, and other animals to move in their habitat.

Additionally, the CSM has an iterative structure. That is, it presents similarities with other metaheuristic techniques. The iterative nature of CSM lies in using a set of candidate solutions, operated under a context of exploration (Lévy flight) and exploitation (nest parasitism), which together achieve optimal solutions for solving optimization problems. It should be noted that, in the same way, the CSM algorithm also uses the concept of survival of the best individual, since, as can be observed, the behavior of nest parasitism indicates that each cuckoo brood throws the remaining broods out of the nest, so that only this one is left and can survive and develop.

10.3 Search Strategy for CSM

The CSM is based on the natural interaction of cuckoo birds with their environment. That is, female cuckoo birds make a journey from one nest to another of different bird species, leaving behind an egg in each of the nests she visits. This causes the host bird of a certain nest to take care of all the eggs in its nest, including those of a cuckoo bird. Naturally, when a cuckoo bird leaves an egg in a certain nest, the egg it leaves will have to have a certain color similar to the eggs found in that nest, this to avoid suspicion from the host birds. The purpose of leaving eggs in nests is for the host bird to take care of the offspring. That is, the host bird is in charge of feeding and protecting the cuckoo brood.

When the cuckoo hatchling breaks its egg, it begins to get stronger day by day, which means that if there are other eggs or hatchlings in its nest, the cuckoo hatchling pushes the rest out of the nest until it is left alone in the nest. The objective of this action is that the host bird feeds and protects only the cuckoo brood, since following the paradigm of natural selection, the cuckoo bird proved to be the strongest individual in the nest.

This survival mechanism of the cuckoo hatchlings can be translated into a search strategy for an optimization algorithm, since, as can be analyzed, at the moment that the cuckoo hatchling breaks its egg, it will try to be the best individual in that population, which means that this individual will seek to have the best position in the nest.

Because cuckoo birds present a complex mechanism of selection and reproduction, abstracting all these natural situations to obtain an algorithmic structure capable of solving optimization problems is a complicated process. In order to simplify the natural process involved in the nest parasitism behavior of cuckoo birds and to obtain a computational representation, it is necessary to propose certain rules that, in general terms, mimic these concepts. Three rules that abstract the interaction mechanisms of cuckoo birds are described below.

  • Each cuckoo bird carries one egg at a time, and deposits it in a random nest from a possible set of nests.
  • The nest containing the eggs that represent the best solution will be taken into account for subsequent generations.
  • The host bird will be able to discover whether or not an egg belongs to its nest. That is, each host bird when it arrives at its nest, it can either attend to the cuckoo egg or get rid of it, or else the host bird can leave the nest, since it could be understood that the nest does not belong to it.

Another of the fundamental aspects to be reviewed when discussing this algorithm is the way in which it can mimic the flight that cuckoo birds make to deposit eggs in host nests. Traditionally, evolutionary computational algorithms use random values in their operators to simulate a stochastic process abstracted from nature, social aspects, and even physical aspects. It is well known that an evolutionary computation algorithm without a random part will tend to fail to obtain the solution of an optimization problem. For this reason, metaheuristic algorithms use Random Walk to produce new solutions in the search space. However, random walk presents some problems when used in multidimensional spaces, as it can produce duplicate values across iterations. Faced with such a circumstance, the need to model more complex behaviors of nature, Lévy flights offer an interesting and powerful alternative without incurring the problems of random walk. The main advantage of Lévy flight is that they can mimic the natural flight of birds, insects, and other animals in a computationally efficient way (Chawla and Duhan 2018).

In response to this discussion, the CSM uses Lévy flights to mimic the flight of the cuckoo bird when depositing eggs in host nests. This causes the CSM to better explore the entire search space involved in the optimization process.

Finally, the CSM, like most metaheuristic algorithms, uses a population of individuals, where each one of them is considered as a candidate solution to a given optimization problem. Computationally speaking, each of the members of the population are elements that make up a multidimensional space.

In order to develop the ideas of the biological process of the cuckoo birds for the formulation of the CSM, the CSM can be described in several stages. The first one consists of the initialization of a population that randomly generates solutions (eggs) where these solutions are interpreted as positions in the search space. The second computational procedure involves the calculation of the random movement within the search space. For this stage, the Lévy flight is used to imitate the flight of the cuckoo bird to deposit its eggs in host nests. The third operation replaces the current solutions following a random principle. Finally, the last stage of this algorithm consists in selecting in an elite way the best solution in each of the generations of the algorithm.

In the following subsections, we describe the population structure in the CSM as well as each of the steps mentioned above in order to formulate an algorithmic structure.

10.3.1 Initialization

Within the optimization process of the CSM, it is required to have a set of N solution vectors (individuals) that will evolve through the generations. For this, in CSM, a population of individuals (eggs) X, will be composed by a set of parameter vectors where each parameter vector , represents a position in a d-dimensional vector space {x1, x2, …, xd} that defines the search space of the problem to be solved.

Like most evolutionary algorithms, the CSM begins by generating an initial population of individuals (solutions) uniformly distributed and spread over the entire domain of the search space. Each individual in the population will act as a d-dimensional vector to solve an optimization problem.

At this stage, the limits under which the population will operate by means of the search operators must be indicated. These limits are defined as lower limit lb = [lb1, lb2, …, lbd] and upper limit ub = [ub1, ub2, …, ubd]. Once these bounds have been specified, each of the individuals will be generated as follows:

(10.1)

where lb and ub represent the lower and upper bound vectors respectively, while r(0, 1) denotes a vector of random numbers within the uniformly distributed interval (0,1).

10.3.2 Lévy Flight

In metaheuristics, randomness is considered one of the pillars under which evolutionary algorithms are defined. Without randomness, many evolutionary algorithms could not work when trying to find an optimal solution to an optimization problem with multimodality. Since a multimodal function contains multiple convexities (minima or maxima) which make it more complicated to solve. Under this circumstance, an evolutionary algorithm without randomness presents stagnation in its performance as well as an algorithm based on derivative.

To solve the problem presented by classical optimization techniques, evolutionary algorithms use randomness as an operating mechanism that allows them to escape from the local minima or maxima of a function so that the search strategy focuses on finding the global optimal solutions (global minimum or maximum).

The technique most used by evolutionary algorithms is the so-called Random Walk. What this technique does is to perturb in a very small proportion the neighborhood of an individual, so that it escapes from a local minimum or maximum or, failing that, helps in the intensification of the search process. The latter significantly improves the exploitation stage of any evolutionary algorithm. However, random walk presents some drawbacks that make it prone to fail in situations when the dimensionality of a certain optimization problem increases.

To overcome these drawbacks, some random mechanisms have been proposed in the literature. Among them, the one that has been shown to perform better than random walking is the well-known Lévy flight. Lévy flight generates random movements using a Gamma distribution to mimic most of the biological processes found in nature, such as the flight of birds, the trajectories performed by a school of fish, etc.

Under this procedure, and following the analogy of cuckoo birds, the cuckoo bird flies through an environment locating possible nests of birds of different kinds in order to deposit its eggs in those nests. This is done by the cuckoo bird so that another bird will be in charge of raising; feeding and protecting the cuckoo egg that was deposited. Since the flight of the cuckoo bird is a complex behavior, the way in which it could be computationally abstracted is by means of the mechanism offered by Lévy’s flight.

The effect of calculating a Lévy flight causes that, during the optimization process, the search strategy for the optimal solution is gradually refined in each generation. Above all, it is important in the exploitation stage of the CS algorithm, remembering that the exploitation stage refers to the way in which search agents use the information of their environment to be able to position themselves in strategic zones of the search space. Thus, increasing the probabilities of finding the global solution to the optimization problem. In order to calculate the Lévy flight, the initialization stage of the algorithm had to be previously executed.

Once the initialization process described in the previous section has been executed, the CS algorithm will use the information provided by the current population and this will be used to calculate the Lévy flight of each of the individuals in the population. It is here that the CS algorithm will aim to relocate the solutions to other areas of the search space to increase the chance of finding the optimal solution. Thanks to the calculation of the Lévy flight for each individual, the CS algorithm has gained popularity in recent years, since, as will be seen later, the calculation of the Lévy flight is not highly complex.

Within the specifications of the CS algorithm, the Lévy flight is used to improve the global search stage. Lévy flights are produced by a Gamma distribution, which significantly improves the exploration stage of the evolutionary algorithm, in contrast to the random movements produced by techniques based on random walk. Lévy flights represent one of the most powerful operators in evolutionary algorithms since they mimic complex behaviors such as bird flight. The calculation of a Lévy flight can be mathematically defined as follows:

10.3.3 Solution Replacement

In the CS algorithm, once the Lévy flight value for an individual is calculated, it has to be decided whether the solution obtained by Eq. 10.6 will replace the current individual . Within the bioinspired analogy of the cuckoo bird, once the cuckoo bird flies into its environment and deposits its egg in the host nest, it is now that the host bird discovers the cuckoo egg. When the host bird discovers that it has an extra egg in its nest, it has three possible actions, one is to abandon the nest, another possible action is for the host bird to drop the cuckoo egg, and the third is for the host bird to adopt the cuckoo egg. If the host bird succeeds in adopting the cuckoo egg, as soon as it hatches and begins to grow stronger day by day, it will do everything possible to throw the other eggs that share the nest.

The cuckoo brood performs this procedure to obtain all the food and care that the host bird provides. This mechanism is based on the idea of survival of the principle of natural selection, which implies that only those individuals that manage to adapt better to their environment will be able to survive in subsequent generations.

The computational way to abstract the bioinspired behavior that takes place between the cuckoo egg with its host nest lies directly in the exploitation stage of the CS algorithm. Recalling that the exploitation stage of any evolutionary algorithm aims to refine the search strategy in promising areas within the search space. In the CS algorithm, the operation of replacing the solutions aims at perturbing the positions of the individuals by considering the information of the neighboring solutions. This mechanism efficiently reflects the cuckoo egg metaphor, increasing the possibility of finding the global optimal solution.

Under this operation, a set of solutions is selected in a random way to be replaced by a new value. Each individual can be selected by a probability paɛ[0, 1]. For implementation, a random number r1 is generated within the interval [0, 1]. If r1 is smaller than pa, the solution is selected and modified by Eq. 10.7, otherwise, the solution remains unchanged. This procedure can be summarized by the following model.

(10.7)

where r(0, 1) is a normally distributed random number, and the subscripts j and h correspond to integer random numbers in the interval [1, N].

10.3.4 Elitist Selection

Another fundamental pillar of evolutionary algorithms lies in the principle of survival described in the process of natural selection. That is, only the strongest individuals will survive, while the weakest individuals will die. Making the analogy of this fact in an evolutionary methodology, in each iteration of the CS algorithm the best solution (global minimum/global maximum) obtained up to that moment will be maintained. This is an illusion to the natural selection process since, during the optimization process, individuals may represent a very good solution, but if the elitist principle is not considered, in the following iterations, it may diverge from the optimal solution. Thus, the algorithm may not be able to solve the optimization problem in question.

The elitist mechanism used in the CS algorithm is an easy procedure to implement, since it is only necessary to check the quality of the solutions and keep the individual (solution) that presents the best value in its evaluation of the objective function.

In the CS algorithm the elitist criterion is based on the following rule. If the value resulting from the evaluation of the produced solution Eq. 10.7, is better than the value resulting from the evaluation of the current solution , then the solution replaces the current solution , otherwise, the solution will remain in the next iteration. This mechanism can be summarized as shown below:

10.4 Computational Procedure

As described in the previous section, the CS algorithm drives the search strategy toward the global optimum value using four operations that define the bioinspired behavior of the cuckoo bird. The first operation is the so-called initialization. At this stage, a set of individuals is created and initialized. This set represents the solution vectors that will act as search agents in an optimization problem.

The next operation is the calculation of the Lévy flight. Lévy flights represent one of the most powerful and efficient mechanisms to mimic complex behaviors found in nature, such as the flight of birds, some insects, and some schools of fish, among others. This mechanism directly promotes the exploration stage of the CS algorithm, since the type of motion obtained causes the solution vectors to spread throughout the search space. The third operation is the replacement of the solutions, this is where the search process is refined in such a way that each of the solution vectors has a higher probability of finding the global optimal solution in promising zones of the search space that are smaller than the zones explored by the Lévy flights. Within the stages of an evolutionary algorithm, exploitation refines the search process, thus improving the approximation of the optimal solution. Due to this fact, the better the performance of an exploitation operator the better the solution obtained. For this purpose, the CS algorithm is based on a simple rule, the current solution will be replaced by a particle that is randomly generated using information from other solutions. This makes the refined search process start to converge gradually to the global optimal solution. Finally, the fourth operation is based on the elitist selection process, which considers that in each generation of the CS algorithm the best solution obtained so far will be kept on record. The final effect of this selection is that the global optimum solution will be maintained, whether it is a minimum or a maximum, depending on the problem statement.

10.4.1 Metaheuristic Operators for CSM

For each of the stages of the CS algorithm seen in the previous section, a set of specific steps is necessary in order to implement the operators required for the CS algorithm. Each of these steps represents a characteristic behavior of the solution vectors in each of the iterations. Since most evolutionary algorithms have configuration parameters, the CS algorithm is no exception. However, the CS algorithm requires only one parameter: pa, which is referred to as the discovery probability. Table 10.1 shows the typical setting of the single parameter of the CS algorithm.

The generic algorithm used by the search process of the CSM can be summarized in the Pseudo-code 10.1:

Pseudo-code 10.1 General Procedure to Implement the CSM

Input: N, Max_gen, k = 0.
Xk ← Initialize(N); Step 1
while k<=Maxgendo
Xk + 1 ← LévyFlight(Xk) Step 2
← SolutionReplacement(Xk + 1) Step 3
g ← ElitistSelection(Xk + 1); Step 4
K ← k + 1
end while
Output: g

In general, for each of the individuals in the population, Steps 2–4 described in Pseudo-code 10.1 are executed generation after generation in order to obtain a global optimal solution. The initialization of the solution vectors is executed only once, which is when the CS algorithm starts, once the evolution process is initiated, the Lévy flight is calculated for each of the solution vectors and in the same way this movement is refined by applying the replacement operation of the solutions so that, finally, the optimal solution of a certain optimization problem is obtained by means of an elitist criterion.

Figure 10.1 illustrates the flowchart describing the complete process carried out by the search strategy of the CS algorithm. As illustrated in the diagram, the CS algorithm initializes a set of initial solution vectors , randomly generated within the bounds of the search space. Subsequently, the algorithm executes the Lévy flight operators, replacement of the solutions and elitist selection criterion as shown in Pseudo-code 10.1 considering the parameter settings described in Table 10.1. Finally, when the total number of generations that make up the whole optimization process of the problem to be solved has elapsed, the algorithm returns the best solution found by this process.

10.5 Implementation of the CSM in MATLAB

In Algorithm 10.1, it is described the MATLAB code for the CSM. To observe the functionality of the algorithm, the code encodes a benchmark function commonly used in performance testing related to the optimization of continuous functions. In this example, the Schwefel function is implemented, so that the reader can observe the functionality of the CSM considering a minimization process.

The Schwefel function exhibits a non-convex unimodal surface in a two-dimensional space and contains single global minima and multiple local minima. The non-convex feature is used to test the scaling of the search strategy of the CSM method when it operates over surfaces with many local optima. On the other hand, the Schwefel function is continuous and non-convex, which indicates that not any optimization technique either classical or metaheuristic can reach the global optimum. The mathematical model of the Schwefel function is as follows:

(10.9)

Finally, so that the reader can see the behavior of the datapoints on the Schwefel function surface, at each iteration the movement of the solutions (datapoints) on the Schwefel surface is plotted.

 

%Algorithm 10.1
%% INITIAL CONFIGURATION FOR THE OPTIMIZATION PROCESS
%Clear memory and Close Matlab windows
clear all;
close all;
 
 
%% Step 1 INITIALIZATION
%The size of the population is established
n = 50;
%The maximum number of iterations is established
N_IterTotal = 1000;
%The number of decision variables is established
dim = 2;
%The limits of the search space are defined
lb = -500;
ub = 500;
%Parameter initialization of the CSM
pa=0.25;
%Iteration counter
iter = 0;
%Initialization of the initial population
if size(ub,2)==1
    nest=rand(n,dim).*(ub-lb)+lb;
end
if size(ub,2)>1
    for i=1:dim
        high=ub(i);down=lb(i);
        nest(:,i)=rand(n,1).*(high-down)+down;
    end
end
%The fitness values of the initial population are obtained
for j=1:size(nest,1)
    fitness(j) = ObjectiveFunction(nest(j,:),dim);
end
%The best solution is obtained from the initial population
[fitnessXbest,K]=min(fitness) ;
xBest=nest(K,:);
%The plot the function to be optimized is computed
 if dim<=2 
    rangeUpLb=ub-lb;
    figure(1)
    x=[lb:rangeUpLb/100:ub];
    y=x;
    [xg,yg]=meshgrid(x,y);
    [row,col]=size(xg);
    for l=1:col
        for h=1:row
            z(h,l)=ObjectiveFunction([xg(h,l),yg(h,l)],dim);
        end
    end
 end
%Iterative process of the algorithm
while iter <= N_IterTotal
   
    %% Step 2 LÉVY FLIGHT
    beta=3/2;
    sigma=(gamma(1+beta)*sin(pi*beta/2)/(gamma((1+beta)/2)*beta*
2∧((beta-1)/2)))∧(1/beta);
 
    for j=1:n
        s=nest(j,:);
        %Mantegna’s Algorithm
        u=randn(size(s))*sigma;
        v=randn(size(s));
        step=u./abs(v).∧(1/beta);   
        stepsize=0.01*step.*(s-xBest);
        s=s+stepsize.*randn(size(s));
        if size(ub,2)==1
                for i = 1:dim   
                    if (s(1,i) < lb) 
                        s(1,i) = rand(1,1).*(ub-lb)+lb;
                    end
                    if (s(1,i)> ub)
                        s(1,i) = rand(1,1).*(ub-lb)+lb;
                    end
                end       
        end
        if size(ub,2)> 1   
                 for i = 1:dim
                    high=ub(i);down2=lb(i);
                    if (s(1,i) < down2)
                        s(1,i) = rand(1,1).*(high-down2)+down2;
                    end
                    if (s(1,i)> high)
                        s(1,i) = rand(1,1).*(high-down2)+down2;
                    end          
                 end
        end
        nest(j,:)=s;
    end
    for j=1:size(nest,1)
        fnew = ObjectiveFunction(nest(j,:),dim);
        fitness(j)=fnew;  
    end
    [fitnessXbest,K]=min(fitness);
    xBest = nest(K,:);
 
 
    %% Step 3 Solution Replacement
    K=rand(size(nest))>pa;
    stepsize=rand*(nest(randperm(n),:)-nest(randperm(n),:));
    new_nest=nest+stepsize.*K;
    if size(ub,2)==1
        for j = 1 : size(new_nest,1)
            for i = 1:dim   
                if (new_nest(j,i) < lb) 
                    new_nest(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(ub-lb)+lb;
                end
                if (new_nest(j,i)> ub)
                    new_nest(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(ub-lb)+lb;
                end
            end     
        end   
    end
    if size(ub,2)> 1   
         for j = 1 :  size(new_nest,1)
             for i = 1:dim
                high=ub(i);down2=lb(i);
                if (new_nest(j,i) < down2)
                    new_nest(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(high-down2)+down2;
                end
                if (new_nest(j,i)> high)
                    new_nest(j,i) = rand(1,1).*(high-down2)+down2;
                end          
             end
         end
    end
    for j=1:size(nest,1)
        fnew = ObjectiveFunction(new_nest(j,:),dim);
        if fnew<=fitness(j)
           fitness(j)=fnew;
           nest(j,:)=new_nest(j,:);
        end
    end
 
    %% Step 4 Elitist Selection
    [fitnessXbest,K]=min(fitness) ;
    xBest=nest(K,:);
    %The plot the population is generated
    if dim<=2
        surf(xg,yg,z);
        title('Schwefel function')
        hold on
        plot3(nest(:,1),nest(:,2),fitness(1,:),'o','markersize',6,
'markerfacecolor','r');
        plot3(xBest(1),xBest(2),fitnessXbest,'o','markersize',10,
'markerfacecolor','g');
        drawnow;
        hold off                        
    end
    %Iteration counters
    iter = iter + 1;
    fprintf('Iteration: %d\n',iter);
    fprintf('Best solution: (%d,%d)\n',xBest(1),xBest(2));
    fprintf('Best fitness: %d\n',fitnessXbest);   
end
 
 
%%OBJECTIVE FUNCTION
%Schwefel function implementation
function fit = ObjectiveFunction(L,dim)
    [N,∼]=size(L);
    for i=1:N 
        fit(i) = (418.9829*dim)-(sum(L(i,:).*sin(sqrt(abs(L)))));
    end
end

In Algorithm 10.1, the Step 1 configures the initial parameters required by the optimization process. Such configuration relies on setting the maximum number of iterations, the population size, the number of decision variables involved in the optimization process, and the definition of the limits of the search space. The Step 2 defines the computation scheme for the Lévy flight calculation based on the Mantegna’s Algorithm. Then, in Step 3 the solution replacement mechanism is employed. Step 4 defines the elitist selection procedure. In the algorithm, the objective function to be optimized is implemented after the definition of the main loop. The objective function considered in this chapter is the well-known Schwefel function.

10.6 Cuckoo Search Method for K-Means

K-Means (KM) algorithm is one of the most widely used partitional clustering algorithm. Partitional clustering methods aim to group data vector by optimizing a specific objective function by an iterative process.

KM is considered as an unsupervised learning method which classifies unlabeled data by grouping them by inherent features of the data vectors rather than predefined (supervised) categories. The objective of KM is to separate data vectors into K different clusters while the position of the centroids for each cluster is adjusted at each iteration based of the minimization of the distance among data vectors to their respective centroids.

KM starts by selecting K representative points as initial centroids. Then, each data vector is assigned to its closest centroid. To measure closeness relationship between data vectors and centroids, distance metrics are commonly employed as spatial relationships to measure similarity among two data vectors. Once the initial assignment of data vectors, the position of each centroid is updated. The position adjustment in this step, is computed as the mean values of each coordinate position. Finally, this process repeats until a stop criterion is achieved. The learning process of the KM is based on the iterative process of these two steps. KM is also considered as a greedy algorithm which guarantees to converge into a local minimum. However, the optimization process (minimum distance) is considered as NP-Hard problem (Maronna 2015).

The basic idea behind the KM algorithm is that attributes of an object can be efficiently represented as vectors in a vector space. Within this framework, the primary objective is to minimize the cumulative intra-cluster variance or, equivalently, the standard deviation. To accomplish this process, KM organizes data vectors into clusters, with each cluster characterized by a central point called centroid. Through iterative structure, each centroid is updated according to continuous data assignation to nearest centroids. KM creates clusters that exhibit minimal variance within themselves while maximizing the separation between clusters. This process produces distinct clusters within the dataset, making KM a representative technique to data-driven applications (Ikotun et al. 2023).

The KM method unfolds through a systematic and iterative procedure that can be summarized as follows:

  1. Step 1: Determine the Number of Clusters (K):

    As the initial stage, this step involves deciding how many clusters the dataset should be divided into. In KM, the number of clusters is represented by the K. Then, the position of each K cluster is determined. Commonly, the initial positions are random within the data space. As can be concluded, the initial position of each cluster, is the most crucial decision and can significantly impact the quality of the clustering process.

  2. Step 2: Initial Partitioning:

    After determining the K number of classes, each data vector is assigned to one of these classes. This assignment can be done in terms of distance relationship among each data vector and each cluster centroid. Data vectors will be assigned to their closest centroids.

  3. Step 3: Centroid Computation:

    After the initial assignment, KM updated each cluster centroid. The centroid for each cluster represents the geometric center of all the data vectors within a cluster.

  4. Step 4: Distance Computation:

    In this step, KM computes the distance between each data vector and the updated centroids from the previous step for all K clusters.

  5. Step 5: Partition Refinement:

    In this step, KM constructs new partitions based on the new distance values from previous step. Each data vector is associated to its closest cluster centroid.

  6. Step 6: Recalculation of Centroids:

    After the new partitions are formed, the centroid for each cluster is updated. These updated positions for each centroid represent the new geometric centers of their respective clusters.

  7. Step 7: Iterative Process:

    Steps 4 through 6 are iteratively repeated until the stop criterion is achieved. The stop criteria occurs when data assignation does not change or may be any other alternative convergence criterion, such as a predefined number of iterations is met, etc.

As it can be discussed, KM is an iterative procedure which learns how the centroids must be located through the dataset. This iterative procedure allows KM to iteratively refine the clustering solution, seeking to minimize the variance within clusters while maximizing the separation between them. The final outcome is a set of well-defined clusters that effectively group similar data vectors.

The main objective of the KM is to determine the optimal positions of K cluster centroids. This strategy is considered as the learning mechanism of the KM. The positioning of these centroids can significantly influence the clustering solution.

The KM method is a partitional clustering algorithm since it operates by the influence of minimizing the distance between each data vector to each cluster centroid. Mathematically, KM divides a set of n vectors x1, x2, …, xn into m groups G1, G2, …, Gm. Each group is characterized by its centroid c1, 2, …, m which is computed by an objective function. Commonly, the cost function in the KM process, is defined in terms of Euclidean distance as follows:

(10.10)

where Ji represents the cost attributed to i-th cluster. The value of Ji depends on the spatial distribution of the vectors belonging to Gi and the position of its centroid ci.

The division of the elements in each group is defined by an element uij. This binary factor determines the correspondence of a vector to a group. Under these circumstances uij is 1 if the data xj belongs to the group Gi and zero in case of nonmembership. Thus considering uij Eq. 10.9 can be reformulated as follows:

The KM method minimizes the objective function J through an iterative procedure that is based on two steps. In the first step, the positions of the centroids are fixed respect to uij in the minimization of the objective function J. In the second step, the objective function J is minimized respect to each centroid ci while the values uij are fixed. These two steps repeat until stop criterion is achieved.

In the first step of the process, the values of uij are first determined.
