10.6.1 Implementation of KM algorithm in MATLAB

In this section, an example of the implementation of the KM method is exhibited. The MATLAB code in Algorithm 10.2 is presented by using the built-in functions of MATLAB to implement the cluster analysis of the KM method with synthetic data.

 

%Algorithm 10.2
%% INITIAL CONFIGURATION
%Clear memory and Close Matlab windows
clear all
close all
 
 
%% Step 1 Set a default random sequence generator to produce
standard random values
rng('default');
 
 
%% Step 2: Set 100 datapoints, this will be the dataset
X = [(randn(50,2)*0.75)+1;
    (randn(50,2)*0.25)-1];
 
 
%%Step 3: Compute K-Means algorithm over the dataset from Step 2
[idx,C] = kmeans(X,2);
D1 = find(idx==1);
D2 = find(idx==2);
 
 
%% Step 4: Plot the clustered data
figure(1)
title('Data in 2 clusters by K-Means')
plot(X(D1,1),X(D1,2),'xk','DisplayName','Cluster 1');
hold on
plot(X(D2,1),X(D2,2),'ok','DisplayName','Cluster 2');
plot(C(:,1),C(:,2),'.k','MarkerSize',30,'DisplayName','Centroids');
legend({'Cluster 1', 'Cluster 2','Centroids'})
fprintf('Centroid 1: (%d,%d)\n',C(1,1),C(1,2));
fprintf('Centroid 2: (%d,%d)\n',C(2,1),C(2,2));

In Algorithm 10.2, Step 1 indicates which random number generator will be used. The ’default’ instruction from rng function uses a random generator whose output will be the same at each execution of the code. This scheme is used for reproducibility purpose, so the reader can follow a generic output from the clustering process. Step 2, generates 100 datapoints in a random fashion. This datapoints will be the dataset used for clustering process by the KM. In Step 3, the built- in function kmeans is used considering two clusters. Finally, in Step 4, the data and the cluster centroids are plotted. The output of the Algorithm 10.2 can be seen in Figure 10.3.

In Figure 10.3, the produced output from KM for the test dataset of Step 2 in the Algorithm 10.2 is shown. As it can be shown, each datapoint from the dataset is associated into one of the two possible clusters.

The KM clustering process is simple to implement but a powerful technique since the user can define the number of classes according to a specific data project. Different cluster division of groups will produce different cluster groups.

10.6.2 Cuckoo Search Method for K-Means

K-means method is one of the most popular unsupervised classification methods. KM starts with an arbitrary number of K cluster centers then; an iterative procedure is applied to update the initial cluster centers. This mechanism is achieved by a minimization criterion, where the algorithm reduces the Euclidean distance among cluster centers and datapoints. However, the inherent nature of the algorithmic structure of the KM allows to reformulate the minimization criterion by considering different optimization approaches.

In this section, the CSM is employed as an optimization technique to assist the clustering process of the KM algorithm. This section allows readers to understand the KM algorithm as an optimization approach, where different implementations of the objective functions allow different cluster outcomes. Under such circumstances, this section considers the use of a metaheuristic algorithm to group data.

The basic idea behind the synergy of CSM and the KM is that the reader can realize that metaheuristics are universal optimization methods and how they can be applied to solve clustering problems. The presented framework has the advantage of both KM and CSM to improve some of the limitations of traditional KM. Within this framework, the primary objective is to minimize the dispersion of clusters among data.

One important aspect to discuss is that traditional KM method can be improved in different ways through applying several optimization approaches. Each of these approaches can reformulate in different fashion each step of the KM method. For example, the selection of the K cluster centroids can be reformulated as an optimization problem prior to the next steps of the KM. Another approach can substitute the spatial relationship among data by considering different aspects such as information entropy, and so on. In this section, the computation of the cluster centers will be formulated as an optimization scheme. This mechanism is one of the most common adaptations of traditional KM.

To accomplish this process, the original structure of the CSM must be adapted to incorporate the required functionality to update the cluster centers. For that, the CSM-KM methodology begins by producing a set of Np population members, each population member will represent a set of K cluster centroids. Then, the evolutionary strategy of the CSM will update the clusters centroids by each individual in the population based on the information retrieved by the objective function to minimize the dispersion of clusters. Finally, when a stop criterion is achieved the final cluster centroids will be obtained.

The CSM-KM method unfolds through a systematic and iterative procedure that can be summarized as follows:

  1. Step 1: Determine the Number of Clusters (K):

    As well as the original KM method, the CSM-KM method requires the decision of how many clusters the dataset should be divided into. Since the same synthetic dataset generated in Algorithm 10.2 will be used for comparison purposes, in the proposed method K = 2 is defined.

  2. Step 2: Population Initialization:

    Within the optimization process of the CSM-KM method, requires a set of N solution vectors (individuals) that will evolve through the generations. For this, in CSM-KM, a population of individuals (eggs) X, will be composed by a set of parameter vectors where each parameter vector , represents a set of cluster centroids . The initial centroid values for each population member are generated by random values considering the lower limit lb and the ub in the dataset to be used.

  3. Then, the fitness for each individual will be computed. Since the main difference of KM and CSM-KM is the way, the data is grouped in this chapter the following objective function will be defined in the entire optimization process:

    (10.15)

    where K is the number of clusters (Step 1, in this case each population member is composed by two pair of values, each pair corresponds to the two-dimensional coordinates), j corresponds to the j-th cluster. xj represents the datapoint belonging to the j-th cluster. zij corresponds to the centroid values for the j-th cluster, and N represents the number of elements of the dataset.

  4. Step 3: Lévy Flight:

    Traditional KM iteratively updates the centroids values based on the assigned datapoints to each cluster. In CSM-KM, the centroid values are computed based on the Lévy flight structure of the CSM. This mechanism improves the search capabilities by exploring over the entire search space. Since each parameter vector is composed by a set of centroid values, each centroid component will be adjusted by using Lévy flight computation.

  5. Step 4: Solution Replacement:

    As well as the original CSM, the CSM-KM will use the straightforward steps described in Section 10.3.3 for replacement of the best solutions been so far.

  6. Step 5: Elitist Selection:

    Within the elitist criterion, the same scheme is applied by the CSM-KM for updating the best set of centroids been so far (Section 10.3.4).

In the following sub-section, the implementation of the CSM-KM will be presented.

10.6.2.1 Implementation of CSM to KM Clustering in MATLAB

An example of the implementation of the KM method as an optimization problem is presented in this section. The MATLAB code in Algorithm 10.3 considers the search strategy of CSM as an optimization algorithm, and the fitness function from Eq. 10.15. To make a fair distinction between Algorithms 10.2 and 10.3, the same synthetic data is used as the input dataset.

 

%Algorithm 10.3
%% INITIAL CONFIGURATION FOR THE OPTIMIZATION PROCESS
%Clear memory and Close Matlab windows
clear all;
close all;
 
 
%% Step 1 DETERMINE THE NUMBER OF CLUSTERS K
%Definition of the number of K clusters
Kclusters = 2;
 
 
%% Step 2 POPULATION INITIALIZATION
%Set a default random sequence generator to produce standard
random values
rng('default');
%Set 100 datapoints, this will be the dataset
Dataset = [(randn(50,2)*0.75)+1; (randn(50,2)*0.25)-1];
%The size of the population is established
n = 10;
%The maximum number of iterations is established
N_IterTotal = 50;
%The limits of the search space are defined
lb = [min(Dataset(:,1)) min(Dataset(:,2))];
ub = [max(Dataset(:,1)) max(Dataset(:,2))];
%Parameter initialization of the CSM
pa=0.25;
%Iteration counter
iter = 0;
%Initialization of the initial population
for i = 1 : n
    nest(i,1) = rand * (ub(1)-lb(1))+lb(1);
    nest(i,3) = rand * (ub(1)-lb(1))+lb(1);
    nest(i,2) = rand * (ub(2)-lb(2))+lb(2);
    nest(i,4) = rand * (ub(2)-lb(2))+lb(2);
end
%The fitness values of the initial population are obtained
for j = 1 : size(nest,1)
    fitness(j) = ObjectiveFunction(nest(j,:),Dataset);
end
%The best solution is obtained from the initial population
[fitnessXbest,K]=min(fitness) ;
xBest=nest(K,:);
%Iterative process of the algorithm
while iter <= N_IterTotal
   
    %% Step 3 LÉVY FLIGHT
    beta=3/2;
    sigma=(gamma(1+beta)*sin(pi*beta/2)/...
(gamma((1+beta)/2)*beta*2∧...
((beta-1)/2)))∧(1/beta);
 
    for j=1:n
        s=nest(j,:);
        %Mantegna’s Algorithm
        u=randn(size(s))*sigma;
        v=randn(size(s));
        step=u./abs(v).∧(1/beta);   
        stepsize=0.01*step.*(s-xBest);
        s=s+stepsize.*randn(size(s));
        if (s(1) < lb(1) || s(1)> ub(1)) 
            s(1) = rand * (ub(1) - lb(1)) + lb(1);
        end
        if (s(3) < lb(1) || s(3)> ub(1)) 
            s(3) = rand * (ub(1) - lb(1)) + lb(1);
        end
        if (s(2) < lb(2) || s(2)> ub(2)) 
            s(2) = rand * (ub(2) - lb(2)) + lb(2);
        end
        if (s(4) < lb(2) || s(4)> ub(2)) 
            s(4) = rand * (ub(2) - lb(2)) + lb(2);
        end
        nest(j,:)=s;
    end
    for j=1:size(nest,1)
        fnew = ObjectiveFunction(nest(j,:),Dataset);
        fitness(j)=fnew;  
    end
    [fitnessXbest,K]=min(fitness);
    xBest = nest(K,:);
 
 
    %% Step 4 SOLUTION REPLACEMENT
    K=rand(size(nest))>pa;
    stepsize=rand*(nest(randperm(n),:)-nest(randperm(n),:));
    new_nest=nest+stepsize.*K;
    for j = 1 : size(new_nest,1)
        if (new_nest(j,1) < lb(1) || new_nest(j,1)> ub(1)) 
            new_nest(j,1) = rand * (ub(1) - lb(1)) + lb(1);
        end
        if (new_nest(j,3) < lb(1) || new_nest(j,3)> ub(1)) 
            new_nest(j,3) = rand * (ub(1) - lb(1)) + lb(1);
        end
        if (new_nest(j,2) < lb(2) || new_nest(j,2)> ub(2)) 
            new_nest(j,2) = rand * (ub(2) - lb(2)) + lb(2);
        end
        if (new_nest(j,4) < lb(2) || new_nest(j,4)> ub(2)) 
            new_nest(j,4) = rand * (ub(2) - lb(2)) + lb(2);
        end
    end
 
 
    for j=1:size(nest,1)
        fnew = ObjectiveFunction(new_nest(j,:),Dataset);
        if fnew<=fitness(j)
           fitness(j)=fnew;
           nest(j,:)=new_nest(j,:);
        end
    end
 
    %% Step 5 ELITIST SELECTION
    [fitnessXbest,K]=min(fitness) ;
    xBest=nest(K,:);
    %Iteration counters
    iter = iter + 1;
    fprintf('Iteration: %d\n',iter); 
end
fprintf('Best solution: Centroid 1: (%d,%d) Centroid 2: ...
(%d,%d)\n', xBest(1,1),xBest(1,2),...
xBest(1,3),xBest(1,4));
fprintf('Best fitness: %d\n',fitnessXbest);
%Plot the dataset and final centroids
figure(1)
plot(Dataset(:,1),Dataset(:,2),'xk','DisplayName','Original Data');
hold on
plot(xBest(:,1),xBest(:,2),'.k','MarkerSize',...
30,'DisplayName','Centroid 1');
plot(xBest(:,3),xBest(:,4),'.k','MarkerSize',...
30,'DisplayName','Centroid 2');
legend({'Original Data', 'Centroid 1','Centroid 2'});
title('Original Dataset and Final Cluster Centroids');
hold off
 
 
for dataIndex = 1 : 100
    dTemp1 = pdist2(Dataset(dataIndex,:),xBest(1,1:2));
    dTemp2 = pdist2(Dataset(dataIndex,:),xBest(1,3:4));
    if dTemp1 < dTemp2
        dataClass(dataIndex,1) = 1;
    else
        dataClass(dataIndex,1) = 2;
    end
end
    tempIndex1 = find(dataClass(:,1) == 1);
    tempIndex2 = find(dataClass(:,1) == 2);
 
 
%Plot the dataset clustered by the final centroids
figure(2)
plot(Dataset(tempIndex1(:,1),1),...
Dataset(tempIndex1(:,1),2),'xk', 'DisplayName',...
'Cluster 1');
hold on
plot(Dataset(tempIndex2(:,1),1),...
Dataset(tempIndex2(:,1),2),'ok', 'DisplayName',...
'Cluster 2');
plot(xBest(:,1),xBest(:,2),'.k','MarkerSize',...
30,'DisplayName','Centroid 1');
plot(xBest(:,3),xBest(:,4),'.k','MarkerSize',...
30,'DisplayName','Centroid 2');
legend({'Cluster 1', 'Cluster 2', 'Centroid 1','Centroid 2'});
title('Clustered datapoints by Final Cluster Centroids');
hold off
 
 
%%OBJECTIVE FUNCTION
%Objective function implementation for clustering
function fit = ObjectiveFunction(L,Dataset)
    [N,∼]=size(L);
    for i = 1:N %Se obtiene el fitness de cada par de clusters
        for dataIndex = 1 : 100
            dTemp1 = pdist2(Dataset(dataIndex,:),L(i,1:2));
            dTemp2 = pdist2(Dataset(dataIndex,:),L(i,3:4));
            if dTemp1 < dTemp2
                dataClass(dataIndex,1) = 1;
            else
                dataClass(dataIndex,1) = 2;
            end
        end
        tempIndex1 = find(dataClass(:,1) == 1);
        tempIndex2 = find(dataClass(:,1) == 2);
        sum1 = sum(pdist2(Dataset(tempIndex1,:),L(i,1:2)));
        sum2 = sum(pdist2(Dataset(tempIndex2,:),L(i,3:4)));
        fit(i) = (sum1 + sum2) / 100;
    end
end

In Algorithm 10.3, Step 1 indicates the number of desired clusters. Step 2 indicates which random number generator will be used. The ’default’ instruction from rng function uses a random generator whose output will be the same at each execution of the code. This scheme is used for reproducibility purpose, so the reader can follow a generic output from the dataset. Step 3 generates 100 datapoints in a random fashion. These datapoints will be the dataset used for clustering process by the CSM-KM. In Step 3, the Lévy flight method is implemented to update the position of each set of centroid values. In Step 4, the solution replacement mechanism is implemented. Finally, in Step 5 the elitist selection scheme is described. The output of the Algorithm 10.3 can be seen in Figure 10.4.

In Figure 10.4a, the produced output from CSM-KM for the test dataset of Step 2 in the Algorithm 10.3 is shown. As it can be shown, each centroid is represented by a filled circle. Each cluster centroids was produced by the optimization process of the CSM-KM method. In Figure 10.4b, the data generated in Step 2 is also exhibited. However, in this case the data is assigned to its corresponding cluster based on the cluster centers obtained by the optimization process.

As it can be shown, the KM method is a powerful and flexible clustering process that can be improved by considering different stages as an optimization formulation. Different optimization formulations may produce different cluster divisions.

11
Metaheuristic Methods for Dimensional Reduction

11.1 Introduction

Dimensionality reduction, which refers to reducing the number of dimensions in a dataset, has increasingly gained the attention of data analysts as the volume of available data in any field keeps growing at a fast rate. In general, datasets with high dimensionality are undesirable since the volume of the feature space can be so big that the available data is too sparse for data analysis techniques to deliver reliable results. One way to overcome this limitation is to increase the amount of data considered for the analysis, which is not always possible and can, in turn, lead to higher computing power demands. A different approach is reducing the number of dimensions in the dataset, removing redundant and irrelevant features to transform the data to a lower-dimensional space in which it retains some meaningful properties of the original data, ideally close to its intrinsic dimension.

Dimensionality reduction techniques are usually divided into feature selection and feature extraction. While feature selection techniques search for a subset of the input features, the latter group transforms the data to a latent space of fewer dimensions. Different metaheuristic algorithms, such as ant colony optimization (ACO), firefly algorithm, flower pollination algorithm, and genetic algorithm, among others, have proved to be useful for feature selection and extraction, mainly in the field of medicine. This chapter focuses on applications of the ACO algorithm to dimensionality reduction techniques. We begin by presenting the ACO algorithm itself; then, we show the generalities of ACO to dimensionality for feature selection and feature extraction.

11.2 Ant Colony Optimization (ACO)

The ant colony optimization (ACO) is a swarm intelligence algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of ant colonies introduced in the early 1990s by M. Dorigo and colleagues (Dorigo et al. 1996). The ACO, like other metaheuristic algorithms for the solution of combinatorial optimization problems (Blum and Roli 2003), does not aim to find the best solution but a good enough approximation within a reasonable window of time.

As it occurs in other social insects, such as bees, termites, and wasps, the highly structured organization of ant colonies allows the emergence of complex behaviors that greatly surpass the individual capabilities of their members. For the development of the ACO algorithm, Dorigo et al. (1996) considered a prime example of complex behavior observed in ant colonies, their collective foraging. When foraging, ants begin by randomly exploring the nest’s surroundings. Once a food source has been located, they analyze essential characteristics such as quantity and quality of the food available and bring some samples with them back to the nest. On their way back to the nest, ants leave a trail of pheromones that other ants later use to find the food source. The strength of pheromones deposited by food-carrying ants directly correlates with the food site’s properties; hence, highly profitable food sources have the best chances of being revisited. As the profitability of food sources decreases, their paths are less transited, with pheromone density decreasing as well. Additionally, since pheromones evaporate, paths leading to lesser-quality food sources fade quickly enough for scout ants to search for other food sources. This dynamic is perceived as a type of communication mediated by pheromones and has been thoroughly studied through various experimental setups (Deneubourg et al. 1990).

To understand the ACO computational procedure, it is essential to remember that it was initially conceived to solve discrete optimization problems, like the traveling salesman problem (TSP). The core idea behind the ACO approach to optimization problems is the incremental construction of solutions. In the same way, ants find their way to a particular food source by following existing pheromone traces and choosing between paths when coming across intersections. Candidate solutions in the ACO are built by a series of probabilistic choices made by artificial ants. The inner process of the ACO algorithm can be divided into three parts: pheromone representation, ant-based solution construction, and pheromone update.

11.2.1 Pheromone Representation

The pheromone representation refers to an array of k different n-dimensional solutions, each accompanied by its function value and an associated weight w. Hence, the pheromone representation consists of a k × n matrix and two k-length vectors (see Figure 11.1).

The solutions matrix is first initialized at random within the limits of the search space. Then, the function values f(Sl) are computed using the problem’s cost function for all k solutions and ranked accordingly. Lastly, the associated weight values w are calculated following the Gaussian function defined in Eq. 11.1, where k is the number of solutions, l is the solution’s position in the rank, and q is a modulation parameter known as selection pressure. Small q values result in weight vectors strongly biased toward the best solution, while large q values result in more balanced vectors.

(11.1)

11.2.2 Ant-Based Solution Construction

To create a new solution, ACO performs two iterative steps. First, a solution element is selected for each of the n dimensions based on the selection probability of each solution (see Eq. 11.2).

(11.2)

Then, a Gaussian sampling is performed for each of the selected elements using Eq. 11.3:

(11.3)

where the mean μ is the selected element and the standard deviation σ = ξD. The parameter ξ > 0 is the learning rate, also known as the pheromone evaporation rate in ACO, and D is the average distance between the selected element and all elements of the same dimension of the remaining k − 1 solutions (see Eq. 11.4).

(11.4)

11.2.3 Pheromone Update

At each iteration of the ACO algorithm, a set of m new solutions is created. Once the set is complete, the function values f(Sl) for all m new solutions are computed using the problem’s cost function. Finally, the m new solutions are appended to the existing solution set and ranked according to their function value. To keep the number of elements in the solution set constant, only the first k solutions are passed by to the next iteration. New ant-based solutions are generated, and the pheromone representation is updated at each iteration till a stop criterion is met. The overall functioning of the ACO algorithm is shown in the flowchart in Figure 11.2.

The implementation in MATLAB of the ACO algorithm to find the minimum of the Rastrigin test function is presented in Algorithm 11.1. To ease its understanding, the code is divided into 6 steps that can also be found in the ACO flowchart (see Figure 11.2).

 

%Algorithm  11.1
%Clean data
close all
clear all
 
 
% Step 1, problem, and ACO parameters declaration
% problem parameters
l_bound = -5.12;      % lower boundary
u_bound = 5.12;       % upper boundary
dim = 2;              % dimensionality
 
 
% ACO parameters
max_it = 300;         % Maximum number of iterations
K = 40;               % Number of original solutions
M = 10;               % Number of ant-based solutions
q = 0.1;              % Selection pressure
zeta = 0.1;           % Evaporation rate
 
 
% Create aux structure
aux_ant.Position = [];
aux_ant.Cost = [];
 
 
% Create Pheromone representation matrix
ANT = repmat(aux_ant, K, 1);
 
 
% Step 2, randomly initialization of the candidate solutions
% (pheromones) within the search space bounds
 
 
for j=1:K
    % Random solution
    Ant(j).Position = unifrnd(l_bound, u_bound, [1,dim]);
    % Evaluation
    Ant(j).Cost = fitness_function(Ant(j).Position);
end
 
 
% Step 3, sort solutions according to fitness
[∼, SortOrder]= sort([ANT.Cost]);
ANT = ANT(SortOrder);
 
 
% Init fitness history
fitness_history = zeros(max_it,1);
 
 
% Step 4, compute the weights associated to the candidate solutions
w_vector = 1/(sqrt(2*pi)*q*K)*exp(-0.5*(((1:K)-1)/(q*K)).∧2);
% Selection probabilities
p = w_vector/sum(w_vector);
 
 
% ACO main loop
% Step 5, generate new solutions through ant-based solution
% construction
for it=1:tmax    
    % Means matrix
    means = zeros(K, dim);
    for j = 1:dim
        means(j,:) = ANT(j).Position;
    end
    % Standard deviations matrix
    sigma = zeros(K, dim);
    for j = 1:dim
        D = 0;
        for r = 1:K
            D = D+abs(sigma(j,:)-sigma(r,:));
        end
        sigma(j,:) = zeta*D/(K-1);
    end
    % New solutions set
    new_pop = repmat(aux_ant, M, 1);
    for t = 1:M
        % Init solutions matrix
        Newpop(t).Position = zeros([1,dim]);
        % Solution construction
        for i=1:dim
            % Select Gaussian kernel
            l = RouletteWheelSelection(p);
            % Gaussian random variable
            new_pop(t).Position(i) = means(l,i)+sigma(l,i)*randn;
            % Check that solution is within boundaries
            new_pop(t).Position(i) =...
min(new_pop(t).Position(i),u_bound);
 
            new_pop(t).Position(i) =...
max(new_pop(t).Position(i),l_bound);
        end
        % Cost function evaluation
        new_pop(t).Cost = fitness_function(new_pop(t).Position);
    end
 
 
% Step 6, update population
    % Append new solutions to existing population
    ANT = [ANT
           new_pop];
    % Sort according to fitness
    [∼, SortOrder]= sort([ANT.Cost]);
    ANT = ANT(SortOrder);
    % Keeping only best solutions
    ANT = ANT(1:K);
    % Update fitness history
    fitness_history(it) = ANT(1).Cost;
end
 
 
%*******************************************************************
% PLOT COST FUNCTION AND BEST SOLUTION
%*******************************************************************
% Graphic representation Rastrigin 
range=u_bound - l_bound; 
figure(1)
x1=[l_bound:range/100:u_bound];
y1=x1;
[X1,Y1]=meshgrid(x1,y1);
[row1,col1]=size(X1);
for q=1:col1
    for hh=1:row1
        vector = [X1(hh,q),Y1(hh,q)];
        zz(hh,q)= A*n+sum(vector.∧2-A*cos(2*pi*vector));
    end
end
mesh(X1,Y1,zz, 'edgecolor', [0.5,0.5,0.5]);
hold on
 
 
% Add best solution
plot(ANT(1).Position(1), ANT(1).Position(2),'o', . . .
     'markersize',6,'markerfacecolor','r');
 
 
%*******************************************************************
% FUNCTIONS
%*******************************************************************
 
 
%*******************************************************************
% Rastrigin cost function
%*******************************************************************
function ft = fitness_function(xn)
   A = 10;
   n = size(xn);
   cal = xn.∧2-A*cos(2*pi*xn);
   ft = A*n+sum(cal);
end

In Step 1 of the algorithm are defined the parameters of the problem and the ACO algorithm itself, namely, the dimensionality of the problem, lower and upper boundaries, maximum number of iterations, number of solutions (population size), number of ant-based created solutions, selection pressure (q), and pheromone evaporation rate (zeta - ξ). In Step 2, the first set of solutions is randomly initiated, considering a uniform probability distribution across the entire search space. In Step 3, the solutions are ranked according to their fitness values, and their associated weights are computed in Step 4. The main loop takes place in Steps 5 and 6. First, new solutions are created through the ant-based solution construction method in Steps 5. Then, in Step 6, the new solutions are appended to the existing ones to create an extended set from which only the best k solutions will be kept. Finally, the algorithm iterates over Step 5 and 6 till the stop criteria is met. Figure 11.3 shows the function and the best solution found by the ACO optimization.

 Note

Metaheuristic methods can always be modified to work with different types of problems. However, each method is conceived with a particular kind of problem in mind. In the case of ACO, it is best suited to combinatorial problems that meet the following criteria:

  • Problem Representation: The problem must be representable in the form of a graph with a set of nodes and edges.
  • Cost Function: There must be an effective cost function that measures the “goodness” of node to the next for each possible path in the solution space.
  • Construction of New Solutions: A mechanism to create new solutions must be established.
  • Pheromone Updating Rule: A suitable rule to update pheromone levels at each iteration must be defined.

11.3 Dimensionality Reduction

The amount of data generated daily is constantly increasing, not only in the number of instances but also in its dimensionality. Although ideally, more and better-described data allows for more comprehensive analysis, it also poses a challenge in finding the proper methodology capable of processing such a vast amount of data while being cost-effective regarding computational power requirements. One way to deal with this issue is to reduce the dimensionality of the data to analyze. Dimensionality reduction removes irrelevant or redundant data, improving, in turn, the performance of the analysis.

Dimensionality reduction techniques can be classified into two broad groups: feature extraction and feature selection. Feature extraction techniques transform the data from its original representation space into a new latent space in which the complexity of the data is reduced. Among the most popular methods for feature extraction are the principal component analysis algorithm (PCA) and latent semantic analysis (LSA). In recent years, convolutional neural networks (CNN) have also gained popularity as an alternative to traditional approaches to feature extraction. On the other hand, feature selection techniques, as its name suggests, aim to find a subset of features that retains all meaningful properties of the original data set. The feature selection classification encompasses three kinds of methods: filter, wrapper, and embedded methods. The firsts are based on a statistical analysis of the features. Wrapper methods explore the feature space in search of the best subset of features. Meanwhile, embedded methods integrate feature selection and data classification into one single algorithm.

Metaheuristic algorithms, as one of the best approaches to solving combinatorial problems (Blum and Roli 2003), have proven to be successful in solving the feature selection problem following a wrapper-based approach. Among the metaheuristic algorithms that have already been applied to feature selection are the Ant Lion Optimizer (ALO) (Emary et al. 2016a), Grey Wolf Optimization algorithm (GWO) (Emary et al. 2016b), Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) (Hancer et al. 2018), Grasshopper Optimization Algorithm (GOA) (Mafarja et al. 2019), Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) (Hajihashemi et al. 2019; Mafarja and Mirjalili 2018), and the ACO (Ke et al. 2008; Li et al. 2013).

The use of ACO has been particularly prolific for feature selection tasks. In Kanan et al. (2007), an ACO-based feature selection method is tested with the ORL (Olivetti Research Laboratory) faces database, outperforming a GA-based method with fewer features and execution time. Patil et al. (2009) proposed an ACO/random forest-based hybrid filter-wrapper search technique whose performance, when tested with a database of biological active molecules used during the CoEPrA competition, compares well with the available competition results. Robbins et al. (2007) presented a modified ACO to work on high-dimensional gene expression datasets, able to identify small subsets of highly predictive and biologically relevant genes. Yu et al. (2009) introduced an ACO/SVM classifier capable of selecting tumor-related marker genes.

 Note

There are several benefits of applying dimensionality reduction to datasets, among the most relevant:

  • It removes redundant and noisy data.
  • Reducing dimensions may allow for visualization.
  • Improves the classification process.
  • Data storage space is reduced.

11.4 ACO for Feature Selection

To solve the feature selection problem with ACO it is first necessary to reformulate it in a graph-like problem. If each one of the features in the dataset are seen as nodes and the edges connect consecutively chosen features, effectively forming a path graph. This way, the search for the optimal features in the context of ACO can be interpreted as the ants traveling between n different nodes, where these are selected one at a time based on a transition rule. This scenario is illustrated in Figure 11.4, where the ants look for feature subsets within an 8-feature space. As examples of how the ant-based solution construction occurs, consider the following: the first ant starts its path at node a and can choose among any of the remaining 7 nodes to add to its path; after choosing node c based on a selection rule, it repeats the process adding nodes d, g, and b, to end with the feature subset {a, c, d, g, b}. Following the same procedure, the second ant arrives at the feature subset {h, g, f, e, d}.

Since ACO was initially conceived to solve the TSP, when solving a feature selection problem all candidate solutions would consist of a fixed number of elements. Hence, maybe the most straightforward way that comes to mind for solving feature selection with ACO is to set the algorithm for a fixed number of features right from the beginning.

Nevertheless, it is still possible to generate subsets with a different number of features using the original ACO. One valid approach would be to allow features to be included multiple times within the candidate solutions but to consider only one instance when computing their fitness. A different approach is used by Kanan et al. (2007), whose overall process is illustrated in Figure 11.5. First, the solutions population is initiated by randomly selecting k features. Each of the features chosen represents the first node from which each ant starts its path construction. Ants add new features from their initial positions, one at a time, following a probabilistic transition rule until a stopping criterion is satisfied. Once all solutions have been built, their fitness is computed to update the pheromone. Then, new solutions are created to renew the solutions population. The process is executed iteratively until the performance goal is achieved or the maximum number of iterations has been completed.

The probabilistic transition rule proposed by Kanan et al. (2007) is represented by Eq. 11.5.

(11.5)

where k is the number of ants (solutions), nij is the heuristic desirability of adding feature j to the solution when at feature i, is the set of nodes next to node i that have not yet been added to solution k. α ≻ 0, β ≻ 0 adjust the relative importance of the pheromone value and heuristic information and τij(t) is the amount of pheromone on edge (i, j).

 Note

Nowadays, it is not uncommon to find applications of metaheuristic techniques in the field of medicine. In particular, they have been widely used in healthcare data to diagnose, yielding better results than traditional methods. A study conducted by Kaur et al. (2023) on “metaheuristic optimization techniques for feature selection in disease diagnosis” found that between 2011 and 2022 over 150 impactful papers with these characteristics were published. The metaheuristic techniques found in these papers include spider monkey, cuckoo search algorithm, lion optimization technique, moth flame technique, bat-inspired algorithm, grey wolf algorithm, whale optimization, and dragonfly optimization technique. Regarding their applications, they were used to select and optimize the features to predict diseases such as diabetes, liver disease, Alzheimer’s disease, brain disorder, heart disease, and COVID-19. As the amount of available healthcare data increases, metaheuristic techniques will gain terrain in the field of medicine, not only in the last step of diagnosis but also as part of data preprocessing before feeding the data to other machine learning algorithms.

12
Metaheuristic Methods for Regression

12.1 Introduction

Regression analysis is a statistical procedure in which the main objective is to investigate the relation between two or more variables in order to predict the value of one of them through the knowledge of the value of the others. Regression is one of the most employed supervised learning that builds a model using a well-known dataset. The dataset contains the training data of N elements, where is the input vector or independent variable, and the output vector or dependent variable. The main objective of the regression is to generate a model that better fits the training data such as the real function where the data is obtained as possible without having any explicit knowledge. Once the model is trained, it can be able to relate the unknown input values x to a certain output y.

Under this consideration, training the model that better characterizes the relation of the input data is necessary to determine the parameters that shape such a model. Several methods are employed for this task, but most of them are based on deterministic techniques that in some cases determine suboptimal solutions due to the complexity, high dimensionality, and nonlinear nature of many applications. In this chapter, the most known and used optimization approach is presented. The Genetic Algorithm (GA) is a bioinspired technique proposed by John Henry Holland (1992). It is based on the behavior of the genes and their interaction, and it is described in detail below.

12.2 Genetic Algorithm (GA)

GA was presented in 1992 by Holland inspired by the gene combination of the chromosomes of the living beings where parents procreate chromosome children that heredity their information. GA employs crossover, mutation, and selection to extract the chromosome’s combination and perform a search strategy. GA employs the principles of natural selection to determine the feasible solutions (chromosomes), under such circumstances, the chromosomes that have better qualities have better chances to survive. A cost function is necessary to measure each chromosome regarding the problem to be treated to determine which chromosome has a certain quality associated with it.

12.2.1 Computational Structure

From the computational implementation point of view, the GA optimization process considers a set of N candidate solutions (chromosomes) that evolve through generations in the search strategy. Under such an approach, GA generates a population of chromosomes (individuals) defined as composed of a set of parameters where each vector represents the position in a d-dimensional vector space which defines the search space of the problem to be solved and sometimes known as set of decision variables. Each vector (chromosome) is modified by the operators of the GA; crossover, mutation, and selection which are used in the optimization process.

After the population is generated through the search space, each element is evaluated using the objective or cost function required by the problem to be solved. This implies that for each chromosome a fitness value is associated with it. It is worth noting that the fitness value gives us valuable information about the search space by the decision variables. The initialization process and the operator employed in the GA optimization process are described below.

12.2.2 Initialization

As most of the optimization techniques for the initialization process, a set of individuals are randomly generated using a normal distribution. In this stage, the upper and lower bounds are determined by the user according to the problem to be solved, these bounds are defined as and respectively. These bounds are the domain of the decision variables of the problem, once the bound are set each chromosome is generated as below:

(12.1)

where and are the upper and lower bounds, and is a vector of normally distributed random numbers within the interval [0, 1].

12.2.3 Selection Method

To select the elements of the population that continue with the optimization process, a selection method must be considered. Proportional approaches are the most used selection procedures in the optimization tasks which are based on certain information such as the fitness value of each chromosome. Within this category, there are the roulette wheel and stochastic reminder which are described below.

12.2.3.1 Roulette Wheel Selection

This selection method was proposed by De Jong (1975), and is the most used selection approach due to it employing the information on the fitness value of each chromosome to generate a probabilistic model that assigns the chances of the chromosomes to be selected as the parents to the crossover process. To visualize this selection method graphically, Figure 12.1 represents the probability distribution of five solutions where the element with more probability of being selected for the crossover is p1 with 30% and the less probability is p5 with 5%.

For determining the probabilistic value associated with each chromosome, Eqs. 12.2–12.4 are performed respectively. Then, a uniformly distributed random number r is generated and compared with the individual, if the probability is higher than the random number (), it is selected to continue with the iterative process. This process is computed for each element of the population and repeated throughout the complete optimization procedure.

12.2.3.2 Stochastic Reminder Selection

This approach has shown a better performance regarding roulette wheel selection due to it employing a generation of parents to a later crossover which considerably increases the diversity of the generated solution. Nevertheless, this method presents some flaws such as premature convergence. For computing this method, it is necessary to determine the expected value for each element of the population as described below:

(12.5)

Under this approach, the number of parents is indicated for assigning an identification number and computing the expected value of the selected parents. The integer part () of the expected value represents the times of copies that the chromosomes previously selected are generated, and the roulette method is used to determine the number of previously selected parents.

12.2.3.3 Rank-Based Selection

This selection method is mainly based on the stochastic reminder in which hierarchies or ranks are assigned to each chromosome regarding the fitness value of each individual. The main purpose of this method is to rank each solution in the interval of [0, 1] where 1 is the better element. This approach sorts the individuals regarding the fitness function of the problem to be treated and the expected value is computed as follows:

(12.6)

where M and m are 1.1 and 0.9 respectively. Such values are experimentally defined for solving several engineering problems, these parameters can be considered as adjustment values.

12.2.3.4 Tournament Selection

Most selection methods are based on the expected value of each candidate solution. In contrast, tournament selection employs a more direct technique using the value of the cost function or the population. This approach focuses on the selection nature of the individuals, which means a direct competition between chromosomes, stronger elements are capable of survival.

To perform this selection procedure, N elements are randomly selected from the population, and then an individual is selected considering two possible options: the best rank element based on its fitness value is selected, or a random number is generated and compared with a number previously preset by the user. If the last condition is fulfilled, the best element of the population is considered, otherwise, the worst individual is selected. As can be seen, different selection methods can be performed to determine the elements that are considered to continue with the iterative process, and the best selection approach depends on the application to be treated.

12.2.4 Crossover

Crossover is a biological abstraction of the genetic material recombination in nature, in which the individuals’ information is shared to generate a new population with better capabilities to survive than the last one. Under this consideration, following the biological metaphor, the children are generated using the information of both parents. Still, at the same time, the children must have their own characteristics which means that such chromosomes must be modified in a later step. To perform the crossover approach, two particles (chromosomes) and are selected considering a previously described selection method. For this example, a chromosome of eight decision variables is contemplated as below:

12.2.5 Mutation

As mentioned before, this operator is employed to generate new chromosomes based on some individuals previously selected. As in nature, children are born by the combination of parents’ genes but certain mutation in the descendant is performed which implies that each individual is unique, this metaphor is extrapolated to the main process of GA. Computationally, this process is carried out to produce a new population with particular characteristics; for a better understanding of this process the following example is described.

Considering that and are individuals generated by the crossover from two parents, the mutant operator modifies some of the chromosome’s variables. The mutant operator is controlled by a mutation rate , and the process can be summarized in the following steps. A uniformly distributed random number is generated in the interval [0, 1] for each element of the population and compared regarding the mutation rate, if no action is performed, but if the condition is fulfilled the change of a variable of the chromosome is conducted. To illustrate the complete functioning of the GA can be shown in the flowchart of Figure 12.2, and the complete computational implementation is reported in Algorithm 12.1.

 

%Algorithm 12.1
%Clean data
close all
clear all
 
 
%%Step 1, problem, and GA parameters declaration
dim=2;
lb = -2*pi;
ub = 2*pi;
Popusize=50;   
 
 
%Crossover rate, number of childs, mutants, and mutation rate
cr=0.7;
nch=2;              
nm=round(0.3*Popusize);
mr=0.1;            
 
%Selection parameter
beta=8;            
 
%% Stet 2, randomly initialization of the particles and first cost
function evaluation
temporal.Position=[];
temporal.Fitness=[];
pob=repmat(temporal,Popusize,1);
 
for i=1:Popusize 
    pob(i).Posicion=unifrnd(lb,ub,[1 dim]);
    pob(i).Fitness=sin(pob(i).Posicion(1))*...
exp((1-cos(pob(i).Posicion(2)))∧2) +...
cos(pob(i).Posicion(2))*...
exp((1-sin(pob(i).Posicion(1)))∧2) +...
(pob(i).Posicion(1)-pob(i).Posicion(2))∧2;
end
 
%% Sorting population
Costs = [pob.Fitness];
[Costs, SortOrder] = sort(Costs);
pob=pob(SortOrder);
 
%% Storage best and worst solution
xbest=pob(1);
xworst = pob(end).Fitness;
 
%% Step 3, Main iterative process
iter=100;
for it=1:iter
    
    %% Compute the probability of the selection method by the
roulette approach
    P=exp(-beta*Costs/xworst);
    P=P/sum(P);
    
    popc=repmat(temporal,nch/2,2);
        for k=1:nch/2    
        r=rand;
        c=cumsum(P);
        i1=find(r<=c,1,'first');
 
        r=rand;
        c=cumsum(P);
        i2=find(r<=c,1,'first');
 
        i1=randi([1 Popusize]);
        i2=randi([1 Popusize]);
       
        p1=pob(i1);
        p2=pob(i2);
 
        %% Step 4, Crossover procedure 
        x1 = p1.Posicion;
        x2 = p2.Posicion;
        alpha=unifrnd(-cr,1+cr,size(x1));
 
        popc(k,1).Posicion=alpha.*x1+(1-alpha).*x2;
        popc(k,2).Posicion=alpha.*x2+(1-alpha).*x1;
 
        popc(k,1).Posicion=max(popc(k,1).Posicion,lb);
        popc(k,1).Posicion=min(popc(k,1).Posicion,ub);
 
        popc(k,2).Posicion=max(popc(k,2).Posicion,lb);
        popc(k,2).Posicion=min(popc(k,2).Posicion,ub);
        
        % Fitness function evaluation of new solutions
        vector = popc(k,1).Posicion;
        popc(k,1).Fitness=sin(vector(1))*...
exp((1-cos(vector(2)))∧2) +...
cos(vector(2))*exp((1-sin(vector(1)))∧2) +...
(vector(1)-vector(2))∧2;
        vector = popc(k,2).Posicion;
        popc(k,2).Fitness=sin(vector(1))*...
exp((1-cos(vector(2)))∧2) +...
cos(vector(2))*exp((1-sin(vector(1)))∧2) +...
(vector(1)-vector(2))∧2;      
    end
    popc=popc(:);
 
    %% Step 5, Mutation approach
    popm=repmat(temporal,nm,1);
    for k=1:nm
        
        i=randi([1 Popusize]);
        p=pob(i);
        x = p.Posicion;
        dim=numel(x);
 
        nmu=ceil(mr*dim);
 
        j=randsample(dim,nmu);
 
        sigma=0.1*(ub-lb);
 
        popm(k).Posicion=x;
        popm(k).Posicion(j)=x(j)+sigma*randn(size(j));
 
        popm(k).Posicion=max( popm(k).Posicion,lb);
        popm(k).Posicion=min( popm(k).Posicion,ub);
        vector = popm(k).Posicion;
        popm(k).Fitness=sin(vector(1))*...
exp((1-cos(vector(2)))∧2) +...
cos(vector(2))*exp((1-sin(vector(1)))∧2) +...
(vector(1)-vector(2))∧2;    
    end
    
    pob=[pob
         popc
         popm];
     
    %%Sort population
    Costs=[pob.Fitness];
    [Costs, SortOrder]=sort(Costs);
    pob = pob(SortOrder);
    
 
    pob=pob(1:Popusize);
    Costs=Costs(1:Popusize);
    
    %% Storage best solution at iteration it
    xbest=pob(1);
    xworst = pob(end).Fitness;
    
    %% Graphic representation at each iteration 
    if dim<=2 
        rango=ub-lb; 
        figure(1)
        x1=[lb:rango/100:ub];
        y1=x1;
        [X1,Y1]=meshgrid(x1,y1);
        [row1,col1]=size(X1);
        for q=1:col1
            for hh=1:row1
                vector = [X1(hh,q),Y1(hh,q)];
                zz(hh,q)=sin(vector(1))*...
exp((1-cos(vector(2)))∧2) +...
cos(vector(2))*exp((1-sin(vector(1)))∧2) +...
(vector(1)-vector(2))∧2;
                
            end
        end
        mesh(X1,Y1,zz);
        hold on  
         for j = 1: Popusize

           plot(pob(j).Posicion(1), pob(j).Posicion(2),...
'o', 'markersize', 6, 'markerfacecolor', 'r'); 
         end
        drawnow;
        hold off
    end
 
 
    %% Step 6, Display best solution at each iteration
    fprintf('Iteracion: %d\n',it);
    fprintf('Best individual: (%d,%d)\n',...
xbest.Posicion(1), xbest.Posicion(2));
    fprintf('Best fitness: %d\n',xbest.Fitness);
end

Algorithm 12.1 shows the computational scheme of the GA approach where Step 1 performs the GA and problem variables initialization. Then in Step 2, the GA initializes the population through the search space considering the lower and upper bounds by a normal distribution, after that each chromosome is evaluated by the cost function (quality measure), and the population is sorted to order the solutions. In Step 3, the main iterative process starts where the probability of the selection method is computed. Then the crossover of the elements that fulfill the condition of crossover rate is carried out. Once the mutation of some elements of the population is performed, the cost function is employed to determine the quality of the new population. When the iterative process reaches the stop criterion, the best solution is finally displayed with its respective cost function value. Figure 12.3 shows the function and the best solution that the GA performs.

12.3 Neural Network Regression with Artificial Genetic

To perform an example where the GA is employed for improving the regression, a case of study of marriage-divorce data set is employed. In this example, different variables are considered such as education, age, and mental health, just to mention a few are considered. Under such considerations, the GA improves the rate learning of a neural network (NN) to perform the analysis of marriage-divorce regression (Muhammad et al. 2017). Algorithm 12.2 presents the complete functioning of the regression employing NN-GA. First, the marriage-divorce data is loaded and separated into Targets and Inputs, and then the number n of neurons is defined by the user (in this example the number of neurons is set at 9). Once the NN is generated, in Step 3 an error function is defined to determine the quality of the solutions employed through the complete optimization process. Step 4 performs the GA as in Algorithm 12.1, the main difference is the cost function to be optimized and the dimension of the problem. GA searches the parameters of the NN that better fit the regression response regarding the data. Finally, the result of the optimization process is used to perform the NN in its final form, and the error metrics are computed to measure the quality of the solution determined by the GA. The graphical representation of the regression is calculated in Step 5 and Figure 12.4 shows the result. In the section of functions, the cost function and the complete GA are declared which are employed in the complete application process.

 

%Algorithm 12.2
%Clean data
close all
clear all
 
 
%Step1, Loading the data and divide into Target and Inputs
Data=load('Marriage_Divorce:DB.mat');
Inputs=Data.Marriage_Divorce:DB(:,1:end-1);
Targets=Data.Marriage_Divorce:DB(:,end);
 
 
%Step 2, Defining the number of neurons and perform the first model
n = 9; %Neurons
net = feedforwardnet(n,'trainoss'); %NN
[net, tr]= train(net,Inputs', Targets');
 
 
%Step 3, evaluation of error
h = @(x) NMSE(x, net, Inputs', Targets');
sizenn=size(Inputs);sizenn=sizenn(1,1);
 
 
%Step 4, iterative process of the optimization process
[x, cost] = GA (h, sizenn*n+n+n+1);
 
 
%Final NN optimized by GA
getwb(net);
 
 
%Outputs and errors are obtained.
Outputs2=net(Inputs');
Outputs2=Outputs2';
Err_MSE2=mse(Targets,Outputs2);
CC= corrcoef(Targets,Outputs2);
CC= CC(1,2);
 
 
%Step 5, Graphical representation of the regression is displayed
[population3,gof3] = fit(Targets,Outputs2,'poly3');
plot(Targets,Outputs2,'o',...
'LineWidth',0.7,...
'MarkerSize',5,...
'MarkerEdgeColor','g',...
'MarkerFaceColor',[0.9,0.3,0.1]);
title(['GA R =  ' num2str(1-gof3.rmse)],...
['GA MSE =' num2str(Err_MSE2)]); 
hold on
plot(population3,'b-','predobs');
xlabel('Targets');ylabel('Outputs');   grid on;
ax = gca; 
ax.FontSize = 12; ax.LineWidth=2;
legend({'GA Regression'},'FontSize', 8,'TextColor','blue');hold off
 
 

 
%% Functions
function NMSE_calc = NMSE( wb, net, input, target)
 net = setwb(net, wb');
 error = target - net(input);
 NMSE_calc = mean(error.∧2)/mean(var(target',1));
end
 
 

 
%% GA
function [xbest, y]= GA (fit, dim)
lb = -5;
ub = 5;
Popusize=10;   
 
 
% Crossover rate, number of childs, mutants, and mutation rate
cr=0.7;
nch=2;              
nm=round(0.3*Popusize);
mr=0.1;            
 
% Selection parameter
beta=8;            
 
%% Randomly initialization of the particles and first cost
%% function evaluation 
temporal.Position=[];
temporal.Fitness=[];
pob=repmat(temporal,Popusize,1);
 
for i=1:Popusize 
    pob(i).Posicion=unifrnd(lb,ub,[1 dim]);
    pob(i).Fitness= fit (pob(i).Posicion);
end
 
%% Sorting population
Costs = [pob.Fitness];
[Costs, SortOrder] = sort(Costs);
pob=pob(SortOrder);
 
%% Storage best and worst solution
xbest=pob(1);
xworst = pob(end).Fitness;
 
%% Main iterative process
iter=100;
for it=1:iter
    
    %% Compute the probability of the selection method by the
roulette approach
    P=exp(-beta*Costs/xworst);
    P=P/sum(P);
    
    popc=repmat(temporal,nch/2,2);
        for k=1:nch/2    
        r=rand;
        c=cumsum(P);
        i1=find(r<=c,1,'first');
 
        r=rand;
        c=cumsum(P);
        i2=find(r<=c,1,'first');
 
        i1=randi([1 Popusize]);
        i2=randi([1 Popusize]);
       
        p1=pob(i1);
        p2=pob(i2);
 
        %% Crossover procedure 
        x1 = p1.Posicion;
        x2 = p2.Posicion;
        alpha=unifrnd(-cr,1+cr,size(x1));
 
        popc(k,1).Posicion=alpha.*x1+(1-alpha).*x2;
        popc(k,2).Posicion=alpha.*x2+(1-alpha).*x1;
 
        popc(k,1).Posicion=max(popc(k,1).Posicion,lb);
        popc(k,1).Posicion=min(popc(k,1).Posicion,ub);
 
        popc(k,2).Posicion=max(popc(k,2).Posicion,lb);
        popc(k,2).Posicion=min(popc(k,2).Posicion,ub);
        
        % Fitness function evaluation of new solutions
        vector = popc(k,1).Posicion;
        popc(k,1).Fitness=fit (vector);
        vector = popc(k,2).Posicion;
        popc(k,2).Fitness=fit (vector);      
    end
    popc=popc(:);
 
    %% Mutation approach
    popm=repmat(temporal,nm,1);
    for k=1:nm
        
        i=randi([1 Popusize]);
        p=pob(i);
        x = p.Posicion;
        dim=numel(x);
 
        nmu=ceil(mr*dim);
 
        j=randsample(dim,nmu);
 
        sigma=0.1*(ub-lb);
 
        popm(k).Posicion=x;
        popm(k).Posicion(j)=x(j)+sigma*randn(size(j))';
 
        popm(k).Posicion=max( popm(k).Posicion,lb);
        popm(k).Posicion=min( popm(k).Posicion,ub);
        vector = popm(k).Posicion;
        popm(k).Fitness=fit (vector);    
    end
    
    pob=[pob
         popc
         popm];
     
    %%Sort population
    Costs=[pob.Fitness];
    [Costs, SortOrder]=sort(Costs);
    pob = pob(SortOrder);
    
 
    pob=pob(1:Popusize);
    Costs=Costs(1:Popusize);
    
    %% Storage besto solution at iteration it
    xbest=pob(1);
    xworst = pob(end).Fitness;
    y = xbest.Fitness;
end
end

12.4 Linear Regression Employing an Artificial Genetic

A linear regression problem employing the GA is performed as a final example of regression. For this task, a set of data randomly generated is used to determine the better model that fits the training data to generalize new input data to the model. As was previously explained, linear regression consists of generating a line that minimizes the distance between all data and the linear model. Under such circumstances, the slope and the y-intercept of the line must be determined by the optimization approach (GA).

Algorithm 12.3 shows the complete optimization process for determining the best linear model that fits the random training model. As in previous examples, the code is explained using steps, which are just three simple steps. In Step 1, the training data is generated using uniformly distributed random numbers, which implies that every time the algorithm is performed different training data is generated.

In Step 2, the GA is called as a function previously defined in the Functions section of Algorithm 12.3. After the iterative process reaches its stop criterion, the GA returns the best element which is used to determine the best line for the training data (Step 3). Finally, Figure 12.5 shows the best result determined by the GA in order to a better understanding of the optimization process.

 

%Algorithm 12.3
%Clean data
% Step 1, Training Data
xt=-10:0.1:10;
yt=5 * xt + 6 + 20*rand(1,length(xt));
 
 
%Step 2, GA perform
[xbest, yout]= GA (xt, yt);
 
 
%Step 3, Visual representation of regression
% The best solution is used to determine the line that
% better fits the data
y=xbest.Posicion(1,1)*xt+xbest.Posicion(1,2);
 
 
% The line determined by GA is plotted regarding the data
% for visualization
plot(xt,yt);
hold on
plot(xt,y,'r');
legend('Desired','Output','Location','Best');
xlabel('Input ');
ylabel('Output ');
title('Input/Output Graph');
 
 

 
%% Functions
 
 
function [xbest, yout]= GA (xt, yt)
lb = 0;
ub = 10;
Popusize=100;  
dim = 2; 
 
 
% Crossover rate, number of childs, mutants, and mutation rate
cr=0.7;
nch=2;              
nm=round(0.3*Popusize);
mr=0.1;            
 
% Selection parameter
beta=8;            
 
%% Stet 2, randomly initialization of the particles and first
%% cost function evaluation 
temporal.Position=[];
temporal.Fitness=[];
pob=repmat(temporal,Popusize,1);
 
for i=1:Popusize 
    pob(i).Posicion=unifrnd(lb,ub,[1 dim]);
    y = pob(i).Posicion(1,1) * xt + pob(i).Posicion(1,2);
    e = sum (y - yt);
    pob(i).Fitness= e;
end
 
%% Sorting population
Costs = [pob.Fitness];
[Costs, SortOrder] = sort(Costs);
pob=pob(SortOrder);
 
%% Storage best and worst solution
xbest=pob(end);
xworst = pob(1).Fitness;
 
%% Main iterative process
iter=3000;
for it=1:iter
    
    %% Compute the probability of the selection
%% method by the roulette approach
    P=exp(-beta*Costs/xworst);
    P=P/sum(P);
    
    popc=repmat(temporal,nch/2,2);
        for k=1:nch/2    
        r=rand;
        c=cumsum(P);
        i1=find(r<=c,1,'first');
 
        r=rand;
        c=cumsum(P);
        i2=find(r<=c,1,'first');
 
        i1=randi([1 Popusize]);
        i2=randi([1 Popusize]);
       
        p1=pob(i1);
        p2=pob(i2);
 
        %% Crossover procedure 
        x1 = p1.Posicion;
        x2 = p2.Posicion;
        alpha=unifrnd(-cr,1+cr,size(x1));
 
        popc(k,1).Posicion=alpha.*x1+(1-alpha).*x2;
        popc(k,2).Posicion=alpha.*x2+(1-alpha).*x1;
 
        popc(k,1).Posicion=max(popc(k,1).Posicion,lb);
        popc(k,1).Posicion=min(popc(k,1).Posicion,ub);
 
        popc(k,2).Posicion=max(popc(k,2).Posicion,lb);
        popc(k,2).Posicion=min(popc(k,2).Posicion,ub);
        
        % Fitness function evaluation of new solutions
        vector = popc(k,1).Posicion;
        y = vector(1) * xt + vector(2);
        e = sum (y - yt)∧2;
        popc(k,1).Fitness=e;
        vector = popc(k,2).Posicion;
        y = vector(1) * xt + vector(2);
        e = sum (y - yt)∧2;
        popc(k,2).Fitness=e;      
    end
    popc=popc(:);
 
    %% Mutation approach
    popm=repmat(temporal,nm,1);
    for k=1:nm
        
        i=randi([1 Popusize]);
        p=pob(i);
        x = p.Posicion;
        dim=numel(x);
 
        nmu=ceil(mr*dim);
 
        j=randsample(dim,nmu);
 
        sigma=0.1*(ub-lb);
 
        popm(k).Posicion=x;
        popm(k).Posicion(j)=x(j)+sigma*randn(size(j))';
 
        popm(k).Posicion=max( popm(k).Posicion,lb);
        popm(k).Posicion=min( popm(k).Posicion,ub);
        vector = popm(k).Posicion;
        y = vector(1) * xt + vector(2);
        e = sum (y - yt).∧2;
        popm(k).Fitness=e;    
    end
    
    pob=[pob
         popc
         popm];
     
    %%Sort population
    Costs=[pob.Fitness];
    [Costs, SortOrder]=sort(Costs);
    pob = pob(SortOrder);
    
 
    pob=pob(1:Popusize);
    Costs=Costs(1:Popusize);
    
    %% Storage besto solution at iteration it
    xbest=pob(end);
    xworst = pob(1).Fitness;
    yout = xbest.Fitness;
 
 
end
end
